Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the appropriate term for the indigenous people of Canada, Inuits or Eskimos?
Answer: The indigenous people of the far north who aren’t culturally, genetically or linguistically related to any of the First Nations prefer “Inuit” which means “The People” in their language Inuktitut. “Inuit” is the proper plural. The problem with “Eskimo” is that it’s a borrowed term from Innu-aimun, an Algonquin language spoken by First Nations in Labrador. It’s original meaning is uncertain (probably “a person who laces snowshoes), but the Innu-aimun used it for both the Inuit and the Mi’kmac (another First Nation). the French adopted this term and it spread into English for all the people in the North from Greenland to Alaska.

Question: What is the significance of Palestinians being recognized as a state, despite already having their own government and nation?
Answer: This is Taiwan, or “The Republic of China” or “Free China” Just like Palestine, it has: Moreover, until 1973, it was considered a fully sovereign country. It was not only a member of the United Nations, but a member of the Security Council. By 1980, it had all gone to sh*t. It lost its seat in the UN, which was given to the People’s Republic of China, which also had a defined territory, a permanent population, and a government, but wasn’t universally recognized as a sovereign state (except by other Communist governments and even that was problematic - ties between the PRC and USSR were withdrawn in 1963). Even the United States, a staunch ally, withdrew diplomatic relations in 1980. Make no mistake - Taiwan 1949–1973 is pretty much identical in every respect to Taiwan 1973-present. It’s just that in 1972 it was clearly a “state” and now, it isn’t. This has several consequences. Taiwan is not a UN member, which also means it’s not a member of any UN agency, like WHO. It’s not a part of any international trade agreement, which complicates trade. It’s not a member of the ICAO which controls civilian air travel which complicates flying to and from Taiwan. It only has a handful of embassies, which complicates getting travel visas or making applications to emigrate from the country. It complicates military alliances and trade agreements. You can get things done, but it’s all needlessly complicated. Because Taiwan and Palestine aren’t “states”. They’re outsiders in the international community. So say you’re a Taiwanese national and get arrested in the United States. Under international conventions, you’re allowed to contact your consulate. Except you don’t have one. The best you can do is the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office. But there’s no ambassador or consul-general. If you’re an Olympic athlete, you’re in luck because the IOC recognizes you as “Chinese Taipei”. You’re in luck if you’re a soccer player too because FIFA also recognizes “Chinese Taipei”. However, you can’t display “Taiwan” or your country’s flag.

Question: Is it feasible for Israel to give up some of its territory to the Palestinians as a means of preventing attacks on its borders?
Answer: Back in 1993, as part of the Oslo Accords, both Israel and Palestine agreed the starting point of discussions about their respective territories would be the “Green Line” - the 1949 Cease Fire Line that constituted the de facto border of Israel until 1967. Now, Israel has controlled all former territory of the British Palestinian Mandate since 1967, but has never annexed any of it. None of that territory is recognized by Israel as “Israel”. That’s “Occupied Territory” or “Territory under the administration of the Palestinian Authority”. No other country recognizes any claim by Israel over any of that territory. Israel has said many times in many contexts that they are willing to cede this to the new Palestinian state. Nevertheless, about 700,000 Israeli citizens live on the other side of the Green Line. That includes Israelis living East Jerusalem, which many countries who recognize Palestine as a sovereign nation recognize as the capital of Palestine. That number just keeps growing every year. Although these “settlements” have no basis in Israeli law, they are actively supported by Israeli military forces in the area and are tacitly accepted by the Israeli government, which is doing nothing to stop the formation of new settlements and is not doing anything to get rid of the existing ones. This has not always been the case. In 1980 when Israel handed back the occupied Sinai to Egypt, it dismantled all the Israeli settlements in the area. In 1993 when Israel handed all of Gaza to the Palestinian Authority, it also dismantled all the Israeli settlements. Now, back in 1993, if Israel had simply handed pretty much all the territory over the Green Line to Palestine, Palestine would have accepted that. In 1993, the people in charge of the Palestinian authority were amenable to a settlement recognizing Israel’s claim to everything on their side of the Green Line. However, for practical purposes, which were recognized by the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinians realized that without Israeli help they could not control militants, so a phased handover was planned. That “phase” is now nearly a generation old and it’s gone nowhere. It’s not that the Israelis and Palestinians haven’t been talking. However, even moderate Palestinians objected to portions behind the Green Line remaining part of Israel. In addition to sovereignty issues, there are also land ownership issues - a lot of Israeli territory and settlements are on land owned by Palestinian Arabs who took title to the land before 1947 and haven’t actually had their land appropriated. Under Israeli law passed in 1950, if the Israelis find “abandoned” land, they can hold it in trust. It’s rented out to Israelis who don’t “own” it but are allowed to occupy it. There’s a lot of land in the West Bank that’s subject tot his law as well. It’s not that it wouldn’t be a good idea to adjust the actual border. However, the adjustments some Israeli negotiators want are over territory that’s very important to Palestine for a lot of reasons. It’s almost as if they pick land they know the Palestinians won’t give up. Complicating the fact is that Israel has built physical barriers that also go across the Green Line. Many of these actually cut off one Palestinian community from another. As such, for some Palestinians to go from “Palestine” to “Palestine”, the short way requires crossing two Israeli checkpoints. Going around the barrier usually requires going through even more Israeli military checkpoints. So what’s the solution? Why are you asking me. I haven’t got any idea. However, I am descended from people in Northern Ireland and I have relatives who lived there. One of the ways they solved the problem was taking down the border entirely. The only way you know now whether you’re in Ireland or Northern Ireland is that the maximum speed limit signs change from km/h to mph. Oh, and the pubs on one side take Euros and the other takes Pounds. The border was kept open even after the UK left the EU (Ireland is still in the EU).

Question: Why didn't Palestinians accept the partition plan in 1947? What do Palestinians want?
Answer: Well, let’s look at Palestine in 1947 and find out. First, Jews were only a majority in one part of the territory - Jaffa. They were a substantial minority in Haifa and Jerusalem. Second, there was no part of the country where Jews owned the majority of the land, or even the plurality. In Jaffa, 47% of the land was owned by Arabs. Now here is the partition overlaid over a map of relative population density. Note that Jerusalem isn’t given to either side. The “Jewish State” is about 58% Jewish and 42% Arab, and contains massive tracts of land where Arabs have a large majority, such as the southeast and the northeast. Meanwhile, the “Arab State” is 95% Arab. Both states have roughly the same land area, even though Jews are only about a third of the total population. Lastly, here’s the partition plan itself. The Arab state is split into four pieces (there’s a tiny bit of Jaffa that remains Arab). The partition plan passed the UN General Assembly, but the UK, which administered the territory, abstained on the vote, and both India and Pakistan, which was the result of a partition and resulted in an immediate war, both voted against it. Hindus and Muslims had agreed to the plan to partition British India on one simple rule - areas with Muslim majorities became Pakistan, and areas with Hindu Majorities became India. Both saw that the proposed Jewish state meant Arab majority areas would become part of the Jewish State. It should be noted that Ireland, which has largely supported Israel, wasn’t a UN member in 1947 and finally decided to recognize Palestine this year. The reason for this plan was twofold. One, a state made up solely of a Jewish majority couldn’t survive long - it wouldn’t have much of an economy. Two, the proposal was to solve the Jewish refugee problem (there were about a quarter million Jews who lost their residence in the war) by letting them all come to the new Jewish state. As you can see, Arabs were horrified by this plan, which would put a third of Arabs in the Jewish state but only about 7% of Jews in the Arab state. It put an area that was overwhelmingly owned by Arabs, Hebron, into the new Jewish state. It would essentially make Arabs a minority in half the territory where they were a clear majority. The UK was so horrified by the plan that they refused to implement it, and their position in the region was so tenuous that they felt the only answer was to get out as quickly as they could even though that would almost certainly mean widespread conflict in the region.

Question: Who owned most of the land before Israel's creation?
Answer: From the point of view of sovereignty, the land was British territory. They administered it as a “protectorate” meaning that local government had no real authority and all the decisions were made in London. On May 15, 1948, the British pretty much just walked away so the territory didn’t belong to anyone. If we’re talking about land ownership, in 1948 about 4% of the land was owned by Jews and about 6% by Palestinian Arabs, the rest being a mix of public land, common land with no owner, and foreign ownership (mostly by other Muslim countries, particularly Turkey which had ruled the land before the British took it over in 1919).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why is it commonly stated that Israel took over Palestinian land? Wasn't the land previously owned by other countries such as Egypt or Jordan?
Answer: Not in the least. On May 15, 1948, the United Kingdom, which had been administering the territory, announced it was leaving without putting any other government in charge. On that date, Palestine was officially no-man’s land. The previous day, the Jewish Provisional Government in Tel-Aviv had declared independence. Although the United States recognized this soon after it happened, the British did not and waited until “Israel”, as it now was, had democratic elections in January of 1949. Jewish and Arab militias had been fighting each other from 1936–1939, took a break once the UK banned further Jewish immigration in 1939, stayed on break for World War II, then picked up the fighting again in 1945. The Jews also directly attacked the British, killing and wounding about 250 officials between 1945 and 1948. Arabs were largely supportive of the British (and vice versa) but although the Arabs got outside support (as did the Jews) neither side was afraid of taking any further step while the British were in place. While the British were there, they largely forbade further Jewish immigration and the importation of weapons (although both sides were building their own) and other Arab nations wouldn’t send troops into the area for fear of provoking war with Britain. The Americans offered to take over from the British, but both sides were cool to that idea, although the Jewish Provisional Government seriously considered the possibility, eventually rejecting it in favour of independence. But after the British left, all hell broke loose as several Arab nations sent in armed forces, quickly outnumbering the Jewish militias. Jewish forces were forced way back into the interior of the country. However, the Jewish forces were soon reinforced by Jews from abroad (both refugees and Jews from Europe and the United States who were sympathetic) and by surplus World War II weapons largely purchased from Eastern Europe with the blessing of the Soviet Union (which recognized Israel a week after the declaration and was the first to exchange ambassadors). By late 1948, there were more Jewish soldiers on the ground than Arab ones, and they were working together while the Arabs, working with five different command structures and quickly being outnumbered and outgunned, lost all their gains. The two sides reached a cease fire on the condition that this not be a “border” and drew a cease fire line leaving Gaza in the hands of Egypt and the West Bank in the hands of Jordan. Israel soon consolidated its territory and set up a formal democratic government while Egypt and Jordan argued with themselves about what to do next. No peace talks were ever held and after Israel was soon admitted to the UN the cease fire line became the de facto border. But let’s look at it from another point of view - one that doesn’t involve nation states. At the time of the 1947–48 war, most of the people living in the Palestinian Mandate were Muslim. A vast part of the Jewish population had only arrived in the area since 1933 - prior to that not a lot of Jews though that having a separate state in Israel made sense. It was the beginning of anti-Jewish sentiment in Germany that drove more Jews to Palestine. The idea of a Jewish state in Palestine was first proposed by the British in 1917, but by about 1923 they realized it was a terrible idea because the Arab population was so high and widespread. By 1947, Jews were only a majority in one part of the country (near Tel-Aviv). The 1947 Partition Plan passed the UN, but the UK itself though it bad and abstained. Pakistan and India, who were at war at the time, both were vehemently opposed to it. The plan was fundamentally flawed as the “Jewish State” proposed would have been about 55% Jewish and 45% Arab. Simply put, you could not create a primarily Jewish state in Palestine unless it was very small and simply could not support any economic output. Even Jews realized that without a substantial number of Arabs within their state, there was no way they would have sufficient labour to support an economy. Even the Israeli Declaration of Independence welcomes Arabs in the state. A solely Jewish state in the area was, and remains, an impossibility and not just because Arabs live everywhere in the territory. One of the reasons for this is that by 1947 the Arabs didn’t have any real leaders, but the Jews did. Most Arabs who might have been able to create a nation state were dead, either killed by Jews, killed by the British, or killed by other Arabs. Even today, Palestinian Arabs are a deeply divided people. Part of that is because the Palestinians willing to work with the Israelis can’t seem to get anything done to settle the territorial disputes. People on both sides were very hopeful in 1993 when the Oslo Accords were reached, but both sides started working against them practically from the moment they were signed. But let’s face it - there are still millions of Arabs in the territory. Over what used to be British Palestine, there are roughly equal numbers of Arabs and Jews. Some Arabs, those within the cease fire area controlled by Israel, are Israeli citizens. However, millions of Palestinian Arabs are descended from people who were born in what’s now Israel. They’re not going anywhere. Some of them still own land in Israel.

Question: How do I build a social life in Canada?
Answer: That depends on where you live. In most places in Canada, even medium sized cities, it’s not going to be a problem. People there talk to each other all the time. I was in Niagara Falls and people just chat with people they pass on the street. Madness. Here in Toronto, that’s not going to work. Talking to strangers on the street, on transit, in restaurants, bars or cafes is just rude. Mind your own goddamn business. People get friendlier the further away you get. My sister lives in Oshawa now after moving from Scarborough. She lives near a busy community center and the people who work there chat with her non-stop. Here in Toronto, you have to work on it. That means seeking out people with common interests and hoping for the best. I’m a stamp collector. Most of my friends are too. There are several stamp clubs left in the GTA and they’re all very nice. Your interest may differ, but there’s probably a club for you too. Or movies. It used to be easier when you had to line up for hours, but I met so many people standing in lines for movies. But there are still street festivals. Torontonians at street festivals will love talking to you because they’re all at the street festival. They hold Toronto Pride right outside my house and that’s a great place to meet people if you’re 2SLGBTQA+. However, we have the Caribbean festival and the TIFF film festival and the Italian festival and the festival next to the Dufferin Mall and it’s easy to find people to chat with. We have a big comic convention too. Not a weekend goes by when there’s not some sort of festival or show or whatever.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How are chimps related to humans and other species of great apes? How did this relationship come about?
Answer: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor that lived about five million years ago. Eventually, it appears one branch of those ancestors stayed living in forests, while the other branch left the forest and started living on grasslands. Forests initially had more and better food, but it turned out that resources on the grassland could be exploited with a little greater effort. This led to chimpanzees keeping characteristics that favoured living in tress and not travelling long distances, while humans developed characteristics that favoured long distance travel (like walking upright) and larger, more complex social networks (which required larger brains). The main defining characteristic in the skeletons of the two species is the size of the braincase, which is much larger in humans. Conversely, chimpanzees retained the very strong muscles typical of other apes, which allowed them to chew less nutritious but more plentiful food in the forests. Going further back, humans, chimps and gorillas shared a common ancestor somewhat further back. Gorillas still lived in forests, but stuck mostly to the ground rather than the trees, which allowed them to get much larger (no fall risk) which had the side benefit of making them difficult for predators to attack. A fully grown make gorilla weighs from 300–500 pounds, meaning most predators won’t try to attack it. Going even further back, humans, chimps, gorillas and orangutangs also shared a common ancestor. It’s most likely orangutangs, which spend almost all their times in the trees, separated from other apes which spent most of their time on the ground. Early apes are distinguished by their shoulder joint, which has a much wider range of movement than monkeys. For example, Baboons, which are large but still monkeys, don’t have flexible shoulders and can climb trees only with difficulty. Large apes have no problem climbing trees due to that flexibility, so were able to be larger than arboreal monkeys who relied on their low weight to make climbing easier. All apes have brains substantially bigger than monkeys of the same size, most likely to support more complex social relationships than exist in monkeys, which includes a longer attachment to their young. In gorillas, chimps and humans, this includes close attachment to fathers and not just mothers.

Question: Can someone provide the correct pronunciation for Toronto, Canada and Montreal, Quebec?
Answer: No one in Toronto pronounces it “Tah-ron-toe”. If you hear someone call it that, they’re almost certainly Americans. The most common pronunciation here in the city is “T’rah-noh”. In any event, you never, ever, ever pronounce that second “T”. If you’re from rural Canada, “T’ranna” is perfectly acceptable. French speakers in Montreal also hate the “T” sound so it’s “Mohn-ray-ahl”. That “O” sound is very nasal. Flipping it around “Toh-rohn-toh” is a perfectly acceptable French pronunciation of the city name, and “Muhn-tree-all” is fine for an English speaker.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the origin of the name "Toronto" and why was it chosen over other options like "York" for this Canadian city?
Answer: The name derives from the Mohawk “T’karanto” meaning “the place where the trees grow in the water” or “fishing weir”. Originally, the name was applied to a stretch of water between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching near what’s now Orillia, Ontario, but eventually the usage spread south. “T’karanto”. This usage was recorded by Samuel de Champlain as early as 1615. The trees still there and are now called the Mnjikaning Fish Weirs By 1632, the French had compiled a dictionary of Wyandot terms, and “toronto” was listed as the equivalent of “plenty”. “Toronto” wasn’t used on any French maps until 1650 and in 1675, a French map referred to what’s now Lake Simcoe as “Lac Taranto”. Another map in 1678 called the same lake “Tarantos Lac”. In 1680, another map called it “Lac de Taranto”. In 1686, what we now call the Humber River, which links Lake Ontario to the highlands northwest of the city and was an important trade passage was called “Passage de Taranto” and later the “Riviere Taranto”. In the 1750s, the French built a fort in the river’s delta and called it “Fort Toronto”. But in 1797, the area came under the control of the first lieutenant governor of Upper Canada, who chose the site as the colony’s new capital. The new governor, Lord Simcoe started re-naming everything with more British names so “Lake Toronto” became “Lake Simcoe” (after his father?), Riviere Toronto became the Humber River and the town got the name “York” after a military hero, the Duke of York. But by the 1830s the new Town of York was becoming more important as a trade and manufacturing center as well as being the colonial capital. Moreover, fourteen other municipalities in Upper Canada also contained the word “York”, including York Township and York County, where the capital was located. Also, some of the older people missed the native name. As such, the Upper Canada legislature passed legislation in 1834 changing the name of the capital from the “Town of York” to “Toronto” to make it distinctive. There are still plenty of “Yorks” to be found in Ontario, such as the old municipalities now part of Toronto the Town of York, North York and East York, plus the neighbourhoods of Yorkdale and York Mills. The area north of Toronto, formerly part of York County, is now York Region.

Question: What are the legal limitations for suing someone in Canada?
Answer: For the most part, the only requirement is that the court actually have jurisdiction over the dispute. The court will definitely have jurisdiction over a dispute where the defendant resides in Canada (as long as you sue in the appropriate province), but the rules regarding suing foreign defendants change from province to province. My home province, Ontario, has pretty broad rules for suing foreign defendants, but they draw the line at times. For example, an Israeli businessman living in Ontario (he had dual citizenship) sued the Tel-Aviv based newspaper “Haaretz” for libel in Ontario for a story they published that was available on their website. The Ontario court rules on a motion over jurisdiction from the defendant that although the plaintiff may have suffered reputational damage in Ontario, that Israel was the most appropriate jurisdiction to hear the case.

Question: What distinguishes monkeys from apes? Why are humans not classified as monkeys despite their similarities to them?
Answer: Another important distinguishing characteristic between monkeys and apes is the flexibility of the shoulder joint. In monkeys’ the shoulder joint is largely fixed in one plane and only allows the arms to be moved through that plane, which is a necessity for most mammals that run on all four legs. This baboon’s front legs can pretty much only move through a narrow range of motion, mostly back and forth. Apes have very flexible shoulder joints which allows them to move their arms in a very wide range of directions. This often aids climbing. Monkeys simply can’t move their arms like that.

Question: If you could rename your town, what would be an appropriate alternative name?
Answer: No need. It was already renamed in 1834, and that was a good idea The area where the tiny little town was founded in the 1890s had been known as “Toronto” for some time, but the new lieutenant governor instead named it after a military hero, the Duke of York, so it became “York” But by 1834, it was clear that the name wasn’t working out. There were fourteen other places in Upper Canada alone named “York”, plus the old city in England and the new one in the United States. Everyone thought the capital should have a unique name so the Upper Canada legislature changed it to “Toronto” officially. The new city started devouring every municipality in its path and in 1998 pretty much covered the entire southern portion of what used to be York County

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: The fakeness of Obama. Saying that outdated housing restrictions need to change so working people can afford them. Yet he lives on a 30 acre compound on Martha's Vineyard. Why not start dividing that property up for more affordable housing to help?
Answer: Well, you’ve pointed out the very issue Obama is concerned about, because if he tried to do that, the municipality wouldn’t allow it. They could get court orders to stop him if he even tried. Frankly, if Mr. Obama wanted to sub-divide his 30 acres into individual housing units, that would probably be very lucrative for him. A 30 acre parcel may be worth a lot of money, but the market for it is limited, so if he wanted to sell it, he would be looking at a very small pool of buyers. Breaking it up into smaller units makes each individual unit more marketable. At typical suburban densities, a 30 acre lot could easily be split into 200 individual single family homes. Now, the municipality has some valid concerns. There are are limits to how much water can be supplied to households and how much sewage can be handled. There’s a reason why new suburban sub-divisions need approval, and the main issue is supplying them with drinking water. However, in many cases, laws that prohibit multi-unit residential buildings (even duplexes and semi-detached homes) or closely packed housing aren’t there because of resource limits. They’re deliberately exclusionary to prevent affordable housing from being built in an area. Let me draw a comparison. This is Willowdale, one of Toronto’s inner suburbs, and right on a subway line. As you can see, there are big buildings on the arterial road, but everything around it is detached homes. It’s illegal to build more big buildings on the land with the single family homes, even though it makes sense to do it because it’s close to transit. Conversely, this is Laval, an outer suburb of Montreal, but connected to it by a metro system. As you can see, there are densely packed building all over the center of the city, and it looks like they’re expanding into the single family home zones that still exist. And you don’t need high rises This is Leslieville, a “street car suburb” that’s in the old core of the city of Toronto and dates from the 1920s. As you can see, the houses are right next to each other, and there are still a few apartment buildings. Housing in neighbourhoods like this can be affordable. But this is a new development, built in the last few years, in a semi-rural area within commuting distance of Toronto. As you can see, nothing but big houses on big lots. As you can guess, none of these are affordable, and probably never will be. This is a place for rich people. Naturally, there’s no transit.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the reason behind people calling the police when someone is on their property?
Answer: My mom once called the cop when she spotted a suspicious man lurking in her suburban neighbourhood. The 911 operator checked and it turned out the suspicious man was actually an undercover police officer doing surveillance on someone in the neighbourhood. Just because someone is on your property doesn’t make them a trespasser. There are people who have a perfect right to be on your property - law enforcement officers, surveyors, city workers, mail carriers, process servers, political canvassers and so forth. Most people are not comfortable confronting someone on their property and in most jurisdictions, you have no right to use force to get someone to leave your property - they must be confronted and arrested by a police officer if they don’t leave. You can delegate that function to the police, who will arrest someone with no right to be on the property.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: If you were in charge of renaming Canada’s national animal, what would you pick and why?"
Answer: The common name of our industrious, indefatigable, furry national animal is the “Beaver”. It appears that pretty much every language in Europe used a similar word for this animal, which several hundred years ago was widespread throughout that continent until we got a taste for wearing hats made out of its pelt and hunted them to near extinction. Luckily, it recovered and there are about 1.2 million European beavers at the moment. However, although Canadian beavers and European beavers are the same genus, they’re different species. Their genus name “Castor” comes from the Latin word for “wood”. The European species is “Castor fibre” as “fibre” is the Latin for the animal (and it’s a cognate of “beaver”, from the same root). Here in North America, they’re “Castor canadensis” or “Canadian wood”. They’re much more common here, and estimates are that there are about 15 million of them. Beavers are often treated as a nuisance, but they help with old growth forests (they prefer younger, faster growing, more tender trees, leaving older trees room to grow) and it turns out their dam building prevents things like loss of soil and wetlands. One farmer who let beavers have the run of his property found that even during dry times, his crops never lacked for water. So maybe they need a more majestic name. Luckily, the beaver is well known to the First Nations. There are, of course, many indigenous names for the animal, but I’m going with Algonquin for this one as they did a lot of trading. So our new name will of course be “Amik”, which is what they called it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can the New York Times be sued for libel if it keeps on publishing comments calling our president, Donald Trump, "the greatest fool" or "a buffoon"?
Answer: His biggest hurdle in this case is that a defamation has to be “factual”. Statements of opinion, even if negative, aren’t actionable in defamation. For example, movie critics and art critics can’t be sued over their critiques. People who leave reviews on Google or Yelp can’t be sued over whether or not they enjoyed the experience. For example, if you say in a review that you sat in a restaurant for half-an-hour before someone took your order, that’s a “fact”. It’s “actionable”, even if true. However, if you just say “the service was slow”, that’s an “opinion” and it’s not actionable. Calling someone a “fool” or a “buffoon” is pure opinion. There’s no way to independently confirm either of those.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Has a star ever been observed collapsing into a black hole?
Answer: Regrettably no. Although on a universal scale, the type of event that can result in black hole happens all the time as stars die, it doesn’t happen much locally over human time scales. Now, since the invention of the telescope, we’ve been able to observe about 10,000 supernovae, the massive explosion of a star that could leave a black hole behind. Unfortunately, the number of those that took place in our own galaxy is precisely - zero. Like I said, in the universe as a whole, it happens a few million times a day, but the universe is a big place and we can only see a teeny, tiny part of it really well. The last verifiable supernova in our own galaxy observed by humans was in 1604 C.E. and it’s really nothing to write home about. The one we know the most about is designated SN (supernova) 1054 (from 1054 C.E.). It was recorded in several places and described “as bright as the moon during the day”. Luckily, we were able to trace it to something we now can still see. The Crab Nebula. All that stuff you see around it is debris from the supernova (it’s in false color for different types of radiation, but it’s no problem observing it, even in just visible light). Unfortunately, it didn’t create a black hole, only a ho-hum neutron star that is a pulsar. It’s one of the only pulsars we know about that gives off visible light, and it has one of the fastest rotation speeds of any known pulsar, making a full rotation in 33/1000ths of a second. But “collapsing” isn’t quite right. Before collapsing into a black hole, the star must explode, which blows a lot of mass out into space. However, what’s left has no way to resist gravity from collapsing it. A neutron star resists total collapse by crushing whole atoms into atomic nucleii, but the resulting neutrons resist further compression. In a black hole, there’s just too much gravity for even neutrons to resist compression.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the correct pronunciation of the letter R? How can someone learn to pronounce it correctly if they struggle with using their tongue while speaking English as a second language?
Answer: There isn’t one. Lots of languages with a Latin alphabet use “R”, but its pronunciation varies wildly, even across different accents of English. Here’s the IPA chart of related sounds, which includes all the ways “R” is pronounced across languages All of these pretty much involve holding your tongue somewhere on the top palate of your mouth, but the tongue position, how hard you hold the tongue, and whether you vibrate the tongue while making the sound vary widely. In English, “R” is usually pronounced by briefly touching the forward part of tongue (not the tip) hard against the frontal part of the palate a bit behind the teeth. That’s inappropriate in German, where the touch is much less pronounced, giving a softer sound. Making it harder is that the “R” in English isn’t used in most oriental languages. “L” is a related sound in English, made by holding the tip tongue much further back on the palate. In most Asian languages, there is a related sound, but it’s made by holding the tongue about midway between where an English speaker would hold their tongue for an “R” or an “L”. Although, for example, Japanese people learning English will pronounce “L” and “R” the same (largely because they both sound like the middle sound they make) to an English hear the “mid sound” sounds like “L” in an “R” word and vice versa. And even native speakers find it hard to pronounce the sound. The average age for an English speaker to master the sound is seven, so it’s one of the last sounds native speakers master. For non-native speakers, it’s just as difficult. Even adult English speakers sometimes have problems with the sound. “Welease Wodgah!” Many English speakers, including famous ones like Johnathan Woss, I mean Ross, substitute a /w/ sound for an /r/ sound in words. However the two sounds are actually very close and if its subtle, you might miss it. Moreover, it’s getting more common. One of the things you might want to try is pronouncing /w/ and then not moving your lips, but moving your tongue a little forward. That’s often close enough.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How do black holes form in space and why are they not visible on Earth? Would their massive gravitational pull affect us on Earth?
Answer: Black holes form when very massive stars go supernova at the end of their life. A star has to be about 2.5 times as massive as the sun for this to possibly happen. So, the first thing to remember is that a “main sequence” star, one that has normal behavior, is still a massive battle between the force of gravity trying to collapse a cloud of hydrogen and helium and thermonuclear forces deep inside the star (which are ironically due to the pressures caused by this collapse) trying to push the gas cloud apart. In a star like our sun, hundreds of millions of tons of hydrogen in the very center of the star are fusing into a similar amount of helium every second , but there will be a mass difference (about 3 million tons a second) and under Einstein’s E=mc2, that’s a buttload of energy trying to get out of the star. It actually takes several hundred thousand years for photons created by a nuclear fusion at the center of the sun to work its way through the plasma cloud around the core and escape the sun on their way to us. But at the end of every star’s life, there simply isn’t enough hydrogen left to continue the same rate of hydrogen fusion that kept the star from collapsing. In a supernova, as the center of the star collapses, weird things happen with fusion and before you know it, the star has one last hurrah where for a short period of time it releases more energy than the rest of the galaxy does. The star blows off its outer layers and leaves just a central mass of mostly hydrogen and helium that cannot prevent further collapse. In many stars, this collapse is prevented by the fact you can only compress atoms so much before the protons and neutrons in those atoms will not collapse any further. These are “neutron stars” because the gravity forces the electrons and protons together into neutrons. These neutron stars still give off a lot of energy and many of them become what we call “pulsars” because the radiation coming out of their poles can be detected as the star is spinning - sometimes over a few days, but sometimes over a few seconds. But in supermassive stars, there’s so much gravity that even neutrons and protons stop being able to resist the collapse. At this point you can throw everything you know about classical physics out the window because you get a “black hole” which has a mass, and affects an area, but fundamentally has no volume. Unlike neutron stars, black holes don’t give off a lot of radiation, so they’re pretty much impossible to “see”. However, stuff still falls into black holes, and often that stuff is hot and bright. You can see that part and we have. Black holes also still have a lot of gravity, and you can see stars going around a black hole, or otherwise being affected by them. I believe these are still theoretical, but in theory if a black hole were close enough to a star, matter from the star would head towards the black hole, forming an “accretion disc” as the matter orbits the black hole waiting for it’s turn to get in. This disc would be very flat and bright, so you should be able to see them. But this is the best picture we’ve been able to get. This is a very massive black hole. The bright stuff around it is matter orbiting the black hole at very high speeds so it gives off energy we can see.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What happens to the frequency of a light beam when it moves towards an observer?
Answer: It’s frequency rises, shifting to the blue end of the spectrum (or closer to x-rays if it’s really travelling quickly). In astronomy, that’s “blueshift” and is only exhibited by a handful of galaxies close to us, and only by a little bit - a small fraction of the speed of light, but still detectable in the galaxy’s spectrum. However, it’s speed relative to the observer remains constant, which means if I stand still and point a laser at you, then start running, the laser gets a little less red but the speed of light you measure would be identical.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Are there any real life counterparts to Dr. Gregory House in the medical field?
Answer: Not a single person, but there is a voluntary organization The UDN works with doctors all over the country to attempt to get diagnoses for patients with unique conditions that defy the experts. However, unlike the show, the efforts of the doctors often last for years even if they do make a breakthrough. Even then, they only successfully come up with a diagnosis for about a quarter of the cases they accept. They’re partly funded by the National Institutes of Health. It largely operates as a research group so they regularly publish their results. So fare, the UDN has identified 31 new medical syndromes. Other institutions, such as the Mayo Clinic and McGill University, have also set up smaller equivalents.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is there a limit to how many times a joke or gag can be used in a movie and still be funny?
Answer: Not at all. The only rule is that the joke has to fit the situation within the story. If you can do that, you can do it as many times as you want. The common term for this is “running gag”, and there are some classic ones. In “A Funny Thing Happened On The Way to the Forum”, one of the characters (an elderly man) is distracted by telling him he has to walk around Rome’s seven hills seven times. We feel that this is probably the last time we will see him, but no. Sometime later, he appears and announces “first time around!” This happens at a particularly tense point in the plot so it acts as comic relief. It also sets a “countdown clock” because if he does by some miracle complete the task, our protagonist is toast. By the time he gets to “third time around!” you wonder when he will show up next. Another one is the swan in “Hot Fuzz”. The action takes place in a small West Country village in England where it seems our protagonist, urban supercop Nicholas Angel, is going to die of boredom. An escaped swan becomes one of the tasks he’s assigned to sort out. Angel comes close to capturing the swan several times, but is always tasked with something more important. However, by the end of the film he’s uncovered a dangerous conspiracy and he’s managed to turn the police force against their corrupt inspector. But still, you’ve got to do your duty when you can. And so, in a life or death situation when your life is on the line, you still have to deal with the swan.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How long would it take to travel to another star system at light speed if we started one million miles away from it?
Answer: Well, if you were travelling at light speed, one million miles is nothing. It takes light about four to five seconds to traverse that distance. The problem is that other start systems aren’t “millions” of miles away or even “billions” of miles away. They’re “trillions” of miles away. You can travel millions of miles in minutes at the speed of light, and billions of miles in a few hours, but for trillions of miles, you’re talking years. So say you started your trip at Jan 1, 2025 at 00:01 in the morning at the Sun. At 00:08 you would reach Earth and by 06:00 you reach Pluto. You would reach the nearest large star to our Sun, Alpha Centauri, sometime in June of 2029. Light is fast, but the universe is big.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Do you agree that by increasing the capital gains tax 17 % Trudeaus government has effectively killed investment in Canada? An investor wants to make a profit. This is the highest capital gains tax in the world. Why not invest elsewhere?
Answer: Well, when I look at what I pay in income tax every year as a moderate earner, it comes to about 25% of my earned income. Why shouldn’t investors pay at least as much on unearned income as I pay on earned income? Besides, one of the largest sectors of the Canadian economy is property ownership. In a lot of cases, property investors don’t pay a lot of tax on their rental income because they get to deduct mortgage interest, which is high in the early days and slowly goes down. A really good example is one of those “do it yourself” carwashes you might see. The income from that is just enough to pay carrying costs on the land (mortgage payments, taxes, etc.) so they don’t show a lot of profit - until the owner sells the land at a later date to a developer and makes a bundle. However, none of that sale is “business income” - it’s “capital gains”. And because the Canadian property market is red hot, investing in property is one of the main places where you see consistent capital gains. It’s also captive - you can’t escape it by trying to move your money elsewhere because it’s not portable like stocks are. Another consideration - this applies to people who buy a second property to rent out, which pushes up prices and makes it harder for people to buy their own property for ownership. It’s one of the reasons why the principal residence exemption now requires you to own a property for at least twelve months to take advantage of it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why are Canada’s railroad workers getting set for a strike in 2024?
Answer: Railway workers are pretty well paid, but the hours suck. You pretty much have to be ready to take control of a train when it actually shows up, and since freight trains don’t run on closely controlled schedules that can be “anytime”. For the most part, you’re put on an “on call” basis for a block of time. You don’t necessarily get paid for that time (you only get paid for the time you’re actually operating a train). This block will, of course, include “the middle of the night” and “weekends”. Each member of a train crew is largely assigned a “route”, a stretch of track where you take one freight train out, then come back to your base on a different freight train. One route one of my buddies, a brakeman, commonly ran was “Toronto to Smiths Falls”. It doesn’t exactly follow this route, but close enough. Mostly, he would grab a fully loaded train in Scarborough, ride it out to Smiths Falls, then find a hotel (which was paid for) to grab some shuteye while waiting for a train in the other direction. Unfortunately, freight trains don’t move at 100 km/h. In some sections, the train has to go as low as 20 km/h, so it takes forever, so it’s pretty much a full day to get the train to its destination. Then he has to eventually make the same trip back. Now, one of the incentives for the railway is to have as few crews as possible. That means crews are often on call, and since letting a train sit is done sometimes, it’s not preferred - you want a crew to take over for a tired crew at some point. Now, because crew has to be ready to go on about an hour’s notice, taking transit to and from the train yard isn’t really a good idea - you need to drive, and often you have to do that after being on a train for 8–10 hours at a stretch. You obviously can’t sleep on the train. Now, modern trains aren’t like old ones. Back in the day, you had an engineer, a brakeman and a guard (conductor) to keep an eye on things. Nowadays a single person can do all of that, but it’s not a good idea. The railways want to do away with the guard position. And that’s where safety comes in. Since this involved a runaway freight train that collided with a passenger train, the autopsies were inconclusive, but it appears the engineer had a heart attack, and the brakeman was asleep. They were on a return leg and only had a few hours to rest in a company bunkhouse in between. The brakeman had been complaining about feeling ill. The conductor survived the crash, but couldn’t explain why he didn’t activate the emergency brakes when he lost contact with the locomotive. In the report, the company was blamed for ignoring the need for crew to rest and actively discouraging men from sleeping in the bunkhouse. Some changes were implemented. In this crash, the train was being operated by a single operator. However, at the end of his twelve-hour shift, he pulled over and secured the train with air brakes and hand brakes before leaving to go to a hotel. IN the middle of the night, there was a small fire on the train, and the firemen released the air brakes when they shut off the locomotive. They didn’t re-start it. They operator hasn’t activated enough hand brakes to make sure the train stayed in place, so it started downhill and crashed. In the investigation, the inquiry noted that had the operator activated all the hand brakes, it would have taken him another half-hour before he could leave. Moreover, the only way to safely determine if you have enough hand brakes is to remove the air brakes and see if the train moves. You can’t do that with a single operator. So one of the big issues is ensuring crew gets enough rests between long shifts. That’s a problem when you have so few train crew. You need to train crew (it pretty much works from brakeman to conductor to engineer, in that order). My brakeman friend felt he wouldn’t be able to successfully complete the training to upgrade - it isn’t easy. There’s really no incentive to do it although there are legal maximums for on-duty time. The other issue is also common with airlines - there aren’t enough crews where they need to be. Crew get sick, or have to go on vacation, or need personal days. Unfortunately, the situation has become so bad that there are many parts of the country that don’t have enough crews and probably won’t for the foreseeable future. The railways want the right to move crew for long term temporary assignments. The union opposes that and wants the railways to hire more crews even though in the more remote parts of the country, that’s often difficult. Now, the railway will pay for your accommodation, but it will rip you away from your home and family for months at a time, and nowadays when most crew have spouses and child care obligations, that’s incredibly difficult (yes, there are a lot of female crew now).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the distance between the train station and the airport in Montreal?
Answer: There’s actually a train station right next to Trudeau Airport - it’s called “Dorval” and westbound trains to Toronto and Ottawa routinely stop there. They’re about 2km apart. The main train station downtown, Gare Centrale, is a bit further away, but on weekdays there is service between Dorval and Gare Centrale on the commuter rail network. It’s about 19km away and the best way to get there is on the 747 Express Bus, which connects downtown Montreal to the airport. Montreal is currently building a light rail link (the REM) from the existing network to the airport. It’s scheduled to open in 2027.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is there a ferry service between the United States and Canada (specifically Niagara)?
Answer: No. There are no current ferry services across the Niagara River, although there are four bridges - Queenston/Lewiston, Whirlpool, Rainbow and Peace. The only ferry services between the two countries remaining are: From Wolfe Island from Point Alexandra ON to Cape Vincent NY From Yarmouth NS to Bar Harbor ME And from Vancouver Island to several spots on the mainland of Washington

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the most efficient route to travel between Toronto and Montreal without using toll roads?
Answer: Neither Autoroute 20, which runs from central Montreal to the Ontario border, or Highway 401, which runs from the Quebec border through northern Toronto, is a toll highway, and it’s clearly the fastest route by road. It’s about five and a half hours of driving, and there are service plazas every 100 km or so.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How do I go to the train station from Montreal Airport?
Answer: Which train station? Dorval is literally next to the airport. VIA Rail runs a shuttle every half hour from the airport to the train station, passing hotels along the way. On weekdays, there’s commuter service to downtown Montreal, and VIA trains stop there heading west to Toronto, so if you’re going to Kingston or Ottawa you can catch the train there. Montreal’s transit system also runs regular busses from the airport to the train station and they’re often faster. It is close enough to walk, but it takes about half-an-hour. The main station is Gare Central downtown, and still the easiest way to get there from the Airport is by the 747 Express bus, which runs every 15 minutes and does a loop of the downtown area, including the train station. Montreal is building a light rail link between the two but it isn’t open yet.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How are commuters in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal affected by the lockouts?
Answer: Some people in the GTA had a major disruption to their commute, but most people in the area weren’t affected at all. This is the Milton GO Line, a heavy commuter rail system. It was the only line that was completely shut down by the strike. However, it mostly serves commuters in Mississauga, and they were able to use alternate train lines that head for the same destination. Hamilton GO Centre was also shut down by the strike, but it was the only station on the Lakeshore West line affected. the trains still ran to the next station on the line, Aldershot, and trains that usually run to Niagara Falls were unaffected as they bypass this station anyway. There was also alternative bus service from here to Toronto.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why are raccoons thriving in Toronto?
Answer: Racoons need food and shelter, and Toronto has plenty of both. Food comes from sloppy humans who don’t properly dispose of or secure their food waste. They don’t call the raccoon the “garbage bandit” for nothing, and racoons have been known to figure out how to penetrate “racoon-proof” garbage cans and pass that information along to other racoons. Shelter comes from Toronto’s roughly five million trees, plus lots of uninhabited nooks and crannies in the city. I once found a mother racoon and her cubs living in a narrow alley near a subway station. There was an iron gate, but even a big raccoon could manage to climb it. In addition, some attics aren’t well secured and racoons can easily use them as nests for their young. Raccoons really don’t have a problem travelling, and commonly cross busy roads during less busy periods. I saw a family of them crossing Broadview Avenue once, which carries a streetcar route among other things. Raccoons also have large litters - an average of about five. They can easily take advantage of extra food sources when they arise. They also have quite varied diets - everything from fruit to small fish. But it’s not like we’re overrun. There are only about 20,000 of them in Toronto alone, although the surrounding area shares many of the same habitats like heavily wooded areas next to residential areas.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can you recommend some movies that were set and filmed in Canada? How do these movies reflect the country's geography and culture?
Answer: That’s not a very long list, but there are a few that meet both criteria and are probably worth watching. Set and shot largely in Toronto’s Annex neighbourhood, “Scott Pilgrim” tells the story of a 23 year old slacker who has to fight off seven of his new 24 year old sweetheart’s evil exes. Based on a popular Canadian Manga series. Unfortunately, the neighbourhood has changed a lot since the film was shot. Shot in Ontario and Quebec, “Bon Cop Bad Cop” teams a straight laced by the book Ontario provincial police force with a maverick slob of a Quebec Surete officer after a body is discovered on the border between the two provinces. The film explores several stereotypes each side of the French/English divide in Canada has about the other. Shot mostly in Montreal and the Quebec resort areas, “Duddy Kravitz” was one of Richard Dreyfuss’s earliest film roles (also featuring a very young Randy Quaid). Duddy is a young and ambitious Jewish Montrealer who hopes to impress his family by acquiring land to build his own resort, but winds up alienating them instead. An amateur hockey team becomes involved in a bet over their sponsor’s bar, but the team has loads of external issues they have to deal with. Shot in and around Montreal and one of the few Canadian films that deals with the nation’s obsession about hockey.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the significance of the band The Ramones?
Answer: In the 1970s, “Rock and Roll” wasn’t anything like it was in the 1960s when it became by far the most popular form of music. And the guys who were responsible for most of that change were The Beatles Back when they invaded America The Beatles were a guitar and drum group. Sure, they were experimenting a bit, but pretty much the majority of what they did was straightforward. But just a few years later, The Beatles were incorporating a massive number of musical elements and experimental techniques into their music. After that, “production values” started to become a massive element in rock music and pretty much pushed out all the guitar and drum bands. Instead we got. Mike Oldfield, a 16 year old wunderkind who played dozens of instruments and once shredded a 24 track tape from re-using it so often during recording sessions. Queen, which used vocoders and other electronic techniques that were impossible to replicate live. In “Bohemian Rhapsody”, Freddie Mercury sings all the vocal parts, including the harmonies. The Electric Light Orchestra, which used a number of non-rock instruments and complicated arrangements. It’s not that this music wasn’t good. It was just complicated. it was beyond the capabilities of musicians who weren’t technically savvy and well financed to duplicate. So, into the middle of this, forming in 1974 and becoming rather better known in 1977, were the Ramones. The Ramones were - three guitars and a drum kit The Ramones were one of a number of groups who fought back against the use of highly technical “progressive rock” and tirelessly played live shows with just three guitars and a drum kit. Ironically, they took their name from Paul McCartney’s alias “Paul Ramon”, used when he registered at a hotel. And they were a massive throwback, because you remember how The Beatles started Just like The Beatles launched a lot of other bands in England, the Ramones had the same effect. They were so simply put together that a lot of musicians though they could pull it off too. That fed into the growing movement of “punk” that was going on in the UK at the same time. Some of the musicians who cite the Ramones as an influence are The Beastie Boys, Black Flag, The Dead Kennedys and Green Day. Their influence also spread into other countries, such as Teenage Head from Canada. Other Hard Rock bands also emulated some of their style, like Metallica, Motorhead, The Foo Fighters, Nirvana and Pearl Jam. And they did this without major commercial success. They only had one gold record, and were never able to fill large arenas, instead having a two decade career playing smaller venues (often packed shoulder to shoulder). The El Mocambo in Toronto was a small venue, usually packed, that was a favourite of The Rolling Stones, Blondie and Elvis Costello. This sort of venue was the “bread and butter” for the band.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What was the labor dispute between rail workers and the Canadian government that led to the shutdown of Canadian freight railroads?
Answer: Well, let’s get this straight - this is not a fight between rail workers and the Canadian government. The rail workers are in a labour dispute with their employers, Canadian National Railway (once owned by the government, but not any more) and the Canadian Pacific Kansas City Railway. Between the two, they control the vast majority of rail freight going through Canada. There are many issues on the table, but the primary one is scheduling. Workers on the trains themselves want more guarantees of rest to ensure they aren’t operating trains without sufficient rest. Freight movement is essentially a 24 hour a day matter, but freight schedules aren’t as tightly controlled as passenger schedules so crews can be kept waiting for hours before they actually go on duty, and don’t get paid for the wait time. Crews often have to take trains back to their “base” on the same shift, which means they can have an unusually long work day. That goes to the second major issue - relocation. The railways want to move personnel to new bases, but not permanently - only in response to local labour shortages. These reassignments could last months. At present, most railway workers work a small series of routes - to an out station and then back to their home location, which means they’re at home a lot of the time.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What was the history of French colonization in Canada? When did it occur, how long did it last, and what happened after the British regained control of Canada?
Answer: In 1534, Jacques Cartier, working for France, was sent on a mission to find a western route to Asia. Like other European explorers, he thought he had found it, but he was actually in what we now know as “Canada” Cartier managed to tick off the local First Nations by kidnapping their chief, and the natives clearly understood Cartier was claiming the land for a foreign power, but all’s well that ends well and they eventually agreed to trade if he brought back European goods. Cartier returned in 1535 and found what we now call the St. Lawrence River, which he was sure was a passage to Asia. Unfortunately, he found rapids near what’s now Montreal that barred his way, but he thought the way to Asia lay just over them. He decided to winter over as Marseilles, which is at the same latitude as Montreal, has mild winters, but that was a near fatal miscalculation and soon his crew was freezing and dying of scurvy. Luckily for him, the local First Nations recognized the disease and had a treatment - boiled cedar bark. Recovery from scurvy is nearly instant once you get Vitamin C so he survived the winter and made it back to France. However, about the only good news Cartier had was that the First Nations had lots of fur to trade. Furs were a valuable commodity in the 16th century as the population of fur bearing animals in Europe, particularly the beaver, had been reduced by overhunting to near extinction level. But France didn’t put a priority on their new lands, but no-one else showed up either. There were fur trading expeditions, but they were small scale and weren’t meant to create a permanent population. All that changed with Samuel de Champlain. In the early 17th century (starting in 1601), Champlain travelled to North American to make maps with larger expeditions and learned more about the geography of the area and previous French attempts to explore it. He also started looking at previous attempts to colonize the area, and learned about dealing with the First Nations from the expedition leaders. He spent the next several years in North American looking for a permanent site for settlement, even as far away as Cape Cod. Finally, the merchant who had the French monopoly on the area’s fur trade came to Champlain with a request that he find an appropriate site for a permanent settlement on the St. Lawrence. When Champlain arrived at a narrow point in the river with high cliffs all around, he couldn’t think of a better site than what the First Nations of the area called “The Narrows” or “Quebec”. Champlain, after narrowly escaping assassination, gave his men orders to build houses out of the numerous nut trees in the area. Champlain stayed there to administer the new colony for the rest of his life. But “Quebec City” grew slowly and by 1665 (57 years after being founded), the colony only had about 550 people, and about a quarter of those were members of religious orders. Almost all the women were nuns who ran the hospital. For the next century, almost all of the activity in the colony was related to the fur trade. That discouraged widespread settlement as ships coming to Quebec and it’s upstream neighbour, Montreal, carried bulky manufactured goods and returned with smaller quantities of expensive furs. More settlers also meant more piracy in the fur trade. By 1754, Quebec City only had 8,000 residents and there were only about 80,000 Europeans mostly scattered around the coast, the St. Lawrence River and the Ottawa River, although some enterprising French people established settlements in the Great Lakes, like Sault Ste. Marie (settled in 1668) The British had often made attempts to seize Quebec, even as early as the 1600s when Champlain got the British to agree to abandon it after it was captured by privateers. During the French and Indian War, Quebec City was the base for most of the French military activity in North America. However, in 1759 it was captured by the British and in the subsequent peace treaty, France ceded the colony to Great Britain. That completely ended France’s involvement in the development of the area. After the American War of Independence, thousands of British loyalists fled to Canadian territory and Great Britain had little choice but to keep it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What challenges do late-round draft picks like Kalen King face when competing for a spot on an NFL team's roster?
Answer: Getting drafted into the NFL means you’re good. About 224 players are drafted every year out of a pool of 16,000 college players who have either declared or have used up their eligibility. That’s fewer than 2% of all college football players. But college teams are allowed to have huge rosters - up to 105 players (although you can’t dress all of those for a single game). In the NFL, the roster is 53 players, plus another 17 on the practice squad. There are only 32 teams, so league wide, that’s 2,240 players. But unlike college, there’s no limit to how long you can play, although the average NFL player is on a team for less time than the average college player (3.3 years). But the only guaranteed open spot on a roster is from players who retire. Most players leave the league because they get cut. The salary cap is a big reason why players get cut because rookies can be paid less (the minimum wage depends on how long you’ve been in the league). That’s good news if you’re a rookie. But let’s face it - a team only needs 22 starters (plus kickers), so most roster spots are for back ups. As a late round pick (King went in the 7th round) King is unlikely to be considered for a starter spot, so he’s competing for a backup spot, and that’s almost certainly already filled. Last year, the Packers carried seven cornerbacks on their full roster. Five of those were backup spots. None of them appear to cause problems with salary caps. And King himself poses problem. He declared as a junior - maybe a good idea to make a quick buck (he will get decent money even if he gets cut) but hardly something that’s going to impress the coaches. So a lot of late rounders have to make themselves useful in other capacities, usually on special teams. That’s a high risk proposition - special teams players (even with the upcoming new kickoff rules) are at higher risk of injury. Moreover at 5′11″, 190 lb., he’s not exactly the guy you want as a blocker so he might get one of the more dangerous jobs, like covering gunners off the line (or being a gunner). But one of the problems is that the Packer already have a good corps of cornerbacks as they seem to have a knack for finding talent at the position. He might suffer in the numbers game.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the reasons for some countries not liking Israel, despite it being a democratic country that values human rights and allows freedom of religion for all citizens?
Answer: Well, yes, Israel is a democracy. So is the United States. On the other hand, in any independent assessment, they don’t actually rank that well This is from Democracy Index Israel is the lowest ranked “Working Democracy” Freedom house, which looks at rights, gives Israel a middling score But all of these ratings suffer from one overwhelming problem - Israel effectively controls a territory of roughly equal population who don’t get to vote in Israeli elections. Technically, back in the 1980s, South Africa was a democracy, and so were its Bantustans, essentially a “reserve” for native people. Nowadays, South Africa has universal suffrage and all citizens get to vote. The irony is that Israel relies heavily on cheap Palestinian labour to keep its economy going. Many of your “Made in Israel” goods were actually made in Palestine by Palestinians. Should I use the word “apartheid”. Well, Archbishop Tutu, who is an expert on the subject, definitely did. And that’s from the Jerusalem Post, which is a center right publication that’s not always sympathetic to Palestinian interests. And that’s from Andrew Feinstein, whose mother was Jewish, was involved in the South African anti-apartheid movement and also was an educator on the subject of genocide.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is tea made in China different from the tea we get in the US?
Answer: Maybe a bit, but not substantially. The Chinese used to have a monopoly on the cultivation of tea, but eventually that monopoly was broken. Tea is cultivated in a number of countries, but apart from China, it’s widely cultivated in India, Sri Lanka and Kenya. Tea isn’t that hard to cultivate - it’s even cultivated here in Canada. However, unless you get a lot of rain and sunshine, it doesn’t grow well. Although tea is cultivated in a few places in the United States, most American tea is actually cultivated in Argentina. However, Argentinian tea isn’t very good, so it doesn’t command a high price. Japanese tea, on the other hand, is excellent and people pay a premium for it, so the highest dollar value for imports is Japan even though it’s behind China and India in volume. Although the United States is a “coffee” country, tea is gaining inroads. It’s always been brewed strong, sweet and cold in the American south where it’s ubiquitous.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Are global languages such as English, Spanish, and French becoming standardized?
Answer: Quite the reverse. The more global a language is, the more likely it is to have local variation. All three of these languages show this. Even if you try to overlook the substantial differences between American English and British English, one of the countries that has the most English speakers is India, and in India they freely throw in terms from local languages that have no English equivalent. For example, Indian English is freely sprinkled with the word “lakh”, which means 100,000. In most of the English speaking world, that’s just “one hundred thousand”. Similarly, Quebec French and Metropolitan French have dozens of differences in vocabulary and pronunciation, and that gap is growing, not shrinking. Similar to how a portable phone is a “cell” in the USA but a “mobile” in the UK, it’s a “portable” in France but a “cellulaire” in Quebec, probably because a “portable” is a laptop computer, which in France is a “l’ordinature portable”. Finally, Spanish as it is spoken in Spain is different than the way it’s spoken in Mexico and Argentina, both of which have massive amounts of Spanish speakers. That being said, on a local level, English is becoming more standard. For example, the Canadian accent is practically the same from British Columbia to Eastern Ontario, and the British habit of dropping the terminal /r/ sound in words, which in the south was pretty much restricted to the eastern side of England, has spread throughout the west country as well. Even in the last fifty years you’re seeing fewer regional accents in both the UK and in the United States.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How do freshwater lakes get their water? Are there any lakes that do not drain into another body of water?
Answer: Freshwater lakes are essentially large rainwater reservoirs - big natural holes in the ground that collect water that flow into them. In addition to the body of the lake, every lake has a “watershed”, a group of rivers, creeks and streams that collect the water that falls within a certain area and eventually wind up in the lake. In addition to getting water from Lake Erie over Niagara Falls, Lake Ontario, the “lowest” of the five Great Lakes, also is fed by streams and rivers from both Ontario and New York before draining through the St. Lawrence River. In its early history about 12,000 years ago, Lake Ontario was much bigger as there was a glacier that blocked its water flow, so the water went through what’s now the Hudson River Valley. Note Lake Ontario is fed by other lakes, like New York’s Finger Lakes and Ontario’s Rice Lake.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the reason for French being spoken so much in Canada? Why is English not as dominant in Canada?
Answer: The first French speaking colony in what’s now Canada was established at what’s now Quebec City in 1608. It wasn’t until after the American War of Independence in the 1780s (over 150 years later) that large numbers of English speakers moved into what’s now Canada. Prior to that, the only English speakers were fur traders, and the number of those was kept as small as possible as to not dilute the profits to be made. By that time, French people had set up settlements all over what’s now Canada from the east coast to the west coast. For example, when Manitoba was founded in 1870, it was majority French speaking. French speakers remained the majority in Canada until well into the 1850s when immigration of English speaking immigrants from the British Isles started in earnest.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What makes immigration law a federal issue in the United States?
Answer: Article I, Section 8 of the United States Constitution, to wit: The Congress shall have power….To establish a uniform rule of naturalization… In other words, from the beginning, it was the federal government and not the states who got to make law about who got to live in the United States. That made sense. You didn’t want thirteen different governments making thirteen different rules about who could live where. One of the goals of the 1787 Constitution was to allow for the free movement of people through the country without internal barriers.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are some other notable risky play calls made in NFL playoff games throughout history?
Answer: At the end of the first half of Super Bowl XLIV between the Indianapolis Colts under Peyton Manning and the New Orleans Saints under Drew Brees, New Orleans, the underdog, was trailing 10–6. As they came out for the second half, they decided to do something that under the rules this year would be completely illegal - they made an onside kick. If the kick fails, the Colts get the ball around midfield and probably build on their lead. But it did work, and the Saints scored on a brilliant six-play 58 yard drive where they never even faced a third down. That put them up 13–10. However, the Colts, who figured to get the ball with the lead at the beginning of the half, were completely shell-shocked. Despite Manning moving the ball downfield for a touchdown in response to put the Colts ahead 17–13, that was the last time they scored all game. The Saints added a field goal, touchdown and 2 point convert to lead 24–17. And when the Colts tried to respond in the fourth quarter, Manning was intercepted for a pick-six that put the Saints up 31–17 with three minutes left. The TD after the onside kick was decisive.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: When was the NDP created in Canada? How has its ideology evolved over time, from being socialist to centrist politics? Is the NDP still considered a left-wing party, or has it shifted towards a more center-right stance?
Answer: It’s complicated, but the genesis of the NDP was the formation of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Alberta in 1932. Yes, there were socialists involved (and there still are for that matter), but a lot of the party was made up of farmers, cooperative movements, and labour interests. It made its big breakthrough in 1944 when the CCF under Tommy Douglas won the provincial election in Saskatchewan, and remained the government until 1964. The CCF started getting involved in federal politics in 1935, winning seven seats. However, in 1945 they grew to 28 seats, becoming the third largest party in the House. However, by 1956, the country’s two largest labour unions formed the Canadian Labour Congress, and actively sought out an alliance with the CCF. They finally met in 1961 and formed a new constitution under the name “New Democratic Party”. In its early days, the NDP largely did well in poor rural areas and in regions that were heavily unionized. However, over the years as demographics have changed and rural areas have gotten more conservative, the party appeals more to people who live in highly urbanized areas. And it’s still considered a left-wing pro-labour party despite the fact that the 1991 NDP government in Ontario went head to head with the public service union during a recession.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: If the universe is expanding faster than light, then why can we still see other galaxies?
Answer: The part of the universe we can see is referred to as the “Hubble Sphere”, which is the same distance in light years as the time that has passed since the initial expansion event, usually called the “Big Bang”. We’re not quite certain when the first galaxies started to form, but it was sometime between 200 million and 2 billion years after the “Bang”. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old and we can see galaxies to about 13.2 billion light years away. So, we can see galaxies that are within the 13.8 billon light years we can see because those galaxies, although travelling at a substantial fraction of the speed of light, still aren’t travelling away from us at a speed higher than the speed of light (those ones we can’t see and probably never will see). The Milky Way is also part of a group of 54 galaxies called the “Local Group”, many of which are actually travelling towards us. The Local Group is part of a bigger group of galaxies called the “Virgo Supercluster”, which is part of the Laniakea Supercluster, which is part of the Pisces-Cetus Supercluster Complex. But although the universe is 13.8 billion years old, it’s going to last “forever”, getting bigger all the time. In a trillion years or so, assuming we move to a red dwarf planetary system that can last that long, it’s likely that even the closest galaxies will be so distant it will be impossible to detect them by any means. Our ability to see about a trillion other galaxies as the moment is simply a historical accident caused by a bit of good luck.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the advantages of building an NHL arena in downtown Ottawa?
Answer: The Canadian Tire Centre is remote in the extreme. I believe it’s the furthest an NHL arena is from the city center. 22 minutes by car from the main train station. So what are the comparisons for the other central Canadian clubs? Well, here in Toronto, it’s a two minute walk, all inside In Montreal, it’s nine minutes on foot, although it’s closer to a Metro stop It takes about an hour by transit to get to the Canadian Tire Centre, which is really on the outskirts of the city, from downtown Ottawa.
