That really limits your fan base to people who can drive because hockey games can run late (particularly during the playoffs). Luckily, the stadium is getting long in the tooth (it’s 28 right now, older than Toronto’s Rogers Centre, home of the Jays). Ottawa is trying to get less suburban as it grows so quickly, and many cities, like Detroit, have also moved stadiums closer to the city center after experimenting with the suburbs.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What factors contribute to rich kids getting into Ivy League schools? Is it solely based on their wealth, intelligence, or a combination of both?
Answer: Okay, say you want to get into Harvard. They let in about 1,800 students a year to their undergraduate programs. So they have a screening process. They set certain minimum GPA and SAT requirements. If you don’t meet those, you’re out. Both are incredibly high, but not high enough to only have 1,800 people qualify. After that, they need to see something special about you. One is that you’re from some sort of disadvantaged minority - black, Hispanic, American Indian, bad zip code, farmer, that sort of thing. Few students meeting this description actually meet the first hurdle. Next is that you’re talented - athlete, performer (they have an orchestra) Then there’s the last one - did either of your parents go to Harvard? In other words “affirmative action for rich people”. About a third of new undergraduates get in on this criteria. And it’s very disruptive. Back in the 1980s, I visited Colgate, which also uses “legacies” to qualify undergraduates. However, Colgate used to be a males only school, but went co-educational in 1970. The next cohort of undergraduates was twice as large as the one before, and even by the early 1980s the campus’s facilities were still too small to hold all of them.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the relationship between Pakistan and Israel? Why does Pakistan recognize Tel Aviv as the capital of Israel instead of Jerusalem?
Answer: Okay, first and foremost, only a handful of countries recognize Jerusalem as the capital of Israel. Almost all the countries that recognize Israel keep their embassies in Tel Aviv. The official position of the United Nations and most of Israel’s allies is that Jerusalem is a split city and Israel doesn’t have complete sovereignty over it. Second of all, Pakistan does not recognize Israel and has never had diplomatic relations with it. It’s not that Pakistan has never cooperated with Israel, but it’s mostly informal and both sides use their embassy and consulate in Turkey as an intermediary. Pakistan voted against the 1947 partition plan, as did India. Pakistan is on record that it will not recognize Israel sovereignty until Israel recognizes Palestinian sovereignty over all the land that was not part of Israel before the Six Day War of 1967, including recognizing East Jerusalem as the capital of Palestine. However, if those conditions are met, Pakistan says it will fully recognize Israeli sovereignty over the territory within its pre-1967 borders. Conversely, Pakistan not only recognized Palestine before the Oslo Accords (1993) by recognizing Palestine on November 15, 1988, recognizing the Palestinian Authority the following day, and extending full diplomatic relations since late 1989. The Palestinian Authority has had an embassy in Islamabad since 2017.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Since US food is considered so bad by snobbish Europeans, should the US stop all its massive food aid programs all over the world?
Answer: Absolutely! U.S. food aid is pretty much a disaster for countries that really need money.; Here’s the deal. U.S. food aid is pretty much a subsidy for agricultural producers. It gives the United States government an opportunity to give away food it has already paid for, for free, without worrying about it further depressing prices in the market. For example, in the Indian Ocean tsunami, the United States shipped a lot of rice to the nations affected by the tsunami. The United States produces a lot more rice than it consumes, but there’s no export market for it because other countries either have no problems growing what they need to feed their own population (China, India) or the cost of rice production is heavily subsidized (Japan). Anyway, rice keeps for a long time so the United States had plenty, but here’s the thing - rice production wasn’t affected at all by the tsunami. All the U.S. rice did was depress rice prices for domestic Asian producers, throwing the market into turmoil. Even worse, a lot of the food just helps support dictatorships who have enough food, but keep it away from the people who actually grow it. For example, the Ethiopian famine was partly due to crop failures, but it was mostly due to the Ethiopian government taking food from where it was grown and sending it to the cities to keep the population from starting an insurrection against the government. During the Irish potato famine, there was plenty of wheat being grown in Ireland, but it was all being sent to Great Britain where people would pay more money for it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why is Jordan Peterson being prosecuted and persecuted for his non-compliance in gender pronoun rule/law of Canada? I tried asking someone, and the first time, they were incredibly offended! How does Canada intend to enforce such a terrible law?
Answer: Well, let’s correct all of your misconceptions. First, it’s not “Canada” persecuting him, and he’s not being prosecuted. Peterson is a member of the College of Psychologists of Ontario, which regulates clinical psychologists in the province. Peterson is a licensed critical psychologist. The proceedings are by the College against one of their members for professional misconduct. Secondly, he’s not being persecuted for non-compliance with gender pronoun rules. Peterson did make a lot of posts regarding his feelings that gender dysphoria isn’t really a condition, but he also made posts of a racist nature, complaints about overpopulation, and posts about the COVID pandemic. The college charged him with making posts that were sexist, racist, and transphobic and which were not backed by any current understanding of clinical psychology. For example, he insulted a plus sized model online, the one who was on the cover of Sports Illustrated. Peterson replied to the allegations by saying he realized he may have gone too far and was working on the issue with his own media advisors. The College didn’t think that was a good idea, and required him to go on a College approved course with respect to the use of social media. Peterson refused. It went to the screening panel which ruled that if he took the course, the matter would be stopped and he would not go on to a hearing facing charges of professional misconduct. The panel noted that despite warnings, Peterson just kept attracting formal complaints. The courts upheld the decision because otherwise professional bodies would have no power to control its members when they bring disrepute on their own profession. For example, the College of Physicians and Surgeons is in the middle of disciplining several physicians who spread COVID myths online, including one physician who granted vaccine exemptions without doing a medical examination or finding any sort of medical reason the person could not be vaccinated. So what if Peterson keeps it up? He loses his clinical psychologist license, which he isn’t using anyway because he stopped seeing patients seven years ago.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why do we have to pay insurance for a vehicle in Canada?
Answer: Well, you don’t live in Manitoba or British Columbia obviously - their insurance is worked into the gas tax, which means people who drive more pay more. But in the rest of the country, schemes to compensate innocent people injured in automobile accidents, generally with some sort of “non-insured fund” where the fund would pay you then try to collect from the uninsured driver consistently cost the government money as the people in the uninsured group tended to be the drivers with the highest insurance premiums. But the easy answer is “driving causes a lot of property and personal damage every year”. In 2022, there were over 74,000 automobile accidents in Ontario alone. That year, 359 people died in those accidents. That number just keeps going up. Statistics Canada keeps track of the costs of accidents, In 2020, that was Just under $36 billion adjusted to 2010 currency (which is the base year for comparison). That’s nearly 2% of the country’s total gross domestic product, and about $0.10 for every kilometer driven. Fully 3/4ths of that was the cost of injuries and fatalities. Only about 11% was property damage. Economists call these costs “externalities” - costs paid by society that aren’t charged to the person who causes the costs. Insurance doesn’t cover all of that.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why are democrats so against school vouchers?
Answer: So let’s say you’re a Sikh and you run a kitchen that feeds anyone who wants a meal. You rely on donations and volunteers. That’s pretty much the way the public school system works, except its paid for in taxes and it’s able to provide everyone with an education because it has economies of scale. But let’s say that one day that someone comes to your kitchen and doesn’t like the food, so they ask for something else, then demands that your kitchen pays for it. That’s a voucher system - it requires the state, which already runs a perfectly adequate system, to subsidize your preferences. Now, under the current system, you’re perfectly entitled to pay for a meal elsewhere, but you don’t want people getting free food on donations. It’s even worse. Many states allow you to take a tax credit for any additional tuition you pay, and the federal government also allows you to deduct it separately - two tax deductions for the price of one. The total savings from those deductions can be more than what the state gave you in value for your voucher. As such, there’s no incentive to support the public system, so spending on it goes down, which means you lose the economy of scale you get from a fully public system. The public system tends to only get students who can’t get into “choice” schools, and those students tend to be more expensive to teach, like students with learning disabilities. In addition, it turns out charters often make a profit,. and often don’t do as well as the public system did. If they do do better, it’s because they cherry pick students who will do well.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How many rivers flow from Canada into the United States, excluding those that are part of the same watershed as another U.S. bordering river (such as the Niagara River)?
Answer: There aren’t that many The Columbia - The river that gives “British Columbia” its name starts in glacial fields in the Rocky Mountains in British Columbia, but crosses the border into Washington and empties near Astoria, which is just on the Oregon side of the Washington/Oregon border The Stikine - This short river starts in British Columbia, but crosses into Alaska before entering the Pacific. The Taku - Another river that starts in British Columbia and crosses over the Alaska panhandle The Alsek - The sources is in British Columbia and crosses into Alaska The Milk - It starts in Alberta and eventually feeds into rivers that feed the Missouri. The Missouri - A tiny part of the Missouri’s watershed is in Saskatchewan But that’s pretty much it. East of Saskatchewan the water generally flows into Canada, like the Red (starts in North Dakota, but goes to the Arctic Ocean through Manitoba) and the Richelieu (which starts in the United States at Lake Champlain and empties into the St. Lawrence River).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Do you think there should be separate tracks for bicycles on roads?
Answer: Well, let’s look at it this way. There’s simply no way to address traffic except by getting fewer people to drive. Traffic congestion is not directly related to the amount of traffic. Small drops in the amount of cars can lead to much faster travel times, but small increases can lead to much slower travel times. Now the good news is that the majority of trips taken by car are under five miles (8 km) That’s a distance that can probably be travelled easier by bicycle than by car. But there are two major problems This is Great River Road in Brainerd, MN, one of the cities that’s had the most written about its traffic. This used to be the main business district and you can see the buildings on the right are very old - most from the 1930s. Pretty much the rest of the business district was torn down to widen the highway which has a speed limit of 35mph (about 60 km/h. It looks like it might have a bike land there, but that’s parking for the stores. Now despite being signed at 35mph, if you drive this stretch you will probably only make about 10 mph (15 km/h) because of all the stop lights, which are very long because the road is very wide and crosses other very wide roads. And Brainerd is small, about 6km x 5km. You could easily bike anywhere you wanted to go if you didn’t have to worry about the cars. But it applies just about everywhere. Here’s a place I go to all the time, and I’ve driven, taken transit and even walked the distance - just over 5km. As you can see, in the congested part of downtown Toronto, both transit and biking are faster. I walk it solely for the exercise because that’s just too slow. To be fair, Bloor Street has a really good bike path, and there are bike sharing facilities at both ends of this route. But if you’re on your own bike, here’s what faces you when you arrive Yes, there is a giant parking lot (and it has two levels underneath) but no bike parking. Like I’ve said, I have driven this route (sometimes I’m bringing back a few cases of soda), but most of the time I’m travelling lighter and easily take my haul back on transit.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is tougher policing on the streets a better deterrent to stop crime than capital punishment?
Answer: Not really no. “Tougher policing” usually results in more people being arrested and incarcerated for minor crimes, which means confidence in the police force is drastically reduced, which means the population doesn’t trust the police, which often means they turn to gangs to protect them. Baltimore tried such an approach, tying police officer performance to the number of arrests made, but this led to a massive increase in arrests for minor crimes (driving a bike without lights was one of the favorites) and targeting minority communities because rich white people sue when this sort of thing happens to them. As a result, crime went up as victims refused to cooperate with the police as most of them had negative interactions with them. Conversely, Philadelphia’s police force had been problematic since the early 20th century when they became the inspiration for the Keystone Kops. They hit their all time low when they set fire to an entire block of row houses in an attempt to drop a “non-lethal bomb” on a house occupied by a gang. After that, they started more community policing initiatives, taking officers out of well fortified police stations and putting them in abandoned corner stores. It worked and Philadelphia’s police force got what it needed all along to fight crime - cooperation from the people they were policing.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Who are some of the most notorious criminals in Canada?
Answer: Probably at the top of the list is serial rapist-murderer Paul Bernardo In 1995, he was convicted of two counts of each of first-degree murder and aggravated sexual assault and was sentenced to life imprisonment with no parole for 25 years. He has since been declared a dangerous offender so it’s unlikely he will be released (he’s currently 61 years old). In addition to the crimes he was convicted of, he appears to have committed a number of other sexual assaults between 1987 and 1990, often with the help of his wife Karla Homolka, who was sentenced to (and served) twelve years for her part in the crimes and currently resides in Quebec. One of the victims was Karla’s younger sister, whose death was originally ruled an accident caused by vomiting while under the influence of alcohol and pills. To make it worse, someone else was convicted of one of the murders that was almost certainly committed by Bernardo and served several years in prison before being exonerated.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why does America have a gun culture when many other developed countries do not?
Answer: Someone mentioned the revolution, and that’s part of it, but it doesn’t explain why the culture stuck around. Lots of countries have had revolutions. Hell, England had a revolution. But America’s big problem has always been getting along with its neighbours - the Native Americans and the Spanish. Americans have had a habit of taking land that clearly wasn’t theirs, like most of North America and bits of Mexico. And those people tended to fight back. Particularly the Indians who weren’t in the least bit hesitant to kill anyone who made trouble in what they felt was their territory. As the United States expanded westward, they needed guns because they simply couldn’t make peace with the Indians. The Canadians, who faced the same problem, could make peace with the Indians and sent cops, not soldiers. The Canadian cops broke up booze smuggling and arrested people who killed Indians. The American army looked the other way. You also had a paranoid culture in the south that treated slaves so poorly, they had the idea that if they ever lost control the slaves would immediately set about killing them. That didn’t happen of course, but one of the first gun control laws after the Civil War was to prohibit former slaves from owning weapons. This backfired of course. The modern gun rights movement can be traced back to the Black Panthers, who carried weapons to protect themselves from the police, saying it was their constitutional right to do so. No one had ever made that claim before. At first, white people passed more laws to control guns, but later, they said “if you can’t beat them, join them”. Another thing keeping it alive is the gun industry. Americans have always embraced profitable businesses. Gun manufacturers have always pressed the dangers around everyone, and in the 1960s they started really putting the pedal to the metal as increasing urbanization generally made gun ownership seem unwise. Did you know that Ty Cobb’s mother shot her husband thinking he was a burglar? To be fair, he was trying to spy on her because he suspected her of sleeping around. And the biggest country to have a civil war was China. At many times, China didn’t have enough guns for everyone in its army. Right now, you can’t get a gun for private use in China unless you get a permit for hunting or gun sports. Russia had a massive civil war too, and anyone can own a gun, if you pass a gun safety course and a background check. Oh, except handguns, unless they’re non-lethal.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can you explain the process of chemical reactions with water and why the chemicals do not dissolve in it?
Answer: Water is a pretty good solvent, but as anyone who has tried to make a vinaigrette knows there are just some liquids that won’t dissolve in water, not to mention a large amount of solids. So what’s the difference? Well, it all comes down to attraction - is a molecule of what you’re trying to dissolve more attracted to water molecules, or molecules of their own kind. For example, salt dissolves in water because sodium and chlorine ions would much rather be attached to a water molecule than a sodium or chlorine molecule. In fact, if you leave salt in a humid environment, it will “cake” as the few water molecules form stronger bonds than the sodium and chlorine atoms do with themselves. Salt is largely free flowing because the way chlorine and sodium form crystals mean they really don’t feel obliged to attach to any other salt crystals they come in contact with. Water has this property because it has both positive charges and negative charges, while for most molecules those charges are perfectly balanced out, and for most ions they’re either entirely negative or entirely positive. That’s because of water’s weird structure where the hydrogen atoms are close to each other on one side and absent on the other. By contrast, Carbon Dioxide doesn’t have this property. It equals out the charges so that the molecule itself has pretty much the same charge in each direction. In water, the hydrogen side seeks out negatively charged ions (like chlorine) and the oxygen side seeks out positively charge ions (like sodium). By contrast, iron won’t dissolve in water because each individual iron atom is strongly tied to other iron atoms. Iron atoms will react with oxygen molecules (slowly) but not with the oxygen side of a water molecule. Similarly, this vegetable oil molecule here would much rather stick to other oil molecules, although it will also stick to water molecules - it just prefers sticking to oil molecules. As such, even if you shake up the oil in the water, when the tiny oil globules touch each other, they stick together, and since oil is a good deal less dense than water, it floats to the top. Of course, then you have pure metallic sodium. Oxygen molecules in water would much rather be attached to a sodium atom than the hydrogen atoms, and this attraction is instant and gives off a lot of heat, also leaving the hydrogen behind, which usually reacts with other oxygen in the atmosphere to form new water. Kaboom!

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are some reasons why people may stop taking prescribed medication without consulting their doctor?
Answer: In countries with a functioning health care system (i.e. not the United States), patients often stop taking prescribed medication for two reasons. So let’s discuss my personal experience. For the first, I had an undiagnosed ulcer when my gall bladder surgeon figured out I had one. Eating hurt so much I had lost 30 pounds. I was given seven doses of medication to see if the problem would go away. After day four, my appetite had returned and the pain was gone. Someone else might have said “I’m cured! I can stop taking the medication!” I knew better and finished all the doses. For the second, I had been on a couple of blood pressure medications with varying degrees of success when my doctor started me on something new. He warned me that I should NOT stop taking the medication for any reason as my blood pressure might skyrocket. My pharmacist said the same thing and told me of his aunt, who had stopped taking the same medication against his direct advice, then had a stroke and died. She stopped the medication because one of its side effects is it makes you feel tired, and that goes away when you stop the medication. Loads of medications have terrible side effects, while the main side effect is “you stay alive”. A lot of people on medication for their mental health stop taking it because it substantially changes their personality. For example, a person with manic depressive illness is satisfied that the depressive episodes are gone, but comes to miss the manic episodes where they had lots of energy and creativity.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the costs involved in constructing and maintaining a new subway line? How do these costs vary between cities and countries?
Answer: Toronto is currently working on two subway lines The Ontario Line will be just under 16km long and updated estimates have put the construction and early operating costs at $19 billion, about double the original estimate. The Line 2 extension will run just under 8 kilometers, but it will be a bargain at about $5 billion. Calling it $1 billion a kilometer wouldn’t be out of line. But tunneling is just one of the costs. In fact, building the new stations are one of the most expensive parts of the process. In the early days of Line 1, stations were constructed almost entirely underground and only had tiny street exits to ground level. However, many modern stations have to have room for bus platforms, which means they have a large above ground footprint. For example, here’s one of the entrances to Museum Station on Line 1. There are two others that are similar. And this is Warden Station at the eastern end of Line 2. Most of it is above ground (you can see the tracks) and there’s a massive bus bay (center right) which is going to be demolished soon because it’s not handicap accessible. There’s also a small parking lot. Also look at the bus entrance at bottom left that makes left turns into the station unnecessary, as well as a pedestrian bridge to a much larger parking lot and a housing development. Stations like these are expensive. The existing station at University and Queen (known as Osgoode after the nearby law courts) is like most in downtown Toronto, but the new Ontario line, which runs under Line 1, requires a completely new entrance to avoid disruptions to Line 1 service (any construction on the existing station would shut down the entire line) That requires two at grade buildings and a complicated set of escalators to get you down to the proper level. But even existing stations are inadequate. Yonge Bloor station was never intended to be a junction for two subway lines so the construction was more or less jury rigged when the new line was put in in the early 1960. It already underwent one redevelopment in the 1990s to widen the platforms, but that’s still inadequate as now the Line 2 platform is just too narrow to handle the crowds. Over $1 billion will be spent on new platforms and entrances.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why don’t the wealthy agree to pay more taxes? They are still able to afford their luxury such as a yacht?
Answer: This is Abigail Disney As you may have guessed, she’s quite wealthy. Walt Disney was her great uncle. She admits she grew up in a life of privilege as the Disney Corporation became larger and richer, which mostly happened after Walt died and the business started charging more for its theme parks and expanding its media empire. I believe she got one of those art degrees that everyone tells you is so useless. Now, she’s never done any animation and pretty much did anything she wanted while her trust fund paid the bills. But she will tell you that while she was growing up it was ingrained into her by both her family and their advisors that government would waste any money that it got its hands on. Giving money to the government was like permanently throwing it away, never to be seen again. The equivalent of burning the damn stuff. Rich people and businesses she was told, used their money frugally and efficiently, and their output provided far more beneficial output for regular people than the government could ever do. In fact, it was your duty to avoid paying taxes and to lobby for laws that allowed you to keep as much of it as humanly possible. Abigail Disney no longer believes this of course, and is one of the biggest advocates for higher tax rates on wealthy people like her. In fact, one of the issues is she really doesn’t control her fortune - it’s all administered for her and her brother (and they’ve been in litigation with each other, and Abigail once sued her trustees about the way her money was being administered).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why are most wealthy people very frugal?
Answer: Well, this is a massive myth, and one place you can see it very clearly is Monaco. Monaco only has rich people living there because the tiny country provides pretty much nothing in the way of social services. However, as you can see, the harbor is full of yachts and if you look at those cars they’re all high end luxury models. They’re all parked illegally too because private parking is prohibitively expensive. Yes, you hear stories about how Warren Buffet has lived in the same house for forty years and drives an old beat up car. But here’s his private jet. To be fair, it was built in 1986, but it’s still a private jet. Donald Trump has a much larger private jet, and he can’t even afford to keep it in the air. In case you have not owned an airplane of any kind they’re extremely expensive to store and maintain. Speaking of yachts, about $4 billion worth of new ones are sold every year. That’s more than the nominal GDP of about thirty countries. And if you think planes are expensive to maintain, you’ve obviously never owned a boat. And although it might not sell for this price, here’s the most expensive home listing in Toronto - a condo on the 80th floor of “The One”, the city’s currently tallest residential building. All yours for a mere $34 million. I think it’s a bit of a rip off because you can get this much larger single family home for a measly $29 million. By comparison, the average house in the Greater Toronto Area goes for about $1.1 million. If you say “but it’s a good investment”, you obviously haven’t been reading about forced sales in the real estate news recently. Just ask Michael Jordan what he will take for his mansion, which has been on the market for (checks) ten years.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What happens to a society, when the men of that society are constantly rejected, looked down upon, and undervalued?
Answer: Author Susan Faludi looked at this very issue in her book “Stiffed: The Betrayal of the American Man” But you have to realize that the people who caused this problem were other men. In other words, although some men have blamed the rise of women and people of color for their problems, it’s clear that men have been betrayed by the rich, who in the past promised them employment for loyalty but instead shut down massive sectors of the economy when it turned out to be cheaper to ship the jobs abroad. It’s not like the highly educated were left out of this either - when aviation companies shut down, some of the smartest people in the United States found themselves out of work for the first time. “The Simpsons” is actually a throwback to a lifestyle that was actively dying when the show premiered in the late 1980s. Homer Simpson is a high school graduate whose salary can support his stay-at-home wife and three kids in a single family home. The series itself lampshaded this with the character Frank Grimes - a much better educated man who couldn’t dream of the lifestyle Homer takes for granted. The result has been that men have pretty much blamed everyone except the people who are actually at fault - other men. Rich men. Men who want for nothing. Men with 20 cookies who will give you one and tell you to watch out for the guy without any cookies whatsoever. And, if you’ve seen “Barbie”, Ken is a guy who is clearly underprivileged who learns about “The patriarchy” and how men are in charge everywhere, leading him to the conclusion that he should be in charge because he’s a man. Barbie has no-one to blame but herself as she realizes that she’s ignored Ken as a human being and realizes Barbieland can only survive if Kens have the same rights as Barbies.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the purpose of canals or rivers in cities? Is it just for aesthetic purposes?
Answer: Until about 200 years ago, the only way to economically transport low value high volume goods, like grain, was over water. That’s why a lot of big cities either sit on a river, or are where a river meets a larger body of water like a lake or an ocean. For example Tokyo Delhi and Shanghai The three largest metro areas on the planet are all next to a river. Other major cities on or near a river are London (on), Paris (on), New York (near), and even St. Petersburg (more on that later). Navigable rivers allow you to trade all the way to where the river meets falls or rapids, which explains why Montreal is where it is The Lachine Rapids drop about 30 feet from Lac de Deux Montagnes to the Port of Montreal, which means ships can’t use that channel. Back in the 1840s, you can see what they built to get around them, the Lachine Canal. The Lachine uses a series of locks to raise boats to the lake, after which there are more locks on both the St. Lawrence River and the Ottawa River allowing barge type vessels to take goods to Ottawa, Toronto and beyond. But in 1959, they built an even better canal for larger ships which is still in commercial use, the St. Lawrence Seaway. That and two other canals allow ships to get all the way to Minnesota. The St. Lawrence Seaway through Montreal, on the far right and bottom of the picture - longer and wider than the Lachine, it can carry ocean going ships. Because controlling a river is so important to trade, many river deltas have been completely changed to ensure control over the waterway. To allow the water to continue to flow through, several channels are dug that serve double duty as drainage and transportation corridors. For example: St. Petersburg Amsterdam Now, railroads made lots of canals obsolete. Railroads don’t require a constant flow of water, and it’s easier to run a rail line over a gorge than a canal, although it is possible. The Pontcysyllte Aqueduct in Wales finished in 1805. Now only used for recreational purposes. 38m above the River Dee, it’s the highest navigable aqueduct in the world. But lots of canals have fallen into disuse, like these ones in Quebec that were replaced by the St. Lawrence Seaway Old lock on the Soulange Canal, north of the St. Lawrence River. The Newmarket Canal, obsolete while it was being built in the late 19th century. But for a lot of cities, the river is their lifeblood - their reason for being. The Detroit River, as it goes by Detroit (right) and Windsor, Ontario (left). The river allowed the raw materials for car manufacturing to be easily shipped to automobile factories, and allowed the finished product to be shipped by sea as well.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is Edgar Wright going to do to The Running Man remake that is more "outrageous" than the original?
Answer: Well, I have not seen “The Running Man”, but I have seen all of Edgar Wright’s movies, so I have a pretty good idea. As I understand it, in the dystopian future, convicted criminals are given a chance at freedom by participating in a televised show where they try to escape confinement while being hunted down by professional assassins. No one ever makes it, but the audience has fun betting on the outcome. But in the movie, wrongfully convicted ex-policeman Ben Richards is given his chance on the show. He performs better than expected. He performs so well that for the first time, the audience starts to root for him to escape and asks to bet on him to score the next kill. So who is Edgar Wright? Well, he’s a youngish British director who got his start in British television, moved onto comedies, and then made a car chase movie and a psychological thriller. His trade mark is insane attention to visual detail which provides clues to the audience about what’s going to happen next. He relies heavily on “callbacks”, references in the film to elements that had already been disclosed in previous scenes. For example: In Hot Fuzz, early in the film, our protagonist Nick Angel meets his new partner Danny Butterman who sits down to watch two movies with him - “Point Break” and “Bad Boys 2”. But later in the film, after Nick makes a narrow escape with the help of Danny, he stops at a convenience store and sees a rack of DVDs - featuring “Bad Boys 2” and “Point Break”, making him return to the dangerous situation. Wright’s attention to visual style is legendary, allowing him to tell a story without dialogue through the way he frames a shot alone. Five old friends, from “The World’s End” The brass ganging up on you, from “Hot Fuzz” Complete and utter despair, from “The World’s End” A troubled team, except for a couple of people, from “Baby Driver” Confusion and despair, from “Last Night in Soho” Determination and absurdity, from “Hot Fuzz”. So enjoy the upcoming visual feast.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the biggest problem facing advocates of universal basic income?
Answer: It’s going to be expensive. There’s no sugar coating it. We’re talking levels of money similar to what governments regularly spend on old age pensions or health care. In theory, the benefits should cover the cost. We’re talking about more people actually getting involved in the workforce. We’re talking about people getting better educations. We’re talking about people moving away from places where there’s no economy to speak of to places where they have a chance to get a job. We’re talking about economic stimulus as well as essentially eliminating poverty, homelessness and reducing crime. Moreover, practically all the money in the program will be going to beneficiaries. The big problem with current anti-poverty programs is they don’t work, actually create disincentives to work and education, cost a fortune to administer, and give benefits that are impossible to transfer to another area of need (e.g. you can’t use SNAP benefits if your rent is due, or subsidized housing to get a bite to eat). UBI will probably cost more than all the anti-poverty programs but together (apart from old age pensions) but will most likely have collateral economic benefits that will pay for the program indirectly.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How do donations turn into votes? You cannot pay voters to vote for you.
Answer: Hi! I’m Joanie Noname, a candidate for the U.S. Senate. Well, I’m making a primary run against a well known local businessman and the former mayor of the state’s largest city, and whoever wins that primary goes up against the incumbent Senator who represents the other party. And you’ve never heard of me. And it’s “Noh-naym” not “No-na-mee”. Well, I think I would make a terrific candidate. I actually went to West Point and finished fourth in my class, and served as a logistics officer in Iraq during my four year hitch. After that, I got a master’s degree in education and taught school before making principal and deciding to get into the U.S. foreign service where I worked my way up to the Ambassador to Paraguay. Did I mention I speak fluent Spanish? After coming back and running the state department of education and moving the state up from 30th to 15th in the U.S. rankings in four years, I ran for the state senate and eventually became the majority whip. As such, a lot of people in the party know who I am and that I have the ability to get things done. Frankly, the businessman and the mayor are at odds with the party because they keep sucking up to businesspeople who support the other party and the mayor actually cut programs as an “austerity measure”. But you’ve heard of them. You haven’t heard of me. And the only way I’m going to win this primary and the senate race is if people learn who I am . Frankly, it’s going to be an ugly primary fight but the businessman has plenty of money for his own campaign and the mayor has lots of rich donors to support his run. We’re trying to put together a grass roots campaign starting with people who know me well who may be able to chip in a few bucks so we can do more fundraising. Because despite my qualifications in politics, there’s no way I’m going to win if no-one in my own party knows who the hell I am. I also expect the incumbent, who everyone knows, to fight dirty and avoid the issues. Even if I lose, it’s still going to cost a lot of money, and I just don’t have it. In 2022, the 33 Senate races saw a total of $3.1 billion in total spending, or about $100 million each. And this is a small state, but it doesn’t matter because all Senate seats count the same. And if I don’t raise money, the press will think I’m not really serious about winning. Honestly, six years ago, we lost this seat 51–49 so it’s clearly winnable for our side. If I don’t raise serious money, they will think I’m setting myself up to become governor or a later run for congress instead. And, yes, you can’t pay voters to vote for you. However, voters will vote for someone they dislike long before they will vote for someone they’ve never heard of.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why do you think the movies "Furiosa" and "The Fall Guy" failed to draw crowds?
Answer: Well, first and foremost, I would like to say I saw and enjoyed both movies. I thought “Furiosa” was a much better movie than “Fury Road”, and “The Fall Guy” managed to mash up an action movie, a whodunit, and a romantic comedy in a massively entertaining way. But to paraphrase Yogi Berra, if people don’t go to the movies, you can’t stop them. So, were these movies “bad” or just “not entertaining”. It doesn’t appear so So what went wrong? Well, marketing is most likely. In a nutshell, the movies you thought you were going to see are not the movies you actually saw. “Furiosa” is of course the follow up and prequel to the amazingly successful “Fury Road”. However, it’s still based on the “Mad Max” formula which although it was a cinematic breakthrough particularly on its miniscule budget, was pretty much abandoned in “Fury Road” for star power and spectacle. “Fury Road” was led by Tom Hardy and Charlsie Theron, both people whose movies you really want to see. Instead of relying on the previous Mad Max formula of interesting characters and deep character development, “Fury Road” focused on spectacle and cinematography. For “Furiosa”, which unlike the other four films takes place over a matter of years rather than days, we cut back on the star power and use a very talented Anya Taylor-Joy and a charismatic Chris Hemsworth. However, instead of focusing on spectacle, “Furiosa” focuses on character development, which makes it a very different film, so if you were hoping on non-stop action, I’m sorry, that’s not what this movie is about. That probably disappointed some people, just not me who liked the Mad Max films because of their insane focus on the characters. As for “The Fall Guy”, its loosely based on the old television series (which I loved) but if you thought it was going to be about stunt men who double as bounty hunters, you’re likely to be severely disappointed. Instead, the Fall Guy is a romantic comedy wrapped around a murder mystery wrapped around stunt performances, and against all odds, it totally works. Ryan Gosling is the “fall guy” three times over - he falls for Emily Blunt, he’s a stuntman, and he’s the patsy for a murder cover up - that’s three fall guys in one! Maybe the movie is just too smart, funny and action packed for its own good.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the reason for using an alphabet in most languages instead of a syllabary or other writing system?
Answer: Syllabaries are great if your language has a limited number of syllables, like Japanese or Inuktitut. Japanese has about a hundred, and Inuktitut has about forty, so it’s not difficult to come up with a written system to cover all cases, particularly when Inuktitut’s syllabary has a system to it. But if your language allows pretty much an unlimited number of syllables, it’s nearly impossible to have either a systemic or arbitrary set of symbols for them. English, for example, uses 15,000 different distinct syllables, and can possibly use over 100,000. Also, if you try to have a syllabary, it’s pretty much going to be unique to your language. If you have an alphabet, it’s fairly easy to adjust it to your language to make it fit, which means several alphabets, like the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, can be adapted across several languages, even if they’re unrelated. The Latin alphabet, used for the unrelated languages English and Spanish And again, for the two unrelated languages English and Turkish And, once again, for the two unrelated languages English and Vietnamese. The Cyrillic alphabet, used for the unrelated language Mongolian. Mongolian switched to Cyrillic about 90 years ago to replace their own, but difficult to use, alphabet.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are potential solutions to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict? Is dividing the land between the two sides a viable option?
Answer: Well, you got me on potential solutions, but trying to divide the land into “Israel” and “Palestine” was probably always impossible. Here’s what the UN had to work with when they tried to divide the land in 1947. As you can see, Jews were only a majority in one part of the country (near Tel Aviv, where they were about 70% of the population) but they were not the majority land owners in ANY part of the territory. The resulting partition map created a Jewish territory that was 55% Jewish and 45% Arab, and an Arab territory that was 95% Arab and 5% Jewish. The Arab territory was split up into four parts, and the Jewish one into three. As you can see, the Jewish territory in the south consists of land where there is pretty much no Jewish ownership or population whatsoever. Now, the demographics of the region have changed somewhat with most of Israel being inhabited by Jews with about 20% Arabs, and most of the West Bank and Gaza being inhabited by Arabs with about 10% Jews. The Israelis have no problem with their Arab population, but pretty much all the Jews living in Palestine are considered by the Palestinian Authority to be living their illegally. Moreover, the Jewish population, only 10% of the population of the territory, is widely spread through the West Bank. Now, Israel can dismantle those settlements. They did dismantle settlements in the Sinai when it was returned to Egypt, and in Gaza when it was handed over to the Palestinian Authority in 1993. However, the Israeli population of the West Bank and East Jerusalem, which are “over the green line” which was established as the provisional border by the Oslo Accords, just keeps growing and now stands at nearly 700,000. There is simply no way to draw a border around those areas, least of all one that the Palestinian Authority could accept. The other problem - land ownership between Jews and Arabs has barely budged since 1949. In 1950, Israel passed a law that meant Arab owned land in Israel would be held in trust, allowing Israel to lease the land without claiming ownership of it. Legally, that land is still owned by the Arabs who owned it in 1948 when the fighting started in earnest, and many Arabs have proof of their ownership. Arab Israelis can control their land, but other Arabs cannot, and that includes land that came under Israeli control after occupying the West Bank in 1967. The Palestinian Authority is probably not going to agree to any peace treaty that abandons those lands as most Palestinians have some sort of ownership link to lands now in Israel. Similarly, Israelis aren’t going to let Arabs into Israel to use their land unless they’re already Israeli citizens. Even though the Palestinian Authority has accepted Israeli sovereignty over its pre 1967 borders, it still does not accept that Israel controls land owned by Palestinians. That matter has to be settled, and its unlikely Palestine will accept compensation on behalf of its citizens. This land held in trust also includes land that’s clearly in Palestine and is now occupied by Israeli settlements.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How does Moscow’s public transportation system, including the Moscow Metro, compare to those in other major global cities in terms of efficiency and coverage?
Answer: Apart from being fantastically beautiful and good enough to rely on a daily basis, the Moscow Metro has one thing that most Metro systems lack. So let’s take a look at a map of Moscow’s Metro Take a look at that red circle .It’s important. Now let’s take a look at a scale map of London’s underground network If you look really close at the center of the map, you can see the “Circle Line”, which was cobbled together from other pieces of the system and shares tracks with other lines. But Moscow Metro’s Circle is much further out, which means it’s easy to get from any line in the system to any other line without having to go through the most congested part of the city. Almost every other metro system in the world is missing this. For example, in New York City, there is only one line that doesn’t go through Manhattan. Even for some trips between Brooklyn and Queens, it’s easier to go though the congested part of the system to get from one borough to the other. Chicago’s “EL” is egregiously bad in this respect with all interline transfers being in “The Loop”, which is the busiest part of the city. All of the lines on the Greater Toronto Area’s GO Train heavy rail system meet at Union Station, the city’s busiest transportation center. But in Moscow, the Metro isn’t just for trips from the city center to the suburbs. Because of that ring line that pretty much encircles the city, getting from any one part of the metro area to any other part is straightforward by subway and doesn’t require you to make a trip to the city centre. Paris comes closest, and it avoids concentrating lines in the city center, but it’s still difficult to navigate between points on the outside of the city even if they have metro coverage. You may hav eto make a couple of transfers to make the trip work.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What were the reasons for Quebec voting against independence from Canada, despite being mostly French speaking and having a smaller population than Ontario?
Answer: Well, for one thing, “mostly French speaking” doesn’t mean “entirely French speaking”. Despite English not being an official language in Quebec, 28.8% of people who live there don’t speak French as a first language, with English being most of that, but several other European and Native languages making up the difference. People who don’t speak French as a first language, including most immigrants and most First Nations and Inuit, overwhelmingly opposed to separation. Support for separation also wanes the closer you get to the Ontario border, with even French speaking regions of Montreal and the Outaouais leaning towards remaining in Canada. Montreal based companies, including two major banks (Royal and B of Montreal), a major financial institution (Desjardins) and several other companies (Power Corp., Dollarama, Metro Grocery Stores, Alimentations Couche-Tard. Saputo) have extensive links to the rest of Canada. Most people in Quebec also realize just how difficult sovereignty association will be in practice. Quebec is right next to the United States, and Canada would be separated. The St. Lawrence Seaway is pretty much an international waterway controlled by Canada and the United States, but it starts in Quebec at the Lachine Rapids. People in favour of sovereignty still want to use the Canadian dollar, free trade with Canada, freedom to work in Canada, and a voice in monetary policy. They know that Canada isn’t just going to hand those over.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Who is considered the best Governor-General in Canada and what were their notable achievements and contributions?
Answer: Despite two governors-general donating trophies for sports (Lord Grey and Lord Stanley), you really have to give it to someone who spent most of his time in Canada trying to settle differences between the French, English and Natives. He was incredibly popular and as a result we’ve named a ton of stuff after him. And he has the backbreaking name of Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava, or “Lord Dufferin” for short. Good looking fellow too Dufferin held the job from 1872 to 1878 under two prime ministers, one of whom, Alexander MacKenzie, pretty much hated his guts. Nevertheless, he was a natural diplomat and an excellent writer (a best-seller in fact). Feeling that previous governors-general had just sat on their butts in Ottawa, he made a point to travel throughout the country, including the new province of Manitoba. He spoke fluent French as well as English and actually enjoyed talking to regular people, making him incredibly popular. Perhaps his most notable accomplishment was to prorogue parliament when allegations of corruption were raised against Prime Minister John A. MacDonald, resulting in an inquiry that eventually forced MacDonald to resign. He established the Governor-General’s Academic Medals, which were awarded during his term, and morphed into the Governor-General’s Awards. And he may not have established a hockey or rugby football trophy, but he did start one for curling. When Quebec attempted to tear down its old city walls, Dufferin objected and led a movement to stop the demolition and restore the walls that had been removed. It’s probably why Quebec is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Here in Ontario, Dufferin Street in Toronto is named after him, as is Dufferin County northwest of Toronto.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the differences between the Parliamentary System and American democracy? What is your opinion on the Parliamentary System?
Answer: The major difference is that in Westminster systems, such as the UK, Canada and Australia, the executive is part of and consistently has to answer to the legislature. In the American system, which is shared with other republics like France, the executive is completely separate from the legislature and does not need to answer to it on a constant basis, although there is a mechanism to remove the president. For example, in the UK, the Prime Minister actually has to be in the House of Commons twice a week while it is in session to answer questions posed by members of parliament. The U.S. president is under no obligation to answer to the legislature at any point. But the big difference is what happens at budget time. If the UK government proposes a budget (or indeed any provision to raise or spend money) and it doesn’t pass, Parliament can be dissolved and there can be another election or, at least, a change of Prime Minister. If the U.S. Congress can’t agree on a budget proposed by the president, the government just gets shut down and everyone keeps their job.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are some notable NFL plays, both good and bad?
Answer: GOOD - The “Music City Miracle”. As much as it pains me as a Bills fan, this play was practiced and executed. The Bills had scored late to take a one point lead. However, there was only time for a kickoff as there wasn’t enough time on the clock to catch the kickoff and down the ball to get another play. However, the Titans had practiced a contingency play for just this situation all year, and when the Bills kicked off short, the ball receiver threw a lateral to a teammate near the sideline who had blocking in front of him and he ran for the winning touchdown. BAD - Rocket Screen - Super Bowl XVIII The heavily favoured Washington Redskins were down 7 points with 12 seconds left in the first half, but they were on their own twelve yard line. Coach Joe Gibbs remembered a play called “rocket screen” (a pass behind the line of scrimmage to the sideline) had gone for a long gain earlier that season. However, the team they had run that play against was the same team they were facing - the Oakland Raiders. The Raiders perfectly read the play and intercepted the pass for a pick-six putting them up by 14 going into the half. GOOD - Beastquake Leading by four points in the fourth quarter with about 3:40 left to play in the game from their own 32, the Seattle Seahawks were 2nd and 10 after no gain on the first play. The Seahawks, although playing at home, were underdogs as they won their division with a 7–9 record (to that point, the worst division winning record in history) and were playing the 11–3 Saints, who were just nosed out of first place in their own division. In an obvious passing situation, the Saints decided to play its linebackers wide leaving the center of the field open. The Seahawks attacked the center by handing the ball to Marshawn Lynch who used the lack of linebacker support to push through the initial tackling and find space, then accelerated quickly shedding tackles all the way for an amazing 67 yard touchdown run. BAD - The opening safety - Superbowl XLVIII In the comeback story of the year, the legendary Peyton Manning recovered from a neck injury to win the MVP award in 2014 and lead the Denver Broncos to the Super Bowl. However, on the first play from scrimmage, a miscommunication between Manning and his center resulted in the ball being snapped while Manning looked away and it was all Manning could do to rush back and cover up the ball to concede a safety. The Broncos never recovered and lost 43–8. GOOD - Plexico Burress’s go-ahead touchdown, Super Bowl XLII The 18–0 New England Patriots were heavy favorites over the 13–6 New York Giants, particularly due to the fact they had beat them in the final game of the regular season. However, late in the fourth quarter, the Patriots were ahead only 14–10 with the Giants pressing. However, on the previous play, Giants QB Eli Manning had shed a sack to throw a pass downfield to receiver David Tyree that Tyree caught on top of his helmet. That gave the Giants a first down on the Patriots fourteen with only 39 seconds left. It’s at that point that the Patriot’s defensive captain decided to go with an all-out blitz to try to force the the Giants back and perhaps end the game. However, Eli Manning spotted it and decided to target Plexico Burress who was facing single coverage. Burress ran deep into the endzone and caught a beautiful pass to put the Giants ahead. BAD - The Colt’s flea flicker, Super Bowl III The Colts were the heavy favourites against the New York Jets in the early NFL/AFL format of the first Super Bowls, the NFL had dominated. The Colts had only lost one game that year and had blown through the NFL championship while the Jets had struggled all year and eked out a win in the AFL championship. However, the Colts game plan wasn’t working against the speedy Jets defensive backs and late in the first half the Colts were trailing by more than a touchdown. In an attempt to kick start the team, they called a “flea flicker”, a fake run where the ball would be sent back to quarterback Earl Morrall who would throw it downfield for a big gain. Unfortunately, he missed a wide open receiver and tried to force it to another receiver and got intercepted. The Jets won the game 16–7.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the basis of Israel's claim to land in Palestine? Is there a dispute over the amount of land it has taken over?
Answer: Okay, this is going to get complicated, but here we go. On May 15, 1948, the United Kingdom, gave up all of its claims to the Palestinian Mandate, having refused to even attempt to implement a plan by the United Nations from the previous November that would have split the territory into roughly seven different territories, some of which would be controlled by the provisional Jewish government of the territory, and the others that would be controlled by the local Arabs. Jerusalem would be administered by the United Nations. Here’s the plan, but don’t worry, it won’t be important later. Slightly prior to this, realizing there would be chaos once the British left, the Americans offered to continue a trusteeship of the territory until a suitable partition plan could be worked out, but they had no illusions that this would be pretty much impossible. The day before, on May 14, the Jewish provisional cabinet declared independence at a ceremony in Tel Aviv. This was almost immediately recognized by the United States and by the end of the week, the Soviet Union had also recognized the new government, now known as “Israel”. Israel had no fixed territory and both Jewish and Arab militias had been fighting each other since the end of World War II, with the Jewish militias also taking aim at the British authorities. As such, on May 15, 1948, the territory above belonged to no-one. The Arab-Israeli war, which lasted from May of 1948 to January of 1949, involved the new nation of Israel and a coalition of local Arab militias assisted by the armed forces of surrounding Arab nations. At first, the Arabs dominated the conflict, but by November an influx of Jewish volunteers and weaponry turned the tide, forcing the Arab forces back. In January of 1949 they agreed to a cease fire. All sides agreed the armistice line was not to be considered a “border”, and the Arab allies consistently refused to recognize any of Israel’s claim to any of the land it now occupied. However, Israel’s allies an very quickly after, the United Nations recognized the blue area as Israel’s territory. In the absence of any agreement to the contrary. With the Arab nations refusing to come to the table to discuss a peace treaty, this became the de facto border of Israel for the next 18 years. In the meantime, about 700,000 Arabs who had been living in the blue territory had been forced out, mostly into the West Bank. To make matters worse, Egypt and Jordan essentially asserted sovereignty over the areas that they occupied, but refused to recognize the Arabs living their as citizens. Part of that was that Palestinian Arabs refused to swear an oath of loyalty to the King of Jordan. In any event, the people who lived in Palestine didn’t identify as Egyptian or Jordanian, and the United Nations recognized them as “refugees” and still does. During this time, from a diplomatic standpoint, Jordan was the official representative of the Palestinian people as most Palestinian refugees lived in Jordan or the Jordanian West Bank. This proved to be untenable so in 1964 the Arab League formed the Palestinian National Council as the official representative of the Palestinian people. Unfortunately, Jordan and Egypt did not recognize the territory they occupied as “Palestine” and as such “Palestine” became only the territory that was controlled by Israel. It’s not like the Arabs didn’t try. In 1967, they planned a war to take back Israel. However, the “Six Day War” was an absolute disaster and not only left Israel in complete occupation of the Palestinian Mandate, but the Golan Heights of Syria and the Egyptian Sinai as well. However, Israel made no attempt to annex these territories, although some Israelis, with the tacit support of the government, set up what are now called “settlements” - areas controlled by Israeli citizens with the help of the Israeli military. Through this time, the Palestinian National Council, through their military arm the Palestine Liberation Organization, started a terrorism campaign against Israel in both the occupied territories and Israeli targets abroad (for example, the PLO staged a kidnapping and murder of Israeli athletes at the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich). Another war in 1973 had no effect on the occupied territory, but it continued the shutdown of the Suez Canal (the Israeli’s occupied the west bank of the canal), but the 1973 was had been a close thing and by 1978 both the Israelis and Egyptians were willing to talk. This resulted in the Camp David accords where Egypt agreed to recognize Israel’s claim to its pre 1967 borders in return for the Sinai and cooperation against the PLO. But the terrorism continued and eventually the Israeli government, which had made it treason to talk to the PLO or the PNC, eventually planned a back door conference to be held between two Israeli representatives and a PLO representative under the cover of an academic conference in Oslo, Norway. The conference was successful and in return for a promise to return the occupied territories to the Arabs, the PLO recognized Israel’s claim to it’s pre-1967 borders, The Palestinian Authority was created as the territory’s provisional government and a framework was created to hand control to the PA from the Israeli military. Based on a promise that Israel would withdraw to its pre-1967 borders (the “Green Line”), Jordan dropped its claim to the West Bank and recognized Israel’s territory based on its pre-1967 border. However, there’s still no agreement 31 years later as Israel has built a wall which goes over the green line, and at present about 670,000 Israeli citizens live in the occupied territories, a number that grows every year. Israel did dismantle the settlements in the Sinai and in Gaza, but never the ones in the West Bank and East Jerusalem.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the reasons for universities not offering low tuition?
Answer: Well, back until the 1980s, governments were more than happy to contribute a lot of money to universities to keep tuitions low, but cutbacks in the late 1980s and going forward put a lot of universities in the unenviable position of having to raise money and tuition was the only variable they could control. Now, this hasn’t been universal. Lots of countries provide free or next-to-free tuition to their own citizens - France, Finland, Germany and Slovenia being some of the more notable ones. Part of the reason they can do this is that university in Europe is a “no frills” experience - little in the way of sports or amenities. But particularly in the United States, where you have a mix of public, non-profit private and for-profit private schools, there’s a massive variation in tuition for the same programs (here in Ontario, there are differences from school to school, but they tend to be on the small side). Moreover, many universities provide a massive amount of on-campus amenities to attract students, and many universities use tuition to subsidize their sports programs (a few universities make money on sports, for the rest it’s a massive money drain). There’s also the “prestige” factor. If Harvard (which has a massive endowment and a tiny number of undergraduate students) charged the same tuition as UMass (a public university), people wouldn’t believe it was “better” which, on several metrics, it isn’t. There’s actually very little correlation between what a school charges for tuition and student achievement.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What elements contribute to The Mask being considered one of the greatest films of all time, despite its seemingly absurd premise?
Answer: Well, “greatest of all time” is a bit of a stretch, but “way better than it had any right to be” is a decent description. Jim Carrey made both “Ace Ventura” and “The Mask” before the first film came out and made him a bankable star. “The Mask” showed “Ace” wasn’t a fluke and Carrey’s asking price shot up to $20 million, something the producers of “Ace II” could afford, but which the producers of “The Mask” thought better of to their later dismay. So why was “The Mask” so good? A really good screenplay The comic book version of “The Mask” was Hannibal Lecter level psychopath so the screenwriters (Michael Fallon, Mark Verheiden and Mike Werb) had the unenviable task of toning the character down substantially to get a screenplay Hollywood might just find money for. “The Mask” is a bit of a “Jekyll and Hyde” story to begin with, and the screenwriters borrowed heavily from horror movie depictions to develop a “Mask” who was there simply to live out his revenge fantasies and fight crime in the process. To this, they added a big romantic element where the main character bounces back and forth between a woman he feels he can only impress as the Mask, and another who he feels he will love him for himself. Our protagonist, Stanley Ipkiss, is wonderfully characterized as someone who puts up with a lot from his work but shows sparks of being something better. The story carefully takes Stanley through his dual life and wraps up satisfactorily without having something extraordinary happen to the character to get him off the hook. It also keeps subverting your expectations about what’s going to happen by having some marvelous twists. Jim Carrey At the time, Carrey was pretty much known as an above average sketch comedian with some skills as a stand up, but as his later career showed, Carrey is actually a pretty good actor who took his chameleon like career and used it to devise everyman characters who feel real. You would expect him to excel as the Mask, particularly with his outstanding ability to control his face, but it’s clear he can really sell Stanley too. Without Carrey, the character simply doesn’t work - you might as well get two actors to play the role (or Eddie Murphy). The supporting cast You have to remember when the film was made, Cameron Diaz was pretty much a complete unknown, this being her first movie role. However, someone saw her acting ability, particularly as the “straight man” in comedies (“There’s Something About Mary”, “Knight and Day”). Amy Yasbeck’s talent was already evident in “Men in Tights” and “Wings”. Perpetual foil Peter Riegert was great in the role of the Lieutenant hunting down the Mask, and Peter Green (who worked with Quentin Tarantino in “Pulp Fiction”) was a believable gangster.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can an American citizen become a Canadian citizen through marriage? What is the process for doing so and what are the requirements, aside from marrying a Canadian?
Answer: No. Marrying a Canadian citizen will get you a fiance visa and, eventually, permanent resident status, but like any other immigrant you have to go through the waiting period to be eligible for citizenship (I believe it’s ten years at the moment), then pass the citizenship exam. You still have to apply for your fiance visa (whether you’re married or not) outside of Canada (it doesn’t have to be in the US, but that would be easiest). Once you’re married you can get permanent resident status and can reside in Canada, but you can’t get citizenship in Canada unless you continue to reside here (although you aren’t trapped in the country - you can still be out of Canada up to about 180 days in any given year as long as you have a permanent address in Canada). But please note that Canada has absolutely no respect for the institution of marriage, which means even if your marriage is 100% legit, legal and binding (Nevada anyone?) you can still be turned down if the immigration authorities don’t think the marriage is bona fides (i.e. is just a “marriage of convenience”). Cohabitation is the best way to prove that.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can I earn a P.Eng anywhere in Canada while still a U.S. citizen?
Answer: Wow. So many wrong answers! Everyone seems to think the “P.Eng.” is some sort of academic degree. It is not. It is a professional license. Yes, you do need a bachelor’s degree in engineering from an accredited institution in order to start the process (masters degrees don’t count) but the good news is that all Canadian provincial regulators recognize all American ABET accredited programs as being the equivalent of Canadian programs. Now, as noted, each province and territory, 12 in all (Nunavut and the North West Territories share a regulator for the time being) issues its own licenses. Some of them have unique requirements. For example, Quebec requires you show French language proficiency, and Prince Edward Island requires you be resident in Prince Edward Island. However, none of the regulators require you to be a Canadian citizen or even a permanent resident. Now, after graduating from an accredited institution, you need to demonstrate that you have 48 months of experience (36 in Quebec) and go through what’s now called “Qualification based assessment”, demonstrating that your engineering experience has taught you the basic skills expected of a practicing engineer in your field. For example, if you work on buildings, you have to show experience with relevant building codes. On top of that, every province requires you pass an examination on law and ethics. The most common now is the NPPE, which is a computer invigilated examination. So, as a U.S. citizen and resident, neither of those is any barrier to getting a Canadian license as long as you have an accredited degree and appropriate experience. However, if all your experience is in the United States, you may have problems demonstrating its appropriate.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the ways to determine if a stamp is old or new?
Answer: The way we have printed stamps has changed since they first came into use in the 1840s and a lot of that change has actually come in the last 60 years or so as security printing techniques have improved. The first stamps, like this Penny Black here, were made by an engraving process which incorporated new machine lathes to do the complex curved patterns on the left and right sides. The Portrait would have been engraved by a professional engraver, who would have had to have etched the design, in reverse, in copper. This would be transferred in reverse to a steel die, which would then be hardened before it too was used to make impressions in a printing plate. The plate would then be inked and applied with pressure to paper, leaving the design. Unfortunately, this process didn’t allow much detail, so the earliest stamps often look a bit rough. But by the late 19th century engraving techniques had been improved, allowing you to get much better details through this process. But in addition, the cost of engraving became more expensive, so another technique, Lithography, which involves the use of a press where ink is kept off the non-inked parts of the paper by the fact oil and water don’t mix started to be used to produce stamps. This sort of printing dominated stamps right up to the 1950s and became one of the most common ways of printing stamps during this period. Later, photographic plates were used to provide more detail even though the process remained pretty much the same. Not too long after, two passes of the stamp through the press allowed lithographed stamps to be printed in multiple colors. Again, this was slightly improved upon for the next fifty years. In the 20th century, engraving again got better, but still limited you to one color However, by the 1960s, engraved stamps printed in two colors started to become common, as did mixing lithographic and engraved printing to give you more color options. But by the late 1960s, four color lithographic presses became good enough to print stamps in enough detail that they were more difficult to counterfeit. That was always a problem with lithographed stamps and remains so today. However, by the 1990s, lithographic printing processes started to get incredibly good, using very small dots of color as opposed to the larger dots found in lithographed stamps from the 1960s. By the early 21st century, it became possible to mix a number of printing techniques in the same stamp. This stamp uses engraving, lithography, changing color ink that’s also commonly found on currency, and microprinting to make a stamp with incredible detail

Question: What would have happened if England had won the Revolutionary War? How would it have affected Britain and its colonies?
Answer: Everything changes Remember that at American independence, there were only about 4 million people in the 13 colonies. America’s rapid population growth after that was driven largely by its expansion westward. If that doesn’t happen, America’s population doesn’t grow so fast because even in the late 18th century the Americans had eaten into most of its natural resources. Even George Washington noted how quickly land in Virginia was being exhausted by tobacco cultivation. The new British North American confederation is still lightly populated, and relies largely on trade with each other rather than international trade.

Question: What are some off-the-beaten-path activities in NYC? Are there any lesser-known attractions or hidden gems in the city?
Answer: Too many tourists concentrate on the wonders of Manhattan where there are tons of other attractions in the boroughs. One of the issues is that it takes some time to get to them and they often aren’t near other attractions so it takes some effort. That also applies to some of the attractions in the north of Manhattan. So here we go: The Transit Museum, Brooklyn Tucked into an abandoned subway station, Court Street in Brooklyn, is the main branch of the New York City Transit Museum (there is a small display in Grand Central Terminal as well). The gems of the collection are fully restored subway cars from pretty much every decade the subway has operated. It’s not a big collection and you can easily see it in 90 minutes, but the admission is on the inexpensive side. One of the problems is that it’s not easy to navigate too as Brooklyn’s street grid isn’t as logically laid out as Manhattans, but it’s worth the trip. It is only a five minute walk from Jay Street. The Museum of the Moving Image, Queens Housed in a former production studio in Astoria, The museum dates back to 1988 but has only been permanently installed in its current location since 2011. It concentrates on cinema and television technology, but has lately also been documenting digital productions as well. It is kind of hard to get to though, being an 8 minute walk from the nearest subway station on 36th Avenue. It’s also only open Thursday to Sunday. It’s reasonably priced at $20 for adults. The Cloisters, north Manhattan A branch of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Cloisters features medieval art and architecture in a building designed along the lines of early French architecture. Again, getting to it can be a pain as it was deliberately put on top of a hill (they don’t call it Washington Heights for nothing). It’s a 12 minute climb from the nearest subway at 190th Street, but there is a free shuttle for people with mobility issues and one city bus line runs to the door. It’s $30, but that also includes admission to The Met.

Question: The Supreme Court just overturned Chevron, a 1984 case that gave agencies the authority to pass regulations that are essentially laws. Only Congress can make laws. This is HUGE! Will liberals meltdown?
Answer: No, courts are going to melt down because for the past several decades, they have not had to look deeply at federal policy when the law was not entirely clear. And this could be a boost to liberals. People forget that in Chevron, Chevron was the winner because they were being sued by an environmental interest group that alleged the standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency were too lenient. The Supreme Court ruled the EPA had no obligation to use the “most restrictive” standard and a “reasonable” standard was fine so the only way to challenge the EPA was to prove their standard was “unreasonable”. That actually happened when the EPA ruled carbon dioxide wasn’t a “pollutant” and the Supreme Court overruled them. That means everyone opposed to any project that has to be approved by some federal administrative authority (airports, railway lines, dams, nuclear plants, military bases, etc, etc) can face lawsuits by “tree huggers” who complain the federal agency who has to approve it didn’t properly construe a broad provision and force the matter into the courts, delaying it for years while it works through the appeal process.
