Question: How many states are in the United States? Why do some countries have multiple states while others only have one?
Answer: The United States has forty-six states and four “commonwealths” (Virginia, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and Kentucky) with the commonwealths being treated as states for all purposes. The United States is one of only a dozen or so countries that uses a “federal” system with sovereign sub-units within the main government, with a division of powers between the central government and the regional governments. Most states are “unitary” with only one central government that can pass laws of their own accord. Other countries that use a federal system are Canada, Australia, Switzerland, Germany, Brazil, Venezuela, Nigeria, India, Russia, Syria, Nepal, Pakistan, Argentina, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Comoros, Ethiopia, Malaysia, Mexico, Micronesia, Saint Kitts & Nevis, South Africa, Spain and the United Arab Emirates. Yugoslavia also used to be a federal state, but it split up into individual countries in the 1990s.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What events led to the establishment of the state of Israel? What challenges did it face after gaining independence and how were they addressed?
Answer: On May 12, 1948, the People’s Administration (Minhelet HaAm), which was at that time the provisional cabinet of the provisional government of the Jewish people in Palestine, was facing a crisis. The Jewish population had been in open revolt against the British administration and in armed conflict with Arab militias throughout the region. The Jews had been hopeful that the United Nations proposal to partition Palestine into Jewish and Arab states made on November 29, 1947 would be accepted, but the Arabs refused (probably for good reason - a massive proportion of Arabs would live in the Jewish state) and the fighting continued. The British, whose official position since 1917 had been for the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine abstained on the partition vote in the UN and refused to implement the partition because they too felt it was unfair to the Arab majority. It was clear that the British were fed up with the situation. Jewish insurrectionists had killed or wounded over 250 British administrative and military personnel since the end of World War II. They announced that on May 15, 1948, they were abandoning their mandate over the territory. They made no attempt to create any type of provisional government on the way out, feeling the only choice was to let the two sides fight it out amongst themselves. This put the Jewish provisional government into a very uncomfortable situation. Other Arab nations were already providing the Arab militias with weapons, but had resisted sending their own forces into the territory for fear of provoking war with the British. While they were there, the British had effectively prevented the Jewish militias from importing weapons, but they had set up their own weapons factories and were holding their own. However, the Jews were heavily outnumbered and at that moment, the Arabs were in complete control of Jerusalem, meaning two members of the provisional cabinet were hiding in the city. Another member was in the United States. The remaining ten members of the provisional. cabinet knew that once the British left, Arab forces would rush in. Now, at that point, the Jews would be able to move in their own imported weapons (mostly from Eastern Europe) and more volunteers, but at the moment they were badly outnumbered. Complicating the matter was that the United States, which had become sympathetic to an independent Jewish State after initial reluctance to do so, had made a proposal at the UN Security Council to replace the British trusteeship with a United Nations trusteeship in order to prevent a power vacuum in the region. However, the Americans expected to be in the lead of this trusteeship, and it’s primary purpose was to prevent the implementation of a partition plan, which at this point even the UN had realized was unworkable. The ten remaining members of the provisional cabinet met in Tel Aviv at 1:45 p.m. local time on May 12. Ahead of the meeting, Zvi Berenson, the legal advisor to the largest Jewish trade union, had drafted a declaration of independence. When the ten representatives met, there were really only two alternatives - declare independence or accept American trusteeship. Neither option was terribly palatable. Independence meant the Jews were on their own against the might of combined Arab forces in the region. However, American trusteeship was unlikely to result in any state for anyone for the foreseeable future. They finally decided to bring the matter to a vote just after midnight on May 13. By a 6–4 vote, the meeting decided on the independence option. On hearing about the vote, Chaim Weizmann, who was the president of the World Zionist Organization heartily endorsed it, commenting “What are they waiting for, the idiots?” The provisional cabinet met at 1:50 p.m. the following day to approve the final text of the declaration. They had arranged a secret press conference at 4 pm at the Tel Aviv Museum but didn’t come to an agreement on the text until 3 p.m. That meant a mad dash from the meeting place to the museum which was almost interrupted by a police officer who arrested the car that David Ben-Gurion had commandeered for the trip for speeding, but let it go once he realized what it was carrying. The car got there at 3;59 p.m. and Ben-Gurion started the ceremony with a gavel bang and a song “Hatikvah” (soon to be the national anthem) before reading the declaration to the 250 guests and live over the radio. The following morning, the United States formally recognized Israel as a sovereign state. It took the Soviet Union a couple more days, but within a week they were the first country to establish formal diplomatic relations. That helped the flow of weapons from Eastern Europe to the Jewish forces. Of course, militarily, the new state of Israel was in deep trouble - outnumbered by the Arab forces coming in from all sides and retreating on all fronts. However, within a few months, Jewish volunteers from abroad and a distinct advantage in technology (Israel surprised everyone with an air force) the Jewish forces soon outnumbered the Arab ones and gained far more territory than had been allocated to them by the partition plan, essentially forcing Arab forces back into Gaza and the West Bank by the time a cease fire was arranged in January 1949.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What makes Long Island part of the New York City metropolitan area?
Answer: Mostly the Long Island Railroad (L.I.R.R.) which stretches to the most easterly point of Long Island providing direct connections to Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan. It is ancient in the extreme, having been founded in 1834 - 70 years older than the subway. It’s purpose has always been to carry passengers. Originally, there was a plan to run a ferry from Boston to the L.I.R.R. terminals, but commuter traffic soon became enough to justify it. Ironically, the L.I.R.R. never made money but it became a vital link from New York to communities on the island and is now integrated into New York City’s economy, with the same agency that runs transit running the L.I.R.R. On a typical weekday, over a quarter-million people use the L.I.R.R., mostly to commute to New York City.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the reasons behind people's preferences for universities over community colleges? Is prestige a factor?
Answer: The difference between community colleges and universities is largely one of the philosophy of teaching. Community college students are “trained”. They work mostly on practical projects after getting a grounding in the basic principles used in the field. University students are “educated”. They go much deeper into the basic principles of their field, learning how these principles were developed without immediately jumping into practical applications. Even though not all students make it to the next step, studying for a “masters” where it is hoped they will improve the state of knowledge in their field. I’ve known people who have gone through both and although a community college will teach you a lot of practical skills, sometimes it’s not clear how deep your knowledge goes. That makes it tough when you’re facing a novel problem to even know where to start. Now, a lot of employers prefer community college graduates to university graduates because the former has more immediate knowledge they can put to use right away. However, university graduates, no matter what their field, tend to do better longer term because once they learn the practical skills they can often see the weaknesses in them and how to improve them.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Do you think it's fair for the owners of the Colorado funeral home to be "facing hundreds of criminal charges"?
Answer: Well, I read about the case, so here’s a short description of the facts. The funeral home owners had contracted to take bodies of deceased people and properly dispose of the remains, either by burial or cremation. Instead, they pretty much stored all the dead unembalmed bodies in their facility, pretty much letting them rot until they were finally caught. Unfortunately, this is not the first time something like this has happened. In one case (which was featured on the medical examiner show “Dr. G.” and was actually her first ever case) the funeral home was pretty much putting two bodies in the same coffin, and was still backed up. This sort of thing, of course, poses a massive public health risk, which is why we have laws regarding the proper disposal of bodies. It also goes against several religious traditions requiring bodies to be disposed of in a respectful manner. And, yes, they did this with hundreds of bodies, so hundreds of criminal charges seem justified.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How is the word 'proof' defined in the context of law?
Answer: Black’s law dictionary only defines “proof” in the context of private cases, but it does provide a useful definition of “prove” To establish a fact or hypothesis as true by satisfactory and sufficient evidence. To break this down, “satisfactory” can be thought of as the synonym of “admissible”, that is, evidence the court will accept. “Sufficient” goes to the “burden” of proof and the “standard” of proof, which is different for civil and criminal cases. In civil cases, the “burden” is always on the plaintiff, and the “standard” is “on the balance of probabilities” or “more likely than not”. In criminal cases, the “burden” is on the prosecution, and the “standard” is “beyond a reasonable doubt”, which is pretty much a lack of any rational objection to the evidence. As such, courts never ask for “absolute” proof of any fact. In addition, if a fact is put forward by a plaintiff or a prosecutor, and survives cross-examination, you generally have to assume the burden of proof has been met if the civil defendant or criminal defendant puts forward no evidence of their own to refute it. So let’s give a for instance. This year, I was involved in a case at work where we were trying to get an injunction against an individual for doing things that you needed a license to do. He showed up at the first hearing and said that we had to “prove” it. However, to that point As such, at that moment, we had almost certainly met our burden and our standard (which was “more likely than not”). He didn’t bother to show up for the second hearing and I’m pleased to say we got a massive costs award against him.

Question: Is there an animated movie that accurately portrays human history?
Answer: Well, not a movie, but there is an animated series Consisting of twenty-six twenty-five minute episodes, this animated series, made in France but financed widely by educational television providers all over the planet, covers all periods of human history using the same set of characters throughout. The first episode covers the history of earth from its formation in the solar system until the appearance of Homo Erectus. The last episode covers the period of time from 1945 to the production of the series in 1978, then speculates on the future. The characters (in English) are Maestro (the wise old man), Peter (the ordinary guy), Jumbo (the fighter), Pierette (the lady), The Pest (the villain), The Dwarf (The Pest’s boss), and The Clock (who visually provides the year events take place) Six other series in the “Once Upon a Time…” franchise have also been produced, each covering a less wide scope of time. Many of the episodes are available on YouTube

Question: Why would Pierre Poilievre's policy fail?
Answer: Well, Poilievre doesn’t have much in the way of policy. His strategy so far has been “Trudeau bad! Trudeau corrupt! Trudeau incompetent! Trudeau a laughing stock!” Now, there are people doing poorly in Canada, but that’s largely due to provincial policies, not federal ones. Trudeau is pretty much being blamed for things the federal government can’t do constitutionally. So let’s look at some of the barely enunciated policies shall we? Remover the carbon tax Or as he puts it “remove the inflationary carbon tax” which doesn’t hold up under scrutiny (the carbon tax accounts for only a small part of inflation). The problem is that the carbon tax, which I note that conservative premiers ganged up on to remove and LOST not because they said the federal government can’t impose it (which it clearly can) but because it wasn’t imposed on provinces that had their own carbon tax or cap-and-trade scheme, which two of those provinces already had and dropped, forcing a showdown. The problem is that Poilievre hasn’t told us what will replace it. Canada is one of the biggest per capita carbon dioxide producers (far more than the Scandinavian countries) and one of the problems with the carbon tax is that it’s generally far too low to dissuade people from using carbon based fuels. Yes we do need things like zero interest loans for alternatives (other energy solutions pay for themselves over time, even if there is no carbon tax) but the only reasonable alternative is “cap and trade”, which Ontario had until it dropped it to force a showdown. Quebec still has a cap and trade scheme it shares with California, and we’re already seeing transition (for example, maple syrup producers have switched from fuel oil driven evaporators to electric ones). Both the carbon tax and cap-and-trade were solutions that were developed by conservative leaning economists, and cap-and-trade worked brilliantly to reduce acid rain causing emissions. The left leaning solution would just be banning stuff that uses carbon based fuels. The other thing is that the vast majority of Canadians (85%) get more money from the government than they pay in carbon taxes. That’s because most carbon taxes are used by heavy industry (like the Alberta Oil Sands, which produces more carbon dioxide than all of Quebec). For example, Poilievre tried to use the example of an Ottawa region mushroom farmer whose carbon tax bill was about $100,000 a year, but that meant that the farmer was using more than $1 million of fuel a year in any event and it would probably make more sense to finance a heating system that was more energy efficient. Make housing more affordable The Conservative playbook on this has generally been “open up more greenspace to housing use” but even Ontario’s government, which tried and failed to do this, realizes that it’s not going to solve the problem because new housing on “greenfields” tends to be expensive single family homes and not affordable housing. But Poilievre can complain all he wants but the genesis of the affordable housing crisis was created by the Mulroney government in the 1980s, who followed the policy of the Reagan government and the Thatcher government - get the government out of the housing business and leave it to the market. However, “the market” wants housing prices to remain high to protect their investment. People in the UK who bought their council houses in the 1980s are sitting pretty right now, but they all know their children can no longer afford housing because of it. Now back in the 1970s, governments at all levels were building rent-geared-to-income housing and making money available for cooperative housing and other non-profit housing. I myself live in a 1970s cooperative and I pay about 60% of market for my unit. All that ended in the 1980s and attempts to build such housing since have been scattershot at best. And the big problem is not at the federal level, or even the provincial level - it’s at the municipal level where local zoning laws make it difficult or impossible to build affordable housing. Here in Toronto, local opposition can hold up approval of affordable units for years. One affordable development near by boyhood home, a beautiful location near a regional rail station, is permanently on hold because construction costs will make it unprofitable. Right now, it’s an empty lot. Lowering spending One of the really bad things that happened to the Conservatives last year is that the Liberals delivered a budget with a lower deficit, benefitting from the recovery of the economy after the high spending necessitated by the pandemic. Poilievre has said high deficits are bad, but delivered no alternative to the economic plunge in 2020 which the Trudeau government responded to by making applying for supplementary benefits far easier. That appears to have worked. But if you’re voting conservatives for “lower taxes”, please be assured that this just means “more debt”. Here in Ontario, the Progressive Conservatives got elected partly on the platform that the Liberals were spending too much money, forcing higher taxes. Since being elected, in every single year, Ontario government spending has gone up regardless of revenue projections, which were made worse by things like scrapping the annual vehicle plate registration fee (cost about $1 billion). That’s just meant higher deficits every year. Conservatives are not, and never have been, fiscally prudent. For example, Alberta’s budget still comes mostly from oil revenues, which just aren’t going to be sustainable, which is why they fight so hard against the carbon tax because it benefits provinces like Quebec which produce clean power (Quebec has been investing heavily in hydroelectricity since the 1960s, and it’s paid off big time).

Question: How did Charles Darwin come up with the concept of "survival of the fittest" to explain evolution without knowledge of DNA?
Answer: There were two experience of Darwin that clued him into the concept of “natural selection” The first was his voyages on “The Beagle” where he collected biological specimens to be returned to England to be studied. He did an excellent job of that by the way and when he returned he was able to get a university job cataloguing those specimens. During that trip, he visited the Galapagos Islands where even the ship’s notoriously religious captain Robert Fitzroy had to agree were much less old than the South American mainland. On the Galapagos, Darwin studied the local giant tortoises, finches, and iguanas and noted that despite them almost certainly having common ancestors, it was easy to identify which island they came from by their physical characteristics. He figured that this was due to populations being isolated from each other as it was pretty much impossible to swim from island to island because of the currents. Moreover, the physical characteristics matched their environment, like being able to take advantage of local food sources. Differences of the beaks of finches, unique to each island. Some ate bugs and didn’t need big beaks. Some ate seeds and did to break them apart. Differences in the structure of tortoise shells Differences between iguanas (here with modern information about genetic similarities) The other thing that clued in Darwin was his interest in breeding fancy pigeons Darwin knew a skilled breeder could take a rock pigeon and, within a few generations, turn it into a highly specialized variety by breeding birds with the more desirable characteristics. So knowing human beings could use “artificial selection” to turn “wolves” into several hundred breeds of dogs in a space of about 15,000 years, he figured that given enough time, environmental pressures on distinct populations would have the same effect. The animals most likely to breed and survive to breed again were the ones who were the “best fit” to the local environment. He called this “natural selection” and when he finally published (because another naturalist named Alfred Russell Wallace came up with the exact same idea) it was the first time anyone had suggested a mechanism by which evolution could over time create new species.

Question: Why does inbreeding, especially when it is done generationally, cause birth defects in animals? Shouldn’t inbreeding also increase the chance of getting good genes?
Answer: So let’s talk about genetics. In the vast majority of cases, offspring get two copies of the same “chromosome” or genetic body. Each chromosome has the same sent of genes. One chromosome of every pair comes from the mother and one from the father, except for the weird XY pair in males where the X comes from the mother and the Y comes from the father. In females, one X chromosome comes from the mother and one from the father. Now, the way genetics work is that you don’t use the genes on both chromosomes. In each pair of genes, one is “dominant” and the other is “recessive”. If they’re more or less identical then they both do the same function and it doesn’t matter which gene asserts itself. However, in a pair where one is dominant and one is recessive, the dominant gene is expressed and the recessive gene is suppressed. As such, in any random set of four genes DD, DR, RD or RR, “D” will always express unless you have “RR” when “R” will express. As a simple example, the genes that tend to give you brown hair are dominant while the ones that given you blond hair are recessive. The big exception is the XY pair. Some genes just aren’t found on the Y chromosome, so you express the one on the X chromosome in all cases. So let’s look at this in practice. Hemophilia describes a group of diseases where your blood wont clot properly. That’s very bad because a slight injury can make you bleed to death internally. The genes for clotting are on the X chromosome, not the Y, so if you’re a male who gets a bad X chromosome you get hemophilia. However, if you’re a female with XX, the hemophilia causing genes are recessive, so you don’t get the disease although you can pass it on to your sons. The vast majority of genetic diseases are caused by recessive genes. Luckily, you have to have two copies of the faulty gene for the disease to manifest itself. Otherwise, you’re saved by the other parent’s genes, which will dominate so the disease won’t express itself. But this presumes that breeding takes place more or less at random. If you attempt to breed within a small population, recessive genes tend to accumulate. This is most obvious in dog breeds. Many “purebred” dogs are actually bred with characteristics expressed only when there are two recessive genes. However, these “desirable” recessive genes often carry with them recessive genes that cause congenital problems. Now, I intensely dislike PETA, but they’ve hit the nail on the head here, so credit where credit is due. And that conclusion is scientifically solid Humans are no different, so let’s get back to hemophilia, which rampaged through royal families related to the British royal family for generations. The culprit- Queen Victoria, who carried the gene on one of her X chromosomes So, if you’re a royal female and you marry a hemophiliac, congratulations - no matter how healthy you are personally, all of your daughters are going to carry one X chromosome with the faulty gene, and half your grandsons will be hemophiliacs. It’s even worse in royal families because despite the small breeding pool, they tend to live longer and are more likely to have children than other people who might have it. I mean, they make a lovely couple and all, but they’re also third cousins sharing Victoria as a great-great-grandmother. That’s why my money is on Archie. His parents are distantly related. He’s probably going to keep his hair well into his seventies.

Question: What are your worst experiences in a movie theatre?
Answer: It was the day of release of “Return of the Jedi”. Because I had a life I couldn’t do the “line up first thing in the morning to see it at the massive University Theatre” so a group of friends and I decided to get reserved tickets at the nearby smaller screen Cumberland Theatre for the first evening performance (about 7 p.m.). The place was absolutely packed. Because of the crowds and poor planning, we got started late to begin with, but we were really enjoying the show. Until roughly the point where the film is about to reach its climax, when the film breaks. Now back in the early 1980s at multiplexes, films were projected using a platter system where the whole film sat on a massive horizontal table before a series of pulleys pulled it out of the center, moved it to the vertical to go through the projector, then re-oriented it horizontally to re-wind it around the big reel. The system was actually pioneered for IMAX film projection where the film goes through the projector sideways anyway Flat plate projection systems really put a lot of stress on a film, but they don’t constantly need a projectionist hanging around, so they made multiplexes like the Cumberland (a 4 plex) possible. Breaking on the fourth show overall is very rare, but it happens. The crowd got a little rowdy, and the cinema staff’s communication was less than worthless, but eventually after about five minutes the film was running again, Darth Vader kills the Emperor, Hans and Leia get the shiels down, and Lando destroys the Death Star. Hurray! So we go to the denouement where Luke is burning Vader’s body on a pyre and guess what - the film breaks AGAIN. Right now we’re about twenty minutes after we expected the film to end and we were so close, so the crowd goes nuts again. All’s well that ends well though, so they fixed the film again, we got to see the end of the movie and left about half-an-hour late.

Question: Was Reagan less racist against Mexicans and immigrants than Trump, because Reagan used to work for a living, was born in Dixon, Illinois, and used to be a Democrat & a union organizer? Hasn't Trump always been a spoiled, rich, right-wing Republican?
Answer: I don’t know if he was less racist, but when he was running for the Republican nomination against George W. Bush, both men advocated a legal path to immigration (if not citizenship) for temporary workers. Both men were familiar that the economy of states like California and Texas was highly dependent on agriculture and trying to completely ban temporary workers was a terrible idea. Without them, you were facing a major labour shortage. But neither Reagan nor Bush could get better immigration policy done and unfortunately the next catastrophe was largely put on the feet of the Democrats. In a nutshell, changes in policy over this time made it more intelligent for temporary workers to stay in the United States all year than attempt crossing the border on an annual basis looking for work, then returning when there was none. That’s the status quo now. Trump’s policies are solely self serving. He too relies on mostly Hispanic workers for many of his enterprises. However, by playing up the narrative of Mexican workers and refugees (mostly created by U.S. foreign policy in Central America) by blaming them for crime, disease and unemployment, he has found people will vote for him. It’s not that you can’t legally get temporary workers. There’s a process. However, the process takes forever - more than a year. You simply can’t wait that long. Meanwhile, a lot of Mexicans find it easier to find temporary agricultural jobs in Canada where getting a permit and working legally is pretty straightforward.

Question: What is the maximum distance that can be seen at Niagara Falls?
Answer: The land topology around the falls is kind of weird as the entire area was covered by a post-glacial lake we now call Lake Tonawanda The Canadian side was one of the lake’s shorelines and, as such, the land rises pretty steeply from the river gorge so if you look further into Canada all you will see is an escarpment. The view into Canada - a high hill. The building is the headquarters of the park police. However, the view is better over to the American side as the land there used to be the shallow lake, which eventually filled in. However, it’s a densely built area so you can only see a few miles into the States from the Canadian side. From the Canadian side of Horseshoe Falls, looking north. Canadian side on the left of the gorge. From here, you can see several hundred yards down the gorge, and about a mile into New York State. You can get a better view from some points of the escarpment, but it’s not easy as it’s mostly private property. From the top of Murray Street in Niagara Falls, ON. As you can see, you can’t see much from here even though you’re near the top of the escarpment Similarly, from the top of Clifton Hill, another high point. Not much of a view here either. You can pay for a better view. Unfortunately, the old Oneida Tower (now part of Casino Niagara) has been condemned for years and the Minolta Tower (also free) has been converted to a hotel. The Skylon Tower and the Skywheel both provide views from a height (both about 520 feet above the falls) but even in good conditions there are troubles with sightlines and on a good day you probably can’t see more than about 40 miles. You’re probably not going to even see Buffalo View from the Skylon Tower restaurant

Question: How do scientists see evolution? Why do they brush off creationism as unscientific?
Answer: “Evolution”, a term coined by Charles Darwin’s grandfather Erasmus Darwin, started to come into the scientific consciousness as biologists started to look more deeply into vertebrate anatomy. The harder they looked the more they realized that the anatomy of every single vertebrate is pretty much a variation on the same set of bones. Even though all these vertebrates use their forelimbs for a different purpose, they pretty much have identical sets of bones. Some are smaller, some are larger, but they’re all connected to each other in the same way. Particularly striking is the similarities between bat wings and bird wings in function and basic bone structure, but not in the arrangement of those bones. These similarities can be traced all the way back to early fish, which have five main bones in their forward fins. Charles Darwin saw all these similarities, which only increased between species that appeared to be closely related, as evidence not of “creation” but of common ancestry. For example, take a look at this elephant skeleton - the feet bones are incredibly similar to other animals with complex feet even though the elephant’s foot is large and flat on the bottom And in whale skeletons, you see what appear to be rear leg bones floating apart from the rest of the skeleton, even though they have no function In modern evolutionary theory, what they now look at is how similar the DNA of different species is. However, even when species are separated by a common ancestor that lived billions of years ago, like humans and oak trees, you still find similarities, like the gene for creating energy in the absence of oxygen. And the X and Y chromosomes of mice and humans are pretty much identical. None of this points to each species being created independently. It points to everything having a common ancestor at some point, sometimes very recently (about 15 million years with people and chimps) but sometimes way back in the past. But its always there.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What was the significance of translating all of God's word into English?
Answer: This was a “Protestant” thing, that became a trend in the mid 16th century after several movements (Lutheranism, Calvinism, Anglican) started to break away from the Catholic church, which at least in the western part of Europe more or less dominated Christianity and religion at that time. At this time, and indeed well into the twentieth century, Catholic services were conducted almost entirely in Latin and pretty much every copy of the Bible in existence was in Latin too. Movable type printing had been invented about 200 years before, and the Bible had been one of the first major works printed, But even though the fellow who commissioned its printing was German speaking, the bible he printed was in Latin. Now at this time, literacy was low. Maybe 15% of people in Europe could read, but even then, very few of them could read Latin which was essentially a language for the church and the rapidly growing field of science. However, with church services, including reading of Bible passages, was entirely in Latin, hardly anyone in a church would be able to understand what was being said. The “protestants” who eventually broke away from the Catholic church thought this was wrong. They thought it would be better to conduct services in the vernacular language of the region so churchgoers could actually understand the bible. Martin Luther himself believed people were completely capable of reading and interpreting the bible on their own, and several later protestant churches, like the Baptists, turned away from official interpretations of biblical texts. Up in England, by the 1560s, the country’s monarchs had embraced their own form of Protestantism that put the monarch at the head of the church and pushed for complete separation from the Roman Church. Although Anglicanism kept a lot of traditions of the Catholic Church, thanks mostly to the influence of Calvinism it also embraced the idea of doing church services in English. The first English bible was made available in 1535, but it was far from “official” and as such it wasn’t even published in England - it was from Antwerp in Belgium. Nevertheless, these translations worked their way to England and caused no end of problems as the different versions translated different passages differently. As such, James I who succeeded Elizabeth I in 1603 almost immediately decided to commission an “official bible translation” that would become the standard for the Anglican Church. The work took eight years but since then it’s been the official Anglican bible despite containing what’s now archaic language.

Question: What is the process of becoming an NHL ice hockey player? Is it difficult, considering players are typically scouted at a young age?
Answer: There are several paths to the NHL, and the process has changed substantially in the last thirty years as more non-Canadian players make it to the big league. But if you’re Canadian, or live in the United States near the Canadian border, your goal is to play in Major Junior A Hockey, a form of semi-pro hockey for players from 15 to 20 years of age. There are sixty eligible teams in the WHL (BC, AB, SK, MB), the OHL (ON) and the QMJHL (QC, NB, NS, PE, NL). Three teams in the OHL are located in the United States, as are five teams in the WHL. If you’re American, the best path is to play in NCAA Division 1 Hockey, which usually means you get a scholarship. Major Junior players are not eligible for the NCAA, and some Canadians do take the path of getting into a college program. By amazing coincidence, there are sixty Division 1 college hockey teams. Most of them are from schools that are Division 1 in most sports, but some colleges, like Union in New York State, only compete at the D1 level in hockey. If you’re European, the best path is the European club system, working your way up to the senior leagues and hoping you get noticed by a scout, often when you play internationally. Hockey has both a world championship and a junior championship (18–19 year olds) and the NHL scouts spend a lot of time at both. Your goal is eventually to get drafted by an NHL team. The draft is held every year and teams pick in the reverse order to how they finished the previous season, with the Stanley Cup champion going last.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are some metals that were once commonly used but are no longer in use? What led to their decline in usage?
Answer: The use of silver has declined tremendously in the past thirty years thanks to the growth of digital cameras. Silver, in the form of silver nitrate, was a necessary component in photographic film and the film industry had a tremendous demand for it. It was so strong that it was worth processing developing fluid to recover the silver in it. But once digital photography started to take over, the demand for silver for industrial purposes dropped. It’s still used in some applications, like high end electronics where conductivity is critical, but it’s most common use isn’t coming back.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can the law regarding cell phone use while driving be changed in Ontario, Canada?
Answer: Of course it can. The current provision of the Highway Traffic Act was set by the legislature and can always be changed by the legislature. However, that’s unlikely. All studies point to cell phone use while driving being the equivalent of having a couple of shots of booze. In addition, statistics show that about 80% of accidents in Ontario are caused by distractions, and that includes cell phone use. The number of deaths from accidents in Ontario has doubled since 2000, and that matches the introduction of widespread adoption of cell phones and, later, smartphones.

Question: Is it possible to change the pronunciation of vowels in English? What would be the benefits of such a change, if any?
Answer: Oh yes. That happens all the time, which is why the spelling of many common English words don’t match the vowels used. In the previous sentence alone, we have “uv” and “wurds”. Now roughly between 1400 (the late Middle English period) and 1700 (early Modern English), the pronunciation of the vowels in many words in English underwent a shift. Unfortunately, spelling conventions were based on the pre 1400 language and only became standardized after 1700, which is the main reason English spelling is so strange. But a vowel shift is going on right now with the Great Lakes Accent, a widespread American accent used in the large cities on the Great Lakes like Buffalo, Cleveland, Detroit, Chicago and Milwaukee. For example, the word “job” has stopped being pronounced “johb” and is now often heard as “jahb”. When that happens, other vowels also start to shift so that they can be distinguished in speech.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can you explain the differences between Avenue, Road, Lane, and Street in terms of their locations and usages?
Answer: Historically, these terms meant something different but are not often used interchangeably. So let’s start with “road”. Historically, that was an improved right of way that ran through a rural area between two built up areas. For example, here in Toronto, we have “Kingston Road”, which used to be the dirt road linking the eastern edge of the City of Toronto to the Town of Kingston abut 200km to the east. Similarly, “Markham Road” linked Scarborough Village, a small settlement, to the Town of Markham about 20km north. A “street” is an improved road within a built up area that is usually surrounded by residences and shops. For example, in Manhattan, streets are fairly narrow and have commercial and residential buildings along them. An “avenue” is a very wide road that easily allows for traffic in both directions, but is difficult to cross on foot. In Manhattan, avenues are about 2–3 times as wide as streets and usually much longer. A “lane” is a short narrow connecting street, usually very narrow, that may have shops and services on it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the reason for Canadians having American accents? Is it due to their proximity to the US or another factor?
Answer: The first English speakers in what’s now Ontario, which was really the first large English speaking population in all of what’s now Canada, were refugees from the American War of Independence called “Loyalists”. While the Revolution raged, they steadfastly supported the existing government and, when the British lost, they became pariahs and had to flee the country. They tended to be better educated and richer than the rest of the American population. But almost all of them had been born in the United States. Moreover, in the late 18th century, American and British accents weren’t all that different. Nevertheless the new “British subjects in North America”, who after the War of 1812 became more comfortable with “Canadian” were mostly people who had been born and raised in the United States and spoke just like them. And, strangely enough, it was in the United Kingdom where the language changed the most. Americans still speak roughly like they did 200 years ago, but in the UK there were major changes to the accent - changes that didn’t get transferred to the United States as although there was immigration from the British Isles to both the United States and Canada, they were from groups that often had quite different accents (like the Scottish and the Irish) and, after a generation, the kids “went native” and started talking with an American accent. Meanwhile, the Americans and Canadians stayed close and there was a ton of cross-border immigration well into the late 19th century so people from Canada spoke very much like people from the Great Lake states despite the constant flow of new British immigrants. As such, although it takes an expert and you can distinguish an American and a Canadian by the way they speak, the two accents have the same root and remain similar to this day, and distinct from accents in the British Isles.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can battery cars save the world, or will they harm it?
Answer: Look, it will be nice if we could save the carbon emissions from transportation. That’s a big piece of the pie. Any reduction would be welcome. But the same problem exists. The main problem with private car ownership isn’t pollution (although that’s bad), its that everyone having (and needing) a car has massive effects on society as a whole. Take a minor one - noise. Electric cars are quieter, but a lot of the noise from a car is from the wheels on the pavement. And it won’t help traffic And it won’t affect the massive amount of land that’s dedicated for parking Or the carnage from automobile accidents (about 43,000 a year in the United States) There was fog. Now, electric cars will solve none of this. Building cities you can walk around, making biking safer, and more public transit will solve these problems AND reduce carbon emissions at the same time. Is this so bad? Or this? Or this? Solutions to replace cars, or even making things easier for everyone else, exist. They just have to start to be implemented

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: All Donald Trump asks is to be treated fairly. Will you check your bias at the door and be fair and impartial to him?
Answer: If he wants to be treated “fairly”, why did he ask the Supreme Court of the United States to find that he was immune for prosecutions for all the official acts he took as president? None of the other 44 presidents, including Nixon, who probably would have been charged with obstruction of justice had he not been pardoned, figured that was necessary. If Donald Trump wanted to be treated fairly, why isn’t he subject to prosecution for the same laws every other American is subject to? Donald Trump wants to be treated UNFAIRLY. He wants to be treated BETTER than everyone else in the country. He and his followers have been calling for the prosecution of “The Biden Crime Family” but he feels he should be able to get away with things that anyone else would get months or years in jail for like starting an attack on the Capitol or stealing classified documents. When, in 1971, the New York Times, Washington Post and several other newspapers published details of classified documents, and even though they won a lawsuit allowing them to publish them in the Supreme Court, they knew that by doing so they could go to jail. They did it because they felt disclosing the lie that the U.S. government thought the Vietnam War was “winnable” was too important to keep secret. In fact the government did try to prosecute the guy who leaked the papers, Daniel Elsberg. By contrast, Nelson Mandela here spent 28 years in jail for fighting for racial equality before he was released and became the first black president of South Africa. Hell, the Mahatma here spent 19 years in jail because every time he broke the law (like “making salt without paying the tax”) he asked the court to send him to jail. When offered bail, he refused it. Look, all I’m asking is that Donald Trump sit still and be tried for the crime he’s charged with. If he’s acquitted, that’s fine. Or are you saying that the U.S. justice system is so fundamentally unfair that no-one should trust it?

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How can it make sense for a far-right party to be a "socialist workers' party"?
Answer: Okay, let’s get one thing out of the way from the beginning. Yes, the “National Socialist Worker’s Party” didn’t start out as “fascists” - a group of authoritarian corporatists. Most of the founders of the party were, in fact, socialists. In 1920, Hitler himself gave a speech on the Nazi party economic platform which advocated things like banning loans for interest, nationalizing large corporations and the death penalty for loan sharks. There were lots of socialists in the early Nazi party. But you can’t forget two things: And when you look at the Nazis as they gained public support, their economic platform was both socialist (more public spending on public works) and nationalistic (start making more weapons, reunite Germans in former German territory to Germany). But Hitler was more of an opportunist than anything else. After he was allowed to re-enter politics just in time for the Great Depression, he was living the high life as many of his associates knew lots of rich people who were looking for an alternative to the communists. Hitler cozied up to industrialists and aristocrats and was handsomely rewarded for it - he lived in a beautiful apartment, was driven around in an expensive automobile, and flew everywhere. As such, privately he reassured the rich, the capitalists and the military that they need not worry and when the Nazis came to power their place would be to make massive profits from weapons production and the army would be greatly expanded. This is particularly ironic because back in 1920 Hitler proposed seizing the assets of war profiteers. Finally, Hitler managed to seize power, but he had a problem - there were still loads of socialists in the party and they were wondering when the nationalization of factories would begin and when the army would be replaced by the “people’s army” - the SA, which was the two million strong violence arm of the party. However, by this point Hitler and many of his close allies realized that keeping industrialists and the army onside was critical to his long term plans. So, in 1934, he just killed them all. That included Ernst Rohm, the head of the SA and the one person in the party whose personal support rivaled Hitler himself. Rohm had been pushing the party to do more in a socialist direction ever since he got power, and he was making the Nazi’s rich and military friends nervous. Rohm was Hitler’s best friend - they had been together since before the Beer Hall Putsch in 1923. Hitler just out and out had him murdered. That was the last time “socialism” was an issue in the party. The Nazis ran a state that was authoritarian, corporatist, capitalist, and militaristic. And Hitler continued to live the high life, mostly thanks to the fact the government was buying copies of his book to give out as gifts and he was dodging taxes on the royalties. Not bad for a guy who before World War II was sleeping in hostels.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it possible for someone who doesn't speak French to learn how to correctly pronounce phrases like "Je t'aime" and "bon appétit" and be understood by native speakers?
Answer: Possible? Mais oui! Difficile? Mais bien sûr. French just has a ton of sounds that don’t exist in English (like highly nasal vowels) and combinations of sounds that don’t exist in English either (/ps/ is a perfectly acceptable consonant combination in French, in English we just drop the /p/, e.g. “psychic”). Adding to that is the fact that French has an entirely different rhythm that requires you to pronounce most of the vowel sounds rather than glossing over them in short form the way you do in English. But, as with English, there are tips and tricks you learn where you just copy what French people do and gloss over some of the pronunciation. For example, many non-English speakers have problems pronouncing “comfortable” but many British English speakers just say “cumftable” anyway and that’s a hell of a lot easier. For example “Que-est ce que” is always “kes-ke” in the mouth of a French speaker. And perfection isn’t the goal in learning a new language, progress is. One of the key things to remember is that words don’t exist in isolation in a language. Words always exist in a sentence, and sentences flow so that the words flow together with it. We don’t hear this in our own language and we think “there are pauses between all these words” but those pauses are illusions created by our brain, not the speaker’s mouth. Sometimes, you just gotta (instead of “got to” or “have to”) go with the flow and the flow regularly leaves out sounds. You can too. You’re always going to have an accent. Everyone does. Americans regularly have to understand British people and vice versa. Similarly, Parisians sometimes have to talk to Quebecois. Your way of speaking is, and always will be, unique. Focus on mistakes that are going to confuse listeners like the difference between “mais” (but - pr. “may”) and “maïs” (corn - prl. “maze”) A good start is to practice the typical masculine and feminine endings. Do it a lot; “un” and “une”, “francais” and “francaise”, “bon” and “bonne”. It will also help you hear those differences in speech.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are your three favourite films (movies) of all time, and why?
Answer: Easy peasy. For once, I’m going to do them in order. I was about ten when I saw this for the first time, in glorious Cinerama. It was really the first “grown up” movie I had ever seen, having to that point been fed a steady diet of comedies and kid films. However my dad, to his everlasting credit, thought I might like it and he took me one evening. I was simply blown away by the spectacle of it all, a massive canvas on which Stanley Kubrick painted man-apes, space craft, and an abstract representation of space travel. It’s a beautiful film with a score that just carries you away or makes you sit on the edge of your seat. Unlike most modern films, it relies almost entirely on visuals to carry the plot, characters and exposition forward. The dialogue is actually pretty boring, and the acting pretty naturalistic, avoiding big speeches and overwrought emotion. In addition to all that, the film has so many themes over so many layers that even after seeing it about fifteen times in theatres (the last time in 2019) you’re still finding new things to explore. One of the ones that hit me rather recently was “birthdays” - they’re referred to in at least three places in the film and matches the film’s constant theme of discovery and rebirth. Having grown up on the Adam West Batman series of 1966 (never missed an episode ever!) and being a fan of the character ever since, this exploration of the darker side of the character caught me off guard. The film’s two leads, Michael Keaton and Jack Nicholson, were largely chosen for their amazing acting abilities (Keaton hadn’t been recognized as such at this point, but the director, Tim Burton, had recognized his skill) and in their scenes together they both manage to hold their own. Tim Burton’s directing was like nothing I had ever seen before, with a marvelous mix of moods that still always kept the story moving. Most impressive was his ability to turn a film set, Gotham City, into something resembling a living breathing character like nothing I’ve seen before or since. Add onto that the music, both Danny Elfman’s breakthrough breathtaking score, and Prince’s song interludes. What a beautiful structure with two protagonists unknowingly working towards the same goal. Sean Connery’s Marko Raimius, a veteran submarine captain has decided to defect with a hand-picked group of senior officers fearing his new sub, the “Red October” will force the Americans to make the Cold War hotter. On the other side is Alec Baldwin’s cocky young CIA analyst Jack Ryan, the agency’s expert on Raimius who figures out that the Russian’s claims that Raimius is a rogue captain bent on nuclear war are a front for the fact that Raimius is stealing the sub. The problem throughout the film is no-one believes Ryan and Raimius doesn’t know who on the American side he can trust. The scene where Ryan is dealing with the problem of how Raimius is going to dispose of the crew who don’t want to defect by talking about the problem while showering and shaving is absolute brilliance and when he says “How do you get people to want to get off a nuclear submarine….” and pauses so you can fill in the blank yourself. The back and forth while another Russian sub hunts down the Red October and Ryan has to convince an American sub commander not to blow it out of the water just increases the tension at every turn. The final sub battle at the end is just gravy.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is Canada prepared for a government led by the New Democratic Party (NDP)? Would the changes be too drastic?
Answer: There have been NDP provincial governments throughout Canada since the 1940s, starting with Saskatchewan which got universal health care and paved road out of the deal. But when the NDP scored an upset in 1990 and formed the government in Ontario for the first and last time, it was much ado about nothing. The notoriously pro-union NDP got into a massive fight with the civil service that resulted in a multi-week strike that pretty much shut everything down. True, they borrowed heavily and spent a lot, but that was standard operating procedure for a recession, which is what the whole country was in at the time. NDP governments tend to be very fiscally responsible - they spend, but they also tax so they generally don’t run big deficits. Here in Ontario the Progressive Conservatives got into office by complaining how much the Liberals were spending and how big the deficit was, then they routinely spent more and ran up a higher deficit. Right now, Toronto’s interim mayor, Olivia Chow, who was an NDP MP as well as a long time councilor, has asked for a 9% tax increase because previous governments that leaned towards the Progressive Conservatives have pretty much just tried to run the city on deficits and now the bills are coming due. Toronto’s tax rates are actually on the low side for the region.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can a moon be captured by Earth through gravity or any other means?
Answer: Its possible, just not very likely. Moon formation is still not perfectly understood. For example, it’s only since the astronauts came back with moon rocks that we figured out that our moon was created when a much larger planetary body crashed into the earth in its early history. However, moons are just plain weird. This is Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons. It’s large (1,500 kilometers across), and has a nearly circular orbit around Jupiter near the planet’s equator. It’s also pretty much entirely made out of water. What the f*ck’s up with that. Yes, the outer shell is ice, but the interior is probably liquid water. That’s seriously weird. Now Saturn is seriously f*cked up. It has 146 moons. Plus rings, which are probably made up of a moon or moons that were torn apart by gravitational forces. The biggest is the appropriately named Titan, which is 5,100 km across. The smallest one with a name is Aegaeon, which is about 660m (or .66 km) across. But it’s pretty clear that some moons are “captures” - small planetary bodies that just got too close to a planet one day, but not so close as to hit them. Except the orbital mechanics of trying to make that shot are entirely insane. Most things in the inner solar system that aren’t planets move very fast relative to planets. Further away, things move slower, but Mars’s two moons, Phobos and Deimos, which are both tiny, seem to be captures. Here at Earth, anything that got close probably would be travelling too fast to go into orbit, it would just go off in another direction. So this is just one of those problems astronomers have to keep working on.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the maximum number of degrees you can travel before crossing into another time zone?
Answer: The widest time zone in the world is China, which keeps one time zone for the whole country despite its size (Greenwich +8). That covers just over 61 degrees of longitude (134 degrees 46 minutes to 73 degrees 30 minutes)

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Which major city does not have any interstate highways within its limits, such as New York City?
Answer: New York City has several interstates within its boundaries, including I-95 which passes right through northern Manhattan on its way to The Bronx But the six largest U.S. cities without an interstate in their boundaries are all in California - Fresno, Bakersfield, Modesto, Oxnard, Salinas and Santa Rosa. Fresno has a population of over half a million and it’s not like it’s in the middle of nowhere - It’s about 100 miles (160 km) southeast of San Jose.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it considered incorrect to use the terms "soda" or "pop" to refer to all types of soft drinks?
Answer: It’s strictly a regional preference, and really only applies to English speaking North America. For example, in most of Britain, it’s a “fizzy drink”. Moreover, the preference changes rapidly over time Here in southern Ontario, “pop” is the preferred term, but I use “soda”. Lots of things are like this, like “what do you call a sandwich on a long bun” “Sub” or “submarine sandwich” is now the overwhelmingly preferred term in the United States, but it has not always been that way.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it against the law to overtake a vehicle while going uphill?
Answer: Not on a multi-lane highway. On a two lane highway, yes. There will almost certainly be a solid line in that section marking “no passing”. That’s because you won’t be able to see over the crest of the hill to determine if there is oncoming traffic in the other lane. Even if there is no center line, it’s still illegal. Instances of dangerous passing - you can’t see oncoming traffic over a hill or around a curve.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why does a dog constantly sniff or want to snuggle with a person?
Answer: As a human, you have really good eyesight. You experience the world mostly by looking at it. You identify other people you know by what they look like. Human faces have so many muscles that they’re all slightly different and people are really good at picking up these differences. Dogs, on the other hand, don’t have such good vision. What they do have is an amazing sense of smell. A dog has about three times as many genes dedicated to smelling stuff than a human does, which means dogs can make out the difference to a staggering number of different scents. Where you smell “stew” on the stove, your dog smells “beef, carrots, celery, onion, potatoes and all the different spices you put in”. They’re that good. Now, with other dogs, there’s a specialized scent gland near the anus. Each dog has a unique scent at that spot, and the scent changes depending on the dog’s diet and health. Dogs also have a specialized set of nerves and brain cells particularly to interpret that special spot. To a dog, that scent is how they recognize other dogs, and can tell where dogs they recognize have been. But humans don’t have that scent gland, so your dog is always gathering information about you to ensure that you’re you. To a dog, you’re like a person showing pictures on your phone only the “pictures” are all the scents you’re exposed to. And they like to be around you because, unlike cats, dogs are very social creature and after 15,000 years of living with humans, often enjoy socializing with other species in the same way wolves would associate with their close relatives.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Kamala Harris is asked how she will fix inflation. She answers by saying generic words about what inflation is for a solid 45 seconds. Has there ever been a dumber person running for president?
Answer: Okay, let’s look at her opponent. I see you’re concerned about inflation. Fair enough. Some inflation is okay, but a lot of inflation can be very damaging, as we saw in the past four years. So, you don’t want inflation to get out of control. Fair enough. So, what if I told you one of the candidates has come out and openly said that one of the policies he will pursue as president is merely to create money to pay interest on the national debt rather than borrowing more money to pay that interest. In practical terms, this is identical to “printing money” even though no actual currency is printed. In other words, debt payments and expenditures over revenues will be paid for by increasing the money supply without any effective limit. More money will clearly mean more inflation. Lots of it. Far more than you’re experiencing now. It will also mean the U.S. dollar will drop against every other currency, making imports more expensive. So, who came up with this crazy idea? Donald Trump. You remember him - the guy who increases his cash flow by not paying his bills. He actually said straight out when he was running for President in 2016 that maybe they should just stop making payments on the debt, like he does. So, if you’re worried about inflation, and you vote for Trump, you’re going to get inflation. Lots of it. Bigly.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is every state in the United States considered a municipal corporation?
Answer: No. States are considered sovereign entities, essentially above the law except in those situations where they agree not to be. Now, incorporated municipalities are considered corporations for legal purposes - cities, towns, townships and counties. Unlike the state, they can be sued freely and for most other purposes are treated identically at law to business corporations or non-profit corporations. Laws vary from state to state as to what you can sue a state for, but for example, although you’re allowed to sue the State of Texas for wrongful conviction and incarceration, in order to get paid the legislature specifically has to allocate money in the budget to pay the judgment. Otherwise, you get bupkis.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is your favorite scene in Inglorious Basterds?
Answer: Reading the answers, it’s all a matter of taste, but I have to go with the scene where Col. Landa is sitting alone with Lt. Raine and his subordinate after arresting them at the premiere. We’re reminded through the film that Landa is brilliant and he’s seen through the subterfuge from the beginning so at this point you’re wondering what he’s up to. He makes it clear to Lt. Raine that he’s figured the whole thing out and with one call he can have the plotters arrested and save Hitler. It’s at this point we see that Landa is not thinking about the present, but the future. He’s finally figured out the war is going to be over soon and he’s most likely going to be arrested and executed for war crimes. But in an instant in this situation he has seen a way out and has a new plan to put into motion - become the savior of the Allies, end the war, and be hailed as a hero, escaping all responsibility. It gets better. Raine is trying to hide who he works for but Landa takes a guess and from Raine’s reaction he knows he’s right. It’s at this point, of course, that you realize that Christoph Waltz might be the best actor in history. He’s positively giddy. He realizes everything is going his way. It’s obvious Lt. Raine hates him and wants nothing to do with him, but that doesn’t matter because Landa has all the cards. He knows he’s won. He takes the opportunity to rationalize and try to justify all the terrible things he’s done while all Raine can do for the moment is seethe. It’s amazing that Pitt, who isn’t a bad actor either, can hold his own with this guy, but he does it. It’s a brilliant scent and Waltz plays it to the hilt but still manages to avoid overacting. He’s like a politician who has just won an election or a runner who has won the gold medal. At this point the film, Waltz plays Landa as a guy who knows everything is going his way and he can get everything he wants. Just escaping execution would be a win for him, but he’s so aware of his importance that in the next scene he asks for and gets the moon. But another good thing about this scene is it perfectly sets him up for his eventual comeuppance during the denouement.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What makes a movie "fun-stupid" instead of "time-wasting stupid" like "Jackpot!"?
Answer: I have come to the conclusion that the key factor between a “fun stupid” movie and a “time wasting stupid” movie is the art of editing. One of the best “fun stupid” movies of all time is “Airplane”, an out and out re-make of a dramatic film with the exact same plot. But “Scary Movie” is a “time-wasting stupid” movie even though it’s a similar type of movie - a parody, this time of horror movie tropes. But there’s this one thing… “Scary Movie 3″, despite the lower IMDB rating, is actually kind of good. I liked it much better. That’s because it was made by David Zucker, who was one of the creative forces behind…. “Airplane!” So why the difference. Well, comedy is hard. All movies are hard, but one of the things to remember about comedies is that if you just put in a lot of jokes and gags, you may not, as a result, get a good movie. A good example of this is…. It uses sketches that were on the successful TV program, re-films them, but doesn’t really work as a movie, whereas “The Meaning of Life”, also based on a series of sketches, worked thanks to its overarching theme. So, to make a good comedy you have to be ruthless. You have to remember “I’m making a movie” not “I’m telling a lot of jokes”. Your movie has to make some sort of sense. That means no matter how good a joke is, if it doesn’t fit within the narrative, it must go. One of the first DVDs I ever bought was of one of my favourite comedies, “The Blues Brothers”, which can be described as “stupid brilliant”. However, my copy was an “extended cut” which added more linking scenes. It turned out they were completely unnecessary and superfluous. The release of the film was tightly edited, and it shows in the final product, where the pace of the movie keeps the story moving along. But one scene that detracts from the flow of the movie can ruin it. I’m not a big fan of “Spaceballs” (although it was Mel Brook’s biggest moneymaker) and one of my quibbles is the “diner scene” where Barf and Lone Star stop for a bite to eat after they save the princess. It’s got a brilliant scene where John Hurt re-lives the chest bursting scene from “Alien”. It’s really funny, but it doesn’t belong in the movie. It adds nothing to the plot and doesn’t develop the characters. It’s a distraction from the story (Lone Star gets the girl!). Conversely though the “You idiots! You’ve captured their stunt doubles” scene works on many levels and is a brilliant take on the “close escape” trope. It advances the plot even though it requires suspension of disbelief. I’m sure the producers had a lot more jokes to tell in “Airplane!” but in the end they realized they couldn’t distract the audience from the main plot of the story, so they throw in their gags and jokes and then get right back to the story. “Scary Movie” can’t do this. At it’s heart, it’s a take-off of “Halloween” and when it sticks to that it’s not bad. However, they throw in references from other movies (“The Sixth Sense”, “The Usual Suspects”) without any thought on how it advances either the character or the plot. “Scary Movie 3” avoids that trap even though it has its own faults. So, be funny, but stick to the story. Just throwing jokes in will get stale pretty quickly.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the average time it takes for an earth-sized planet to fall into a black hole?
Answer: Okay, there’s a massive misconception about black holes here, so let’s get one thing straight - black holes are not some super-gravity matter sucking doom hole. They are just a very large amount of gravity in a very small space. If you replaced our sun with a black hole of the same mass (even though our sun isn’t big enough to form a black hole) it would be much smaller, but it would still have the same amount of gravity and all the planets would still orbit around it (although Earth, of course, will freeze solid) At the center of our galaxy is a super-massive black hole with the mass of a million suns. There are similar black holes at the center of all galaxies. However, there are still galaxies, and our own sun has survived about 18 trips around that black hole and will easily survive the next 18 without coming appreciably closer to it. Now here’s the weird thing. Thanks to orbital anomalies, the Earth is actually getting about 15cm further from the sun every year, so there’s no way it’s ever going to fall in. The same relationship means that the moon is also getting further away from the earth every year. by about 2–3 cm and we’ve actually been measuring that since the Apollo missions of 1969–1971 which left measuring instruments there. Now, most black holes form what are called “accretion discs” because pretty much every object in the universe has some sort of angular momentum. It’s actually incredibly difficult to aim a particle so that it actually falls directly to the surface of a body with gravity. As such, some black holes have massive amounts of matter going around them, faster and faster at the center, but not so fast towards the edge of the disc, and they’re all in a spiral path to the black hole’s “event horizon” - the “no exit” of our universe. Black holes with an accretion disc get more massive, but very, very slowly. Depending on the size of the black hole and the size of the disc, it could take millions or billions of years for a particular particle to fall in.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: UiF the Big Bang happened with hydrogen and helium, what created those elements? And if you can answer that, what created their origin? Assuming the Big Bang theory is accurate, how did we end up with such precise detail?
Answer: No. The Big Bang didn’t star with “hydrogen and helium”. Hydrogen didn’t exist for 380,000 years after the Big Bang and helium didn’t come into existence in significant quantities until about 100 million years after that. In the first two minutes of the history of the universe, you had four things - photons, electrons, protons, and neutrons. Those are the building blocks of atoms, but they weren’t atoms yet. About three minutes in, you get hydrogen nuclei, but no hydrogen atoms. That’s because the early universe was incredibly hot and dense. 3 minutes in, it’s only about 60 million kilometers across, but still contains all the matter and energy that will ever exist in the universe. At those temperatures and pressures, atoms simply cannot form and stay together. Electrons and nuclei pretty much float around separately for hundreds of thousands of years until finally its cool enough for some electrons to become more or less permanently attached to a nuclei, forming the first hydrogen atoms. And even then, when we have hydrogen, it’s still too hot and dense for any bodies to be held together by gravity (which is a very weak force compared to the other fundamental forces) . After 100 million years, the universe is finally cool enough for some hydrogen to coalesce permanently under gravity and form a star. At that point, the star starts making helium. To make hydrogen, you need one electron and one proton - that’s it. You can add one or two neutrons, but you don’t really need them. However, only hydrogen atoms with one neutron can fuse to form helium, which has two protons and two neutrons. That’s the same process that powers our sun. And we’ve been able to work all this out using mathematics and looking for clues in astronomical observations, like “how far away are the furthest away galaxies”. You don’t see galaxies at the very limits of observation (only background radiation from the Big Bang) so you can date the formation of stars from the distance between the background radiation and the furthest away galaxies. The rest involves calculating the nature of the universe at every point and determining how much temperature and pressure would have to drop. We can reverse that process on earth (that’s what particle accelerators do) and see how much energy we have to put into a reaction to, for example, destroy atoms The answer is “not all that much and certainly a lot less energy than their was in the very early universe”.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How does the "Big Bang" theory explain the movement of objects since the "big bang" event? Was there anything in existence before this event that could have caused this movement?
Answer: First and foremost, there was no “before” the Big Bang. Time, as we know it, started with the Big Bang and, due to relativistic effects of massive gravitational bodies, which the very early (e.g. first second) was, time got horribly dilated so from our standpoint that period of time from “zero seconds” to “one second” essentially took “forever”. In a nutshell, being in a very strong gravitational field (which still exist in black holes) is the same at travelling at “relativistic velocities” (i.e. very near the speed of light) so any person in a strong gravitational field or travelling near the speed of light would perceive time much more slowly than a person at more or less normal speeds and gravitational forces. You can think of it something like as much time passed between “zero seconds” and “one second” as has passed between “one second” and “now”. And, second, we have a name for the force that not only keeps the universe expanding but makes it expand faster with every passing second. It’s called “dark energy” and we’re just getting our heads around it, but given our observations of the universe there must be some sort of force that counteracts gravity to keep the universe from collapsing in on itself.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Has our world been warmer in the past? How can it be proven that there were periods of significantly higher temperatures?
Answer: It has, yes This isn’t really that long a period, globally speaking, but it does show in the last million years, the temperature has been higher than it is right now. Again, the problem with climate change is that although we’re not AT a high, we’re rapidly approaching one and it looks like we’re going to punch right through it. So how do we know what the temperature was a million years ago, or 10 million years ago, or 100 million years ago. Well, trees have been with us for at least 350 million years, and perhaps as many as 420 million years. One of the things we notice about trees are their leaves. There is a relationship between leaves and temperature. These are leaves of palm trees. Palms grow in tropical and sub-tropical areas. Their leaves, regardless of species, have very smooth edges. These are leaves of birch trees. Birches grow in temperate climates with cold winters. Their leaves, regardless of species, have edges that are very rough, like teeth. And the more uneven the edge of the leaf, the colder the climate is. And leaves do form fossils These leaves had smooth edges. They grew in a warm place. Over time, going through layers of fossils, you can see the edges of leaves wax and wane between smooth and jagged. Using this data, you can hit on the average annual temperature to within about 1 degree Fahrenheit.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: PreviewPoverty in America is a serious issue. How come Democrats have not championed lower taxes to help the poor?
Answer: Because poverty is tied to lower taxes. As a rule, the higher your taxes, the better the society you live in. Low taxes only help one demographic group - the rich. They go from “very high levels of wealth” to “insanely high levels of wealth”. As you can see, for marginal (i.e. taxes on highest tier of income) tax rates up to 38.6%, you don’t see growth more than about 2.5%. Once you raise them to 39.6%, you see levels of growth consistently over 3%. Part of the reason is having a permanent underclass (people who have no choice but to work for minimum wage) and crumbling infrastructure is a recipe for economic disaster. Economic growth is driven by jobs that demand high pay, not by having full employment in low paying jobs. For example, Singapore has always pursued a strategy of seeking high paying jobs, rather than guaranteeing full employment with low paying jobs like those in the textile and clothing industry. It greatly outperforms all its neighbours on all economic indicators. So with low taxes you get this Rush hour traffic on Houston’s Katy Freeway And with high taxes you get this China’s high speed rail network. Without infrastructure like transit, being poor is expensive. You spend a lot of your income on housing, food and transportation. For example, the average cost of owning a car in the United States is about $12,000 a year, and most households need two cars. The average cost of transit is about $1,800 a year. But you can’t have affordable transit without investment raised through taxes, even though roads cost money to build and maintain too.
