Question: What’s your favorite movie based on true events?
Answer: That’s a tough one, but since getting the a VHS copy from one of my best friends in a Secret Santa and realizing she hit it right on the nose, it probably has to be “Patton” Now to say it was “based on a true story” is probably closer to the truth and like any biographical picture it has to take liberties with historical facts in order to fit into the medium (it’s not a documentary!) However, the general brush strokes are pretty close to the truth, and the film has an outstanding narrative and a first-rate performance by George C. Scott, so what’s not to like. As an honourable mention, there is a documentary I like too. “The Thin Blue Line” was meant to be a documentary about a Texas psychologist who specialized in assessing murderers and always came to the conclusion that the person was irredeemable. However, while meeting up with some of the people that doctor had testified against director Errol Morris met Randall Adams, who had been convicted and sentenced to death for the murder of a police officer. Most of the people Morris had interviewed claimed to be innocent, but Adams was the only person who sounded like he was and the more Morris dug into the case the more he disliked. Adams was eventually freed and the real murderer, who had testified against Adams, actually went on to kill someone else

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the potential implications of Wrexham FC's possible promotion to the Premier League?
Answer: Well, it can’t happen this year. Wrexham A.F.C. is in League One this year, which sounds great, but it’s the third tier, two tiers below the Premier League. Now, thanks to its new ownership and more money (Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney took control of the club in November 2020) Wrexham has gone from the National League (tier 5) where it finished first in 2022–23, to League Two, where it finished 2nd in 2023–24 to earn promotion to League One. Making it to the next tier, the Championship, requires them to finish no lower than 6th in the 24 team league. There’s automatic promotion for the 1st and 2nd place clubs, and the other four have a play-off. The bookies seem to think they have a shot and they’re currently paying about 330 on a 100 bet to do so. But it’s not like Wrexham hasn’t been here before. They earned promotion to the third tier in 2002–03 by finishing 3rd in what was then the “Third Division”. However, two years later they were relegated when they finished in 22nd place and it was downhill from there. And Wrexham has never played in the first tier. In 1978–1982 they were in the 2nd tier (then “Second Division) but never finished better than 15th. And League One is full of Premier League teams that couldn’t keep up. A third of the league has played in the top flight at some point. Huddersfield Town was there as recently as 2019. Wigan Athletic was there until 2013 and has an F.A. Cup in its trophy case. And despite the money coming in, Wrexham’s stadium only holds about 12,000 people. There are seven clubs in League One who have stadiums about twice as big, or bigger. And the odds are even longer. In the history of the Premier League (since 1992), only one club, Luton Town, has gone from the National League to the Premiership. In all of English football history, only five other clubs have climbed that far. And higher standing brings much bigger risk. To compete, you need better players. To get better players, you have to sign them for more than a year in most cases. If you get relegated, you most likely won’t be able to keep them, and that may cost you money. And last year, Wrexham lost 5 million pounds. That’s not atypical for a team seeking promotion. That’s despite revenues nearly doubling and the wage bill going up by far less than 2 million pounds. Right now, Reynolds and McElhenney treat their investment as a loan, and the club owes them a total of 9 million pounds. However, even if optimistic revenue projections are met, it’s unlikely the club will take in more than about 11–12 million pounds this season. That would cover the total salary bill of Ipswich Town, but more competitive Premier League sides have salary bills of over 50 million pounds a year.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why aren't time zones based on the already-established longitude lines?
Answer: It sounds like a good idea, but geography doesn’t always make that convenient. In a lot of cases, having a one hour difference between two different places can cause major headaches. Here in Canada, we have eight. Canada is a pretty wide country, and it could be divided evenly, except that would be inconvenient for a lot of reasons For example, the Saskatchewan/Alberta border runs along a very convenient line of longitude. The problem is that Lloydminster was founded before the border was drawn. If the time zone ran down the longitude, which it does for most of its length, east Lloydminster would be in different time zone than west Lloydminster, even though people freely cross the border. Similarly, Flin Flon MB and Creighton SK practically overlap over a very convenient meridian, but most of their activity is between the two. It makes more sense for them all to share a time zone with larger Winnipeg. Most of Canada’s population lives in this box. Sure, you could try to draw the time zone down a line of longitude, but that would separate communities. For example, if you drew it down the line of longitude that forms the northern border between Ontario and Quebec, it would run through the Greater Toronto Area. Moreover, there are major financial markets in both Toronto and Montreal, and it makes more sense for them to be on the same clock. Far northwestern Ontario is a long, long way away from southern Ontario and most of the communities there get their television and radio broadcasts from Winnipeg, which isn’t that far away. As such, it’s more convenient for them to be on Winnipeg time. Most of Newfoundland’s population is in St. John’s, which is quite far east of other cities in Eastern Canada. Moreover, most communities on the island are economically tied to St. John’s. As such, they all are in a time zone that’s half-an-hour ahead of Atlantic time as if they were in the same time zone the dawn and dusk times would be inconvenient. Along the B.C./Alberta border, some communities are most closely tied to cities in Alberta, so they’re in Alberta’s time zone.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What geographical factors led to England becoming an island? Why are countries like Denmark and the Netherlands not considered islands despite being surrounded by water?
Answer: Well, it’s “Great Britain” not “England” that’s the island, and you’re right that there’s no obvious reason for it to be an island. But a new theory supposes that the English Channel was formed sometime about 10,000 years ago when a giant glacial lake over what’s now the North Sea (which is rather shallow - 700m at its deepest point) that was held back by a massive dam of ice broke and sent a massive cascade of water that essentially removed all the land between Dover and Calais in one fell swoop. We know that such geological events have happened, such as in the northwestern United States “Badlands” and near what’s now Montreal, Quebec when what’s now Lake Ontario stopped flowing into the Hudson River and instead formed the St. Lawrence River. Another clue is that the rock formations in Dover are identical in every respect to the ones in Calais, but there’s no evidence of a fault that would have allowed the two land masses to separate. Under the channel, it’s clear that the rock formations are continuous with no evidence of any discontinuity. It was this continuity that allowed the Chunnel to be constructed through a layer of clay that joins the two countries. And, sorry, to be an “island” you have to be completely surrounded by water. Denmark and The Netherlands each consist of dozens of islands, but they’ve also got parts that are clearly attached to the rest of Europe.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What events occurred during or immediately after The Big Bang? Did time begin at that point? If so, how is time measured without an absolute reference frame?
Answer: About one decillionth of a second after the start, the first photons appeared. Next, within one one-millionth of a second - we had the formation of the first electrons. Shortly after that, the universe had its first instance of expanding faster than the speed of light. Newly formed photons simply couldn’t keep up anymore and some photons were in different parts of the expanding universe so this would be the last time you could see one from the other. We can only see about a tenth of the entire universe, our “Hubblesphere”. Photons not inside our Hubblesphere at this time will never be seen by us again. Within the first second, protons and neutrons started forming. Within about three minutes, the first atomic nuclei formed. However, it would be another 380,000 years before the first hydrogen atoms formed. It was simply too hot for any electron to form a bond with an atomic nuclei. And Albert Einstein proved definitively over a hundred years ago that there is no absolute reference frame. Newton, when he first came up with the basic laws of physics in the 17th century, realized that for his system to work, there had to be an absolute reference frame, but the idea of such a thing existing bothered him greatly. Attempts to prove the existence of an absolute reference frame in the 19th century were complete and utter failures, but Einstein took this and came up with his theory showing you didn’t need one. The only thing that was constant was the speed of light, which was the same for all observers everywhere. Even now, due to relativistic effects from earth’s gravity, every single atom in your body has a unique frame of reference. They’re all very close, but they do not ever synch. In a nutshell, the atoms in your feet when you’re standing up age slower than the ones in your head. It’s not much, but it is very, very real. Now, there are some particles, like the Higgs Boson, that are absolutely fundamental to the operation of the universe, but they haven’t existed independently in nature since before photons appeared. The only way to get at them for a look is to create energies that haven’t existed since the period immediately after the Big Bang.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What happened to the Helium created during the first seconds of the Big Bang Theory? Is it permanently lost in space?
Answer: There was no helium immediately after the Big Bang. At that point you had neutrons, protons and electrons, and that was pretty much it. Helium is created when stars form and fuse hydrogen, helium being the byproduct of that reaction. In fact, the universe was too hot and dense to support atoms until about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Even in our own universe we have neutron stars where gravity is so strong it crushes protons and electrons together into neutrons. Once the universe cooled off, protons and neutrons formed nuclei which gave us hydrogen. Moreover, it was another 100 million years before stars could coalesce. That’s when nuclear fusion started and that’s where you first see helium. Then as now, pretty much all the helium in the universe is found inside stars, trapped by the star’s gravity. However, these new stars were super-massive and short lived so within a few million more years they went supernova and started spreading helium through the universe. In our own solar system, about 99.99% of helium is trapped in the sun, where it will remain until the sun sheds its atmosphere entirely and becomes a white dwarf about 5 billion years from now. 99.99% of the remaining helium is trapped in the atmospheres of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Earth’s atmosphere is warm, and it doesn’t have much gravity, so most of the helium that does make it to the atmosphere escapes into space but this amount is tiny compared to the amount in the sun and the gas giant planets. Helium on earth isn’t the result of hydrogen fusion. Helium is also created by alpha-decay, where a high atomic number element like uranium (which is created in dying stars) gives off a helium nucleus during decay which picks up stray atoms. It gets trapped in rock formations from which it can be extracted, usually from natural gas trapped in the same pockets.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why do supporters of the Democratic Party act like they are intellectually superior?
Answer: Because all the data points to Democrats being more educated, and that trend is growing, not shrinking In 2010, for the first time in American history, more Democrats than Republicans had college degrees, and that gap is growing rapidly. At about the same time, and again this is the first time in American history that it’s been clear, more Democrats than Republicans have post-graduate degrees. Not only is the share of Democrats with post-grad degrees increasing, the share of Republicans with the same educational attainment is actually shrinking. In 2016, for the first time in American history, Republican voters said that having higher education is actually a detriment to the United States. Meanwhile, not only do Democrats believe college is a good thing, they have always thought so more than Republicans have. Among whites, in 1995 there was a roughly equal split between the two parties for support from both people who had not graduated college and people who had. By 2019, over 50% of non-college educated whites were voting Republican, but only about 40% of college educated whites were voting Republican. More Democrats have 4 year and postgraduate degrees than Republicans

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How did scientists come to the conclusion that there is an initial singularity "before" the Big Bang?
Answer: You got the number wrong. It was “scientist” By the 1960s the so called “Big Bang” theory was getting more acceptance among astrophysicists but the ones who did believe the theory had arguments about the nature of the early universe - within the first fraction of a second of existence itself. Although the idea of singularities had also been kicking around by this time, many scientists couldn’t imagine how such a homogenous universe could become the universe we had today. Many of them thought that in some way the early universe had to be asymmetrical. We now know that the current universe is actually asymmetrical, but that this asymmetry arose from a very early state of the universe, not its beginning. But no-one could make the early universe work mathematically until a fairly bright grad student at Cambridge presented his doctoral thesis. He probably would not have come up with it had he been supervised by Fred Hoyle, who was his original choice, as Hoyle didn’t believe the Big Bang theory. Instead, he studied under Dennis Sciama, who recognized the man’s incredibly brilliance and thought he might be up to the task. So, in 1966, a young man who had recently been diagnosed with terminal ALS and was given just a few years to live presented his thesis on the problem and then later that year published a paper based on his thesis. His math showed that if general relativity were correct, the early universe had to have been a singularity. There was no other possible state. His thesis panel was suitably impressed and the young newly minted doctor soon became one of the best known scientists in his field. And, in case you haven’t guessed, it was this fellow Stephen Hawking, who could at the time still get around with crutches. He managed to hang on for a good long period after that and made other contributions to his field which determined the fate of the universe as we understand it - bracketing both the beginning and the end. Oh, and if you want to read his thesis, the original is available for free online.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is there a Canadian equivalent to American networks like HBO and Showtime? Why is there a difference in television networks between the two countries?
Answer: Not really. In the early days of pay-TV, we did have similar services, but they didn’t last very long. For the most part, nowadays you subscribe to a “package” which can include movie channels. And we do get HBO in Canada, although its programming isn’t identical. The big issue is media rights, which are broken down by country. As a rule, U.S. cable broadcasters only have the right to show their shows in the United States. Canada is considered a completely different jurisdiction as far as broadcasting rights are concerned, so we get equivalent networks here that show similar types of programing. The other issue is that under Canadian law, cable channels have to show a certain amount of Canadian produced content. Ironically, that means Canadian stations pay less for programs than American ones have to. For example, “The Sopranos” was only available if you had a subscription to HBO. Here in Canada, it was shown on the broadcast network CTV, which you could watch from Buffalo or Detroit if you had an antenna. Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why did Terry Fox run across Canada?
Answer: One thing that seems to have been missed in all the other answers was that before his cancer diagnosis and subsequent amputation of his leg, Fox was a pretty good high school athlete. He had wanted to be a basketball player, but was short so took up cross-country running to keep in shape. He eventually made the basketball team and in his final year he was voted his school’s athlete of the year. He planned to go to university to study kinesiology with a goal of becoming a physical education teacher. Some of that was derailed when he found that the knee he thought he had hurt in a minor traffic accident turned out to be an osteosarcoma. That resulted in his leg being amputated. But that didn’t slow him down. He was fitted with an artificial leg and was back running. Then he met Rick Hansen (later “The Man in Motion”) and was recruited to join a wheelchair basketball team. His team won three national championships and he was chosen as an all-star. But it all changed after he learned about Dick Traum, the first amputee to complete the New York City Marathon. Fox decided to follow in his footsteps (literally) and put his cross-country training back into motion so that he could complete a marathon too. But inside, he was seething. Although he had survived cancer, many of his fellow patients did not, and he found that even though his chances were 50% when treated, only a few years earlier they would have been as low as 15%. He secretly formed a goal of running across the country to raise awareness for the need for funding cancer research. After he finished dead last in a 17km road race (which was greeted with massive cheers from the spectators and other participants), he revealed his plans. His mother tried to talk him out of it, but he persevered and the rest, as they say, is history. He was hoping he would maybe raise $1 million. Instead, he raised $1.7 million by the time he had to cut his run short in Ontario.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: When are the least crowded times to ride the MTA (New York)?
Answer: The MTA is packed during morning (7 am - 10 am) and evening (4 pm - 7 pm) rush hours but the rest of the day it’s not too bad and it can be practically deserted on weekends and holidays. It’s also not bad if you’re heading “in the wrong direction”, for example, you’re in Manhattan but decide to take a trip out to Brooklyn in the morning. But when it’s packed, it’s packed. The Times Square - Grand Central Shuttle will be shoulder to shoulder with a wait for trains during busy times as its a key route. One of the most frustrating things about riding the subway in Manhattan is there are lots of closely packed uptown/downtown routes, but the crosstown routes are spread far apart and there aren’t as many of them.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can a Canadian purchase the rights to a US TV show for broadcast in Canada?
Answer: Yes, and Canadian networks, cable channels and independent stations regularly purchase Canadian rights to U.S. programming, both network and syndicated, every season. But there are problems. Canadian broadcasters (which includes cable channels) have to air a minimum number of hours of Canadian produced programming every week, and the national broadcaster, the CBC, is under a mandate to show as little foreign produced programming as is possible. This leads to some very interesting situations. For example, the new Star Trek shows are “streaming only” in the United States, but here in Canada, CTV (the biggest private television network) owns the rights to show it on their Sci-Fi cable channel, and does so for the regular subscription fees. It also streams the program for free on its website, so it’s easier to watch some U.S. programming in Canada than it is to watch it in the United States. As a rule, the money that producers get for the U.S. rights to the programs they produce pay all their production costs, so foreign sales are totally “gravy” - pure profit. There is a competitive market for U.S. programming in Canada and in the past even an independent station in a large market (Hamilton, Ontario’s CHCH, which reaches about 11 million people in Southern Ontario and the Niagara Frontier in New York) could compete for U.S. programming rights. The big two players are CTV (founded in 1960) which has one network made stations in large markets nationally and another made up of stations in smaller markets (CTV2), and Global (founded in 1973) which has strategically placed stations stations west of Quebec to provide as much broadcast coverage as possible. Both also own a number of cable channels. The little player is Bell Media, which owns a number of independent stations (including CITY and CFMT in Toronto) along with a number of cable channels. There are also French language broadcasters who arrange for sub-titled or dubbed versions of American shows. And then there are still a few independents, like CHCH which was once owned by Global which tried to use it as a new network anchor for independent stations but now has separate ownership and mostly programs independently. It mostly broadcasts reruns and movies on top of local programming, but in the past it regularly showed American network programming.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why do many Americans not follow the "Tour de France" cycling event? Is there a lack of coverage by American media outlets for this sport? If yes, what are the reasons for this lack of coverage?
Answer: Back twenty years ago, I followed the Tour as closely as I could given work and school commitments. But the shine largely came off the race when the doping allegations were proved to be correct. The Tour organizers themselves seem not to have been complicit, but it turned out that pretty much everyone in the race from the stars on down were regularly taking banned performance enhancing substances. One of them, erythropoietin or “EPO” for short, speeds up the body’s production of red blood cells. However, it’s side effects are massive as it can cause clotting conditions, so you’re essentially taking your life into your own hands if you use it for cheating. Is the Tour legit now? It’s hard to say. Certainly, it used to be legit but when Greg Le Monde, the star who made cycling popular in the United States started finishing further and further behind with the same times he had always posted and refused to “dope”, he retired and started pointing fingers. For that he was ridiculed by everyone despite turning out to be right (to be fair, he had been rehabilitated in the sport). But make no mistake - the cycling teams were playing roulette with people’s lives and suffered very little for it. They’ve got a lot of work to do to restore their reputation.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How does QE differ from interest rate cuts?
Answer: You can only cut interest rates so low. How does 0% sound? Yeah, if you’re a central banker a lot of banks are going to take you up on that, but there’s no guarantee they will so anything but sit on the money, and in an economic crisis where there’s deflation and high unemployment that’s the last thing you want. Maybe you could loan banks money and have you pay less money back - negative interest. Same problem. So the deal with Quantitative Easing is that if a bank comes to you showing they loaned out money, you do lend them that money at zero interest. They make money from charging interest on the loan, and it meets the government’s policy of increasing the money supply without the risk that the money will just be sitting in a vault somewhere.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the process for a lawyer to become a judge in Canada?
Answer: Well, there are pretty much three types of judges: The process varies for all three types, but in most cases an opening for a judicial appointment will be advertised in publications likely to be read by lawyers. They will fill out an application form and provide a resume of their qualifications as a barrister and solicitor. Lawyers who practice in court are preferred, but it’s not an absolute requirement - I’ve known people who made associate chief justice based on commercial law experience only, and law professors often become judges. These will go to a local committee who will generally list three preferred choices and cabinet picks one of those three. There is a preference for local lawyers to be appointed, but again it’s not a requirement. There is usually some minimum requirement for having practiced depending on the position. Ironically, the requirement is generally higher for the less senior positions. For example, to be appointed a “master” in Toronto (essentially a mini-judge who rules on motions and construction lien actions) you need 20 years experience. A superior court judge only needs five. One of the reasons for that is that the lower the level of a judge, the more cases you have to handle on a daily basis. For example, a provincial court judge may have to deal with several hundred cases a day, while a superior court judge may not have to deal with more than three.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it possible for someone with a criminal record to be hired by the Canadian government after receiving a pardon?
Answer: It’s possible for someone with a criminal record to be hired by the Canadian government even before they get a pardon. The Canadian and provincial governments have for the past several decades gone out of their way to ensure that persons with a criminal record are considered for job opportunities suitable for them without being screened for their criminal record. The exceptions are jobs where the previous criminal record has a direct bearing on the job. The federal and provincial human rights code all make previous criminal history a protected category - if you fail to hire someone solely on the basis of a criminal record, that’s a human rights violation unless you can demonstrate the criminal record is directly relevant. Pardons Canada has a specific section that deals with the issue. But as a rule, under Canadian law, automatically disqualifying someone for anything due to a criminal record is improper, even if they’re applying to a profession. The professional body must be able to articulate why the conviction disqualifies a person, although they may freely do additional screening for anyone with a criminal record. The rule is “be honest”. Don’t try to hide a criminal record if you’re asked about it. When I applied for an Ontario government job, after the interview they gave me their policy which basically said a criminal conviction would not prevent me from getting the job unless I didn’t tell them about it. In many cases, even if you receive a criminal record suspension, you still have to disclose a conviction. A member of the FLQ was allowed to be a lawyer despite his conviction, and was later pardoned, but lost his judgeship because he didn’t disclose it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How is the Canadian government addressing the housing crisis in Toronto?
Answer: By putting up $82 billion in matching funds for affordable housing projects. But there’s a massive problem. Municipal laws pretty much prohibit the construction of affordable housing. There’s not much the federal government is doing about that. Now, here in Ontario, one of the good things the Ford government did was to require cities to demonstrate that restrictive zoning laws were justifiable, giving the Local Planning Appeal Tribunal, an Ontario government agency, authority to overrule zoning requirements when they got in the way of affordable housing development. The Ontario government hoped that cities would then understand the importance of changing their own zoning laws to allow more development. That didn’t happen. Pretty much every municipality, mayor and local councilor doubled down on restrictive zoning, largely at the insistence of their constituents. They slightly relaxed the rules, but that added so little land as to makes no never mind. The provincial government also promised grants to cities. They set 10 year building targets for every municipality in the province and if you meet your annual goal you get a grant. Some cities, like Toronto, actually exceeded their goals in the first year, but others, like Brampton (an outer Toronto suburb) didn’t even come close (it was about 50%). Now, the thing is that some cities, like Toronto, are fully built out and, in Toronto’s case, have been since the 1980s. As such, to create more housing, that means redevelopment - mostly disused commercial and industrial lands. The problem is those lands aren’t zoned for housing and plans meet a lot of local opposition. One such redevelopment is the Galleria Mall, which lost its last anchor tenant when Target left Canada. The mall lands and a nearby park were subject to a proposal to add housing plus some retail, and the park would be re-worked. One of the problems that arose was that the park would lose its hockey rink and even though there are other hockey rinks in the area, and a skating rink would still be there, the project was delayed. Back in my old neighbourhood, a proposal to build affordable housing on a bit of land that was originally slated to become a freeway was abandoned after challenges and appeals made it unfeasible economically. And there’s nothing the federal government can do about that. The “outer suburbs” are not built up, and there’s lots of land, but part of the issue is the province proposed opening up green space to development, which went over massively badly. It’s not going to help because new development in the outer suburbs tends to be oversized houses on massive pieces of land with no access to transit. Traffic is bad in Toronto and that’s only going to make it worse. So the sort of housing Toronto desperately needs - modest, affordable and transit friendly, takes forever to get going. There’s nothing the federal government can do about that. The problem is mostly local.

Question: What is the origin of precedent in law? Is the source of precedent important?
Answer: In 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, also became King of England and noticed that English law was a mess. Pretty much every location in his realm had different laws based on the custom of the area. As such, as he appointed judges to go out from town to town (“circuit judges”), he decreed that they had to write all their decisions down and make them available at a central place so they could all refer to them. They then had to follow any decision that had previously been made in deciding new cases so that England would have a “common law” that would be the same everywhere. He hoped that this would improve commerce. This system was used alongside Norman law at first, but by 1154 common law was given precedence. This was a brand new system. Most places in Europe either worked on the same “customary” system of laws, or they modified codified Roman law for their own purposes. The oldest common law precedent is generally held to be Furrer v. Snelling, a case from 1220 that prohibited plaintiffs from recovering more in damages than they had actually suffered under the terms of a contract. In that case, the defendant agreed to land rent of 20 pounds a year for 4.5 years (90 pounds) but was sued for 100 pounds. The court only ordered 90 pounds to be paid. That’s still the rule today.

Question: Are helicopters cheaper and safer to use for transportation than airplanes? If so, why aren't they used more often?

A helicopter without power is pretty much uncontrollable.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the origin of using squiggly lines instead of letters when writing words? What is the purpose or meaning behind this practice?
Answer: “Squiggly lines” or, to give it its technical name, “cursive writing”, dates back to Roman times and was developed to deal with some of the technical limitations of writing with a quill. Quills don’t hold much ink, and they’re very easy to damage (they need constant resharpening). Lifting a quill from the page risks ink dripping from it, and when you lift it and put it down constantly the quill wears out more quickly. In England, cursive writing became more common after the Norman Conquest when a massive number of scribes followed William the Conqueror and started taking a census and following William’s decree that judges had to write down their legal decisions for others to read so that there would be “common law” throughout his British realms. The practice caught on because it was much faster to write this way. But cursive writing was horribly inconsistent. It was in the 17th and 18th century that English schools started to teach standardized cursive writing, using consistent strokes, a practice that continued well into the 20th century. But cursive comes with drawbacks. It’s horribly difficult to read, sometimes even for the person who wrote it. To make it easier to read, you have to go more slowly, which defeats the purpose. Besides, writing completely changed in the mid 1950s when Marcel Bich invented a new type of pen the “Bic Crystal” The Bic flowed more smoothly than a fountain pen, but it also didn’t drop ink when lifted from the page and it was difficult to damage. This same basic design has been in use for 70 years now and there have only been marginal improvements. The 100 billionth Bic pen was sold in 2006, and its still going strong.

Question: What British saying is not understood in the US?

That’s when you trap them and instead of defining it, you instead show them examples of how it’s used, which are, as they say on the west side of the pond, “bogus”. Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it true that driving long distances on highways can make your car more fuel-efficient? If so, what is the reason behind this?
Answer: It’s actually the reverse - your car is more fuel efficient when it’s driving on a highway, assuming you don’t go overboard on the speed. “City Driving”, particularly in an internal combustion vehicle, is very fuel inefficient as you stop all the time (but still use fuel) and are constantly changing speeds. Your car is most fuel efficient when it is travelling at a constant speed. Fuel isn’t wasted when you speed up or slow down the engine to adjust to immediate conditions, or by stopping for traffic lights (although stopping for traffic isn’t good either). But there’s a catch - the faster you go the harder your engine has to work against mechanical and road friction to keep your speed up. There’s a “sweet spot” between about 55–65 mph where your car’s engine is the most comfortable and has the highest efficiency. Speeding up or slowing down wastes fuel either because your car isn’t working as efficiently (slow speeds) or you’re using too much fuel to overcome extra forces on your car (at high speeds).

Question: Why are some airports not built near major highways or train stations? For instance, why is JFK airport not located next to a subway station?

But the big problem is that airports require massive amounts of flat land with no obstructions near them. That’s why they often get built out in the middle of nowhere. Sometimes you’re lucky and there’s a big piece of flat land near the city center, or at least you can create one (e.g. Boston Logan, Detroit City) but most of the time to get the necessary land you have to move way out of the city. One of the biggest times this backfired was in the 1970s when the Canadian government thought that Montreal needed a really big airport. Currently, it’s only used for freight traffic. Montreal’s main airport is Pierre Trudeau in Dorval (it’s on the map) and the city is busy building a light rail link there. In addition, some cities, like Dallas, didn’t ever embrace transit. There’s now light rail service to Dallas-Fort Worth Airport from both Fort Worth and Dallas, but its rather recent. No-one really liked where DFW was located, but at the time it was the largest airport in the United States and they needed a lot of room.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How did the United States develop its extensive highway system? Were there any highways before the creation of interstates?
Answer: Easy answer, it spent a sh*t-ton of cash. The legislation that funded the Interstate system was passed in 1957 and allocated $25 billion a year from 1957 to 1969. It was a complicated funding system that required states to chip in, but to give you some comparison, total government general revenues (outside of Social Security) in 1957 were $66 billion, so about 40% of all revenue went to the Interstates (of course, more money was borrowed for the purpose). In other terms, the purchasing power of $25 billion in 1957 is the equivalent of about $275 billion today. Now, were there national highways before this? Yes there were. There were even some very good freeways, like the New York State Thruway from Buffalo to New York City. However, the big problem was that most highways were the responsibility of state governments, and they often made very little effort to connect their highways to highways in other states. Yes, there were “U.S. Highways”, but they were often narrow, hard to navigate as they changed course frequently, and ran through the middle of cities on their way. For example, the famous U.S. Route 66 which ran from Chicago to Los Angeles and was considered one of the best highways in the country kept changing its route, was only two lanes paved in most places, and was horribly congested. For example, somewhere there is an intersection in a town where both streets were once part of Highway 66. The Interstates also made year round travel possible. Particularly in the west, many routes became impassible in winter, or when water levels were high. In 1915, this road, which was simply a series of wooden planks laid across the desert, ran from Yuma to San Diego, just over 170 miles. This was considered a breakthrough at the time. The remnants of the road still exist next to Interstate 8, which eventually replaced it. Today, you can make the same drive in about two-and-a-half hours. Now, it took forever and there are still gaps in the system. I remember coming down I-75 from Detroit to Orlando in the 1970s and at that time there were still two massive gaps that required you to drive on other highways. But it’s amazing what’s possible. This is I-80 in Northern California in winter. It passes through the Donner Pass where in the 19th century a party of people heading to California were trapped when a heavy snowfall blocked their path. Some of them resorted to cannibalism. Even though the Donner Pass still gets heavy snowfall, nowadays the plows come out and re-open the highway.

Question: Can you explain the difference between a run and pass play in American football?
Answer: On thinking about it, the difference isn’t as clear cut as you might first think. Technically, a play is only a “pass” if the ball is thrown in a forward motion by the quarterback (i.e. towards the opponent’s goal line). In other words, only a “forward pass” is a pass play. That’s the case whether the receiver catches it or not. However, it’s not a pass play if: A lot of this has an effect on what’s a legal block. In the modern game, on a “pass play”, which now includes a play where the quarterback runs with the ball, offensive players may extend their hands in front of them as long as they’re not moving forward (if they are moving forward, it’s illegal use of the hands or “holding” in common parlance). It also affects where offensive linemen may go. On a pass play, offensive linemen may not go more than five yards past the line of scrimmage unless they’re in active contact with a defensive player until the ball is thrown. On a running play, an offensive lineman can run as far down the field as they want.

Question: What is the distance and estimated cost of gas for driving across Canada on its highways?
Answer: Well, I’m going to assume you want to go on an all land route, so no ferries, although it won’t make much difference in the long run. So that’s roughly Sydney, Nova Scotia to Vancouver, British Columbia via Montreal through western Quebec (which shaves about 200km off the trip). Those are the two points of the country that are both on the “mainland” or, at least in Cape Breton Island’s case, the body of water you have to cross is fairly shallow and a causeway joins it to the rest of the country. Of course, you will have to cross bridges at Quebec City, near Montreal, and in Nipigon, ON. I’m also assuming you want the all-Canadian route. Going through the United States would be faster, less distant and cheaper with lower gas prices. So over the shortest rout, that’s roughly 6,200 km. Note that this route goes through some very sparsely populated parts of Quebec and Ontario, but most of the rest of it is through fairly well populated parts of the rest of the province. Like I said, going through the more “civilized” route adds about 200 km. to the trip. The average Canadian car has an efficiency of about 8.6L per 100 km travelled, so that’s easy math - the trip will need about 533 liters of fuel. The average cost of gas in Canada is tough to determine because there are big regional variations. However, it appears right now it runs about $1.64 Cdn. a liter, although that will vary a lot. So, roughly speaking, expect your gasoline bill to be about $875 for the trip. Naturally, it’s going to be less in a Honda Civic and more in a Ford F-150. Oh, and please note that in some places along this route, gas stations are few and far between, so be sure to fill up when you can.

Question: What led to the abandonment of elevated trains in NYC? What form of transportation replaced them?
Answer: Well, elevated lines have only been entirely replaced in Manhattan. There are still elevated lines in most of the boroughs of Brooklyn, Queens and The Bronx. But in Manhattan they proved particularly problematic. People really don’t understand how elevated trains dominated a streetscape. This is the Third Avenue El, and as you can see it pretty much covers the whole street. As car traffic started to increase, elevated highways just got in the way. The remaining elevated trains just posed a hazard, as anyone who has seen “The French Connection” can attest to. Elevated trains were also very noisy. That affected both residents and businesses. On top of everything else, elevated trains had to worry about structural issues. Having a buried train with tracks sitting on solid bedrock wasn’t a problem. Having trains sitting on a steel structure thirty feet in the air meant that train weights had to be strictly regulated, and by the 1940s this meant using materials that were as light as possible, including wood. It was soon realized that having light trains was a disaster waiting to happen because they would totally collapse in a crash. Having a steel structure outdoors in New York’s climate also meant you could expect it to deteriorate over time - not a problem for buried tracks. The aesthetics got to be an issue too. Elevated trains were ugly and made the streets they were on look ugly too. Remember it wasn’t too long before that Park Avenue had most of the city’s passenger railways running down the middle of the street. It’s only been in fairly recent times that the trains have been covered up. Third Avenue in modern times. And, indeed, by 1950 Manhattan had surplus north-south capacity. The need for the Third Avenue Line and other elevated railways like the Ninth Avenue Line (the oldest in the city) became less important with subways under Lexington, 6th, 7th, Broadway and 8th avenues. And who knew it was going to take so long to get the 2nd avenue subway built, which was already in the planning stages.

Question: Is it true that the French say "J'aime la France" instead of "Je t'aime la France" when expressing love for their country?
Answer: French has a unique syntax where a pronoun is involved. In most cases, French follows Subject - Verb - Object syntax, just like English. However, if a pronoun is used, it uses Subject - Object - Verb syntax. “Je t’aime” means “I like you”. Even though “you” is the object of the sentence, in French, since it’s a pronoun it goes before the noun. Here, the “t’” is a contraction of the pronoun “tu”, the familiar second person personal pronoun. Technically, “Je vous aime” is fine, but it’s unlikely you would be using such a formal construction to say you liked someone. But “France” isn’t a pronoun, it’s a proper noun. As such, regular syntax applies. It’s the same for any noun - “J’aime les pommes” - I like apples; “J’aime le foot” - I like football. What really bugs me about French is the necessity to use a personal pronoun as the object even if you’re both the subject and the object of the sentence with some verbs like “remember” and “feel”. Je me souvien. Je me sens mal.

Question: How do umpires tell when a swing is checked?
Answer: To add to Mr. Murray’s answer, a swing is “full” if the top of the bat goes over the first base line for a right handed batter, or the third base line for a left handed batter. If the top of the bat doesn’t cross the line, it’s a “check swing” and it’s called either a ball or strike depending on whether the ball went through the strike zone. This rule prevents a batter from pretty much swinging with power from the handle alone without actually moving the top of the bat forward. A decent batter can actually chop the ball without having to move the top of the bat forward too much, but can’t accomplish that unless the top of the bat goes over the baseline. And it’s an appeal play. The home plate umpire can call “strike” without checking, but the batter can ask for a ruling from the base umpire, who can call either “strike” or “ball” based on their view of the swing.

Question: Is it true that baseball is not as popular in America as other sports, despite its long history in the country? If so, what are the reasons for this?

It doesn’t list the Toronto Blue Jays, which technically doesn’t get any cable television revenue. However, the baseball club is owned by Rogers Communications, which runs the Canadian cable network SportsNet, which broadcasts all the Jays games. But think about it - MLB still has a big television following even though it doesn’t have a national television contract. The NBA does and still only pulls in a few more viewers. Moreover, MLB has embraced the internet more than other sports leagues have. Just about every baseball game is now available online, if not live, then in replay. And at the local level, although the number has dropped substantially since the advent of television, there are still 206 MLB affiliated minor league clubs in the United States, Canada and the Dominican Republic. No other pro sport in the United States comes close to that.

Question: Is it more difficult for MLB batters to hit curveballs compared to fastballs due to their unpredictable nature?
Answer: No. All pitches travel in an unpredictable nature as they all leave the pitcher’s arm with some sort of spin and, if they don’t, like a knuckleball, they’re really unpredictable. Curveballs are actually easier to hit because they travel more slowly as they approach the batter, giving the batter an opportunity to predict where they’re headed. Fastballs are hard to hit because the batter gets practically no time to make a decision to swing on the pitch.
