Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it possible to hit a home run off of a curveball in baseball?
Answer: Certainly. It can even be easier if you know a breaking ball is coming because in order to get it to break, the ball has to be thrown slower. That gives the batter more time to spot it and hit it in the sweet spot. If you connect with a fast ball, you can use the momentum of the ball as it bounces off the bat to increase its exit velocity, and that can give it distance, but if you get all of a curve ball it’s not going to be an issue - it’s going for distance. Famously in the movie “Major League”, Pedro Cerrano has difficulty hitting curve balls and is attempting to use his spirit idol “Jojo” to overcome this, but after getting two strikes on curves he decides to stop trying to rely on Jojo and instead crushes the pitch. Now, if you’re in the home run derby you get the pitcher to throw fastballs right down the center of the strike zone. That gives you the best chance of hitting for distance. However, if you have a curve coming outside and hit it towards the end of the bat, the swing actually gives the bat a higher velocity at the end so you get more speed anyway. Pitchers don’t throw curve balls because they’re harder to hit - they’re actually easier to hit because they travel more slowly. They do it because if you feed a hitter fastballs they will connect at some point. Curves work when the batter is expecting a fastball, but don’t when the batter is expecting a curve ball.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How is an error defined in Major League Baseball (MLB) statistics?
Answer: According to Major League Baseball: A fielder is given an error if, in the judgment of the official scorer, he fails to convert an out on a play that an average fielder should have made. Fielders can also be given errors if they make a poor play that allows one or more runners to advance on the bases. A batter does not necessarily need to reach base for a fielder to be given an error. If he drops a foul ball that extends an at-bat, that fielder can also be assessed an error. In modern practice, an error on a batted ball is only assessed if the fielder makes contact with the ball and fails to catch it. If the fielder merely misplays a ball and doesn’t come close to it as a result, allowing it to drop, it’s a base hit instead. However, it’s still an error to make a throw that goes well beyond the ability of a baseman to catch, resulting in it either going into foul territory or the outfield.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why is Toronto’s weather unpredictable nowadays?
Answer: Oh, Toronto’s weather has always been unpredictable. That’s the cost of living in a temperate climate - one that changes from day to day, sometimes drastically. It’s a combination of things - the proximity to the lake (which moderates the temperature, but also creates small scale weather systems), the prevailing westerly winds (which means we get Alberta’s leftover weather most of the time), being on the west side of the coastal mountains (which means weather systems from as far south as the Gulf of Mexico can creep up the west side of the mountains without escaping) and the massive amount of relatively flat land to the west (which means weather systems that form in Arizona can actually make it here). Add to that the city sits in a bit of a depression surrounded by higher land and you get a situation where a lot can happen. But you are right that we are getting more extremes. Storms that flooded the lower Don used to be pretty scarce, but now they happen every couple of years and there’s no way to prevent them despite work being done in the Portlands right now to divert the river into new channels. Heat waves also seem to be more common. That’s most likely climate change making Toronto substantially warmer than it used to be. One of the indications of a warmer climate is this little guy - the American opossum. Many similar species like squirrels and raccoons have been here for ages in the cold weather, but Toronto’s weather was just a tad too cold for this little fellow. That’s no longer the case and you see more of these things with each passing year.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Should America have Christianity as its official religion, like Britain?
Answer: You’re misinformed. Britain’s official religion is not “Christianity”. It’s “The Church of England”. Here’s the head of the church. Of course, nowadays, the King doesn’t actually have any authority within the Church. Back in the day, it was the King who picked bishops and archbishops, but right now if the Church needed a new bishop, here’s the fellow who would pick. Keir Starmer, who is the Prime Minister. High members of the church are now chosen by the government. Now, ironically, hardly anyone in the UK actually goes to Church of England services even though, in theory, about half the population belongs to the Church. That’s misleading because many are members of the Church of Scotland and the Church of Ireland which, although associated with the Church of England, aren’t headed up by the King - they’ve been disestablished, which is what that word means. Moreover, only about 700,000 members of the Church of England show up for weekly services now. That’s not very good for a church that ostensibly has 30 million members. In fact there are more than 700,000 2SLGBTQA+ individuals in the UK, and there are far more people with no religious belief in the UK too. So, despite having an official state church, hardly anyone in the UK is religious now. Religious services are skewing older with every year. And you say “Christianity”. There’s no such religion as “Christianity”. There are about 100,000 distinct religions in the United States alone that are “Christian” and there’s a dispute about some of those (like the Jehovah’s Witnesses and the Latter Day Saints). Although the majority of Americans identify as “Christian” that covers a very large number of independently run religious groups. The Baptists, which are the single largest denomination, are split into about twelve major “conventions” that cover both “mainstream” and “evangelical” rules. And even Baptists change. Jimmy Carter used to be associated with the Southern Baptist Convention, but withdrew over their refusal to allow women to serve as ministers in the church. That had been a rule, and it was not enforced due to a shortage of ministers, but several congregations split from the convention when the convention threatened to remove them over the rule. For example, Joel Osteen here is considered to run a “non-denominational Christian church” which consists of a single very large congregation. However, Osteen was raised in the Southern Baptist convention and became the senior pastor of the Lakewood Church when it was part of the convention, but when it moved to the Compaq Centre in 2005 he broke away from the convention. But one thing that American churches have in common is that none of their religious leaders are appointed by the government. That’s one of the reasons that the Baptists were one of the strongest proponents of the separation of church and state.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why does Canada produce a lot of movies but not many blockbuster hits? Is it due to lack of funding or other factors?
Answer: Producing a blockbuster requires the producer to get about $100-$200 million in funding committed before starting shooting, and that kind of money simply isn’t available in Canada. Banks and investors simply aren’t interested in providing money to film producers as even in Hollywood it’s a very risky business with no guarantee of a pay-out. As such, Canadian films have a different funding model that pretty much guarantees a producer will make some money from a film, but almost certainly won’t make a lot of it. In order to get films made (particularly for the Quebec French-speaking market, which produces the most domestic films every year) there’s a “grant and payback” system where most of the money you need to make a film will be provided by the government, and any money made by the film will go right back to the government for use on future film projects. This is pretty much a break-even proposition, so the only way to make money is to allow the producers to take a fee for their services, something which is completely illegal in the United States. One of the big problems is that Canada is one of the few countries in the world without its own film distribution system. Film distribution in Canada is almost entirely controlled by American studios that treat Canadian film theatres as an extension of American ones. If you want to distribute your film in Canada you either need to convince an American company to distribute it (good luck with that) or find an exhibitor who will give you some screen space for a limited release. A widespread release is pretty much out of the question as providing the necessary copies will probably be out of your budget. You probably won’t have a promotional budget either, or if you do, it will be miniscule. Maudie, a 2016 film about Nova Scotia folk artist Maud Lewis, was a “success” by Canadian standards, making $11.5 million on a budget of 6 million Euros. Oh, yeah, it was co-produced in Ireland. However, note that our two main stars are Sally Hawkins (English) and Ethan Hawke (American). It’s easier to get financing if you can put recognizable stars in the leads. Although the film takes place in Nova Scotia, it was shot in Newfoundland, almost certainly to get a grant from the province to finance production. The government agencies that produce films want to produce a lot of them, so quantity is more important than box office appeal. Moreover, Maudie did well with critics (90% on Rotten Tomatoes) and film festivals (where it won 25 awards). Even audiences liked it (On Rotten Tomatoes it carries an 89% positive rating, and a respectable 7.6 on IMDB). Now, Canadian grants (which come from both the federal government and the provinces, check the credits of your next film to see which provinces provided funding) also finance blockbusters (if they’re shot in Canada) but again give similarly modest amounts. Sometimes those modest amounts can make or break a film’s budget, but no government agency is going to find $100 million where they could make 20 films for the same price. Even if no-one sees it. And my experience with “Maudie” was being at the Varsity Cinema in Toronto with some friends where they were literally giving out free passes to see it about a week in advance. You promote a film the best way you can, even if you have to pay cinemas to show it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What makes something a sitcom?
Answer: Another characteristic of a sitcom is that each episode tells a separate story with a distinct plot that’s resolved by the end of the episode. There may be sub-plots within that story, but each scene will relate back to the main story even if it seems to be independent at first. One of the most famous sitcom episodes in history is “Turkeys Away”, a first season episode of “WKRP in Cincinnati”. It’s Thanksgiving and the station needs a promotion to draw listeners and the station’s manager, Mr. Carlson, takes over the task even though he does very little work at the station. The details of the promotion are kept secret but the story involves Carlson giving directions to the staff and being optimistic about it. In the end, the promotion involves dropping turkeys out of a helicopter, which “hit the ground like sacks of wet cement”. As the staff struggles to deal with the fallout from the disaster, a downfallen Carlson returns to the station to declare “As god as my witness, I thought turkeys could fly”.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it true that English is the language from which all the other languages of the world are descended? After all, isn’t English the language of God himself, because isn’t it the language of the Bible, as King James the First reputedly said?
Answer: That’s not even close to being true. “English” didn’t even exist as a separate language until about 600 C.E. That’s when we see the first texts written in the language and, at that time, the language looked like this: As far as we know, there is no “single root language”, but the oldest languages in the world are traced to the Bushmen, a group of people in southwest Africa who speak about 200 different languages that are mutually unintelligible And assuming that what we know about God is true, the first written texts about him are about two-thousand years older than the English language. And, as has been noted, the King James Bible wasn’t even the first English language bible. It was just the first royal approved translation as the King commissioned the translation and it became the standard for the Church of England thereafter. However, in previous centuries, all the Bibles in England most likely would have been in Latin because that was the language of the Catholic mass. Catholicism didn’t start doing mass in vernacular languages until the mid 20th century.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why are so many Canadians interested in the politics of the United States?
Answer: Pierre Trudeau said this over fifty years ago, but it’s been true for the entire history of Canada, even before Canada became a nation. Since the American Revolution, the United States attempted to take over Canada (1812–1814), got into a dispute about its Pacific border (1840) then nearly got into a war because the border wasn’t clear, got into a dispute about the border between Maine and Quebec (1825), got into a dispute about the border with Alaska (1902), So although Americans can generally ignore Canadian politics with no consequences, it’s foolhardy for a Canadian to think the same is possible. The economies of the two nations have always been inextricably linked (Even during the war of 1812, trade hardly slowed down) and when something catastrophic happens to the United States (like the Civil War) it inevitably spills over (Confederates who robbed a bank in Vermont fled to Quebec during the war - keep us out of it please).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Should the "intelligent design" theory of the origin of life be taken seriously?
Answer: No. Even a cursory examination of anatomy will show structures throughout the body of pretty much any living thing that simply don’t make sense. Just take the human eye, which intelligent design proponents says “could not have come about by chance” or “wouldn’t work if it was incomplete” both of which are just wrong, but more about that later. Now, see the optic nerve. It actually passes into the eye and creates an area, the “blind spot” where there aren’t any light sensing cells. Moreover, all the nerves and blood vessels in the eye aren’t behind the light sensing layer, they’re in front of it, where they actually block light coming in. The eye must keep a roughly spherical shape to work, but it’s supported entirely by the internal pressure of fluid. There’s no such thing as a “detached retina” because the retina isn’t attached to anything - the condition arises when the eyeball starts to leak and the retina collapses into it. Even worse, most people have poor eyesight. I started wearing glasses for farsightedness when I was ten. Then my cornea started to cloud (cataracts, which are very common) and the lenses for that condition fixed my farsightedness, but made me extremely nearsighted. Examples like this abound in nature, like the laryngeal nerve, which for some reason although it links the brain through the throat, passes around the aorta. That’s kind of embarrassing in humans but in giraffes it’s particularly insane. As you can see, the nerve needs to cover less than 30cm in a giraffe because its throat is very close to its brain, but it takes a 5m route. All of this makes sense if anatomical structures once served a different purpose, but not when something was supposed to be “intelligently designed”.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the consequences if a defense lawyer refuses to represent their clients and leaves the courtroom without explanation before a trial? Is this a common occurrence?
Answer: Well, both in criminal and civil proceedings, this is a no-no for the lawyer. Lawyers can always ask to be removed from the case, and they can leave if the client fires them, but as the matter approaches trial, the burden on the lawyer to show they should be excused from the case gets higher. So the judge has the authority to force the lawyer back into the courtroom if, as you say, this happens on the day of trial. If the lawyer refuses, they can be held in contempt. They can even be arrested and brought before the court to answer for their absence. Although a lawyer can withdraw if they’re not being paid, or there’s a breakdown in the client-lawyer relationship, they still need the permission of the court to do so once a trial date has been set. On the date of trial, neither of these excuses will cut it as the lawyer is expected to have settled any such issues well before trial. Now remember, trial dates are carefully coordinated so that the defence counsel is given an opportunity to work it into their schedule. In all cases, the trial date is mostly at the convenience of the defendant, not the prosecution (who shows up to work every day anyway). If the lawyer dodges the court, the court will refer the matter to the bar association, who will almost certainly suspend the lawyer pending a full hearing. So, naturally, this is very rare. Doing it may cost you your license to practice. When it does happen, and it has, its usually because the client has done something outrageous, like assaulting counsel. That will get you excused and the defendant will still go to trial. Illness is, of course, a valid excuse. I know about a trial that was scheduled for several weeks that ground to a halt when one counsel had a heart attack in court. Don’t worry, he recovered.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Are the Jews indigenous to Palestine, or was the latter just promised to the Jews in their sleep?
Answer: Except during the Babylonian exile (587 BCE to 539 BCE) where the Babylonians spent roughly a decade from 597 to 587 deporting Jews to Babylon, the area around Jerusalem has always been inhabited by Jews since the Exodus in roughly the 13th century BCE. Jews remained the majority of people in Palestine until the 4th century CE (so, for about a thousand years) until Christian pilgrims started to outnumber them in the 5th century. By the 12th century, the area was majority Muslim. The low point was in the late 17th century where there were probably no more than 2,000 Jews in the region compared to about 219,000 Muslims and 11,000 Christians, but even in 1800 their numbers had grown to about 7,000 although they still remained only about 3% of the population.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How long does it typically take to obtain a P.Eng license in Ontario after completing an M.Eng degree?
Answer: Well, Professional Engineers Ontario will not give you a license based on a master’s degree, so it’s irrelevant. To meet Ontario’s academic requirement for licensure, there are essentially only two paths: In addition, you can no longer apply unless there’s a chance you meet the requirement for 48 months of engineering experience, which means you have to have received your bachelor degree in or before 2020. Under the current process, you must meet the academic requirement before you apply, so if you don’t fall into category 1, you have to apply to write technical exams. To do that, you need to submit your academic evaluation from WES Once you meet the minimum application criteria, and submit all the documentation for licensure, PEO must make a decision within six months. During that six month period, you have to pass the National Professional Practice Exam.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the worst acting performance in a blockbuster that you have seen?
Answer: Oh, that has to be Dwayne Johnston in “Black Adam” Look. I get it. Johnson is a massive star and can bring box office success simply on the value of his name. Indeed, the film did very well overseas. But DC was betting heavily on this movie to drive the rest of the DC Cinematic Universe. It cost $195 million to make and only took in $168 million domestically. Like many DC films, it also failed to impress critics. Audiences liked it (it has an 88% on Rotten Tomatoes) but it’s clear that Johnson really doesn’t have what you would want to justify a sequel. By contrast, Zachary Levi, who essentially plays the mirror character, is a delight to watch on screen as he goes through a full range of emotions and makes us completely believe he’s a teenage boy in a mature man’s body. “Shazam” struggled at the box office too, but at least it justified a sequel and Levi played well off a good supporting cast. Johnson had a much better supporting cast in “Black Adam” but totally failed to connect with them. Both movies are deeply flawed but both “Shazam” movies have us feeling deeply for all the characters and when Billy sacrifices himself in “Shazam 2” it’s a deeply moving experience. No one cares if “Black Adam” makes it through the movie even though he undergoes a better redemption arc than Billy Batson did.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why do so many people don't realise that if someone doesn't respect your boundaries, they don't respect you?
Answer: Because most of us grow up with social pressure that some people, most notably family members and physicians, are expected to be able to routinely cross those boundaries. Bullies feel free to emulate those people. Most of us get the impression that even having boundaries is somehow “wrong” and that breaking boundaries is somehow normal. This is reinforced by authoritarianism and somehow that if someone doesn’t respect your boundaries, it’s “your fault” because you brought it on yourself. Take the U.S. gymnastics team’s sexual assault scandal. You have a group of teenagers who are pretty much expected to do what they’re told in an environment where it’s clear if they rebel, they’re out, a doctor who is “exempt” from the general rule that people aren’t allowed to violate your personal space, parents who are heavily invested in the process and don’t want to see it all go to waste, and you’ve created an environment where the doctor can freely take liberties without fear of consequences. And parents are usually the worst offenders. Both “tiger parents” and “helicopter parents” expect their children not to be able to make their own judgments and insinuate they know best in every situation.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What factors prevent America from launching a full-scale invasion of Canada, despite having a larger military power than Canada?
Answer: Well, they tried that in 1812. The United States had fifteen times as many people as Canada at that time. And it was an unmitigated disaster. At the end of 1812, all of Michigan was in British hands with the British having taken control of Fort Detroit and Fort Michimakinac. An attempt to invade Queenston, Ontario in October was also a disaster. 1813 was better with the Americans winning everywhere from Ohio to Toronto (then York) but at the end of the year they had had to completely withdraw to Detroit and Buffalo as they simply couldn’t hold what they captured. They held onto Toronto for a whole two weeks before withdrawing. They captured Niagara-on-the-Lake only to be holed up inside the fort for the entire fall and having to abandon it. Invading Canada would probably be trivially easy, but holding on to it would be all but impossible as it’s likely the Canadian population wouldn’t cooperate. That’s what happened in 1813. Despite winning everywhere, the United States faced Canadian forces that would simply withdraw to another strong point and stretch out the existing American forces so they became vulnerable to hit and run attacks. So let’s get back to Niagara-on-the-Lake. Facing overwhelming American force, the British and Canadians simply withdrew about 20km west to Beaver Dams to meet up with their Native allies. The Americans sent a force after them but the British had got word of the attack but were ambushed and surrounded by a native force and had no choice but to surrender to a much smaller British force. The natives spent the rest of the year hiding in the forest in Niagara-on-the-Lake and killing any American who stepped out of sight of the fort. At night, they would dump the body at the gate to make it clear what happened. It’s also likely that what happened in 1814 would happen again - someone would come to Canada’s aid. By the summer of 1814, the British were raiding settlements in the Potomac Basin before finally attacking Washington and setting all the government buildings on fire. The Americans spent over a decade in Vietnam, and lost. They spent over 20 years in Afghanistan, and lost. Faced with an enemy that can hide and won’t surrender, there’s no path to victory. Moreover, it’s not like the United States is far from Canada. Attacking Canada faces retaliation against communities close to the border.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why is Quebec staying in Canada despite its language differences?
Answer: First and foremost, language wasn’t really an issue until the 1960s when the new Liberal government of Quebec essentially disestablished the Catholic Church in Quebec by removing priests, bishops and archbishops from official government positions. This soon extended to the school system, which was also secularized. From the Battle of Quebec until 1960, the big schism in Canada wasn’t language, it was religion. While the Catholic Church had a stranglehold on the Quebec government, and worked with the Union Nationale and rich Anglos to retain it, over in Ontario government, policing, finance and politics was all controlled by the Orange Order, a fraternal organization of Protestants of Irish extraction that worked together with the Ontario Progressive Conservative Party. That monopoly only started to crack in 1959 when a Jew, Nathan Philips, won a three way race for Toronto mayor against two Orangemen and implemented a reform platform. But through the 1960s as Ontario started to get less Protestant thanks to immigration (Catholicism is now the plurality religion in Ontario) and Catholicism started to get more exercised in theory than practice in Quebec, the main issue still wasn’t language - it was local control. Rene Levesque the new Minister of Public Works under the provincial Liberals, had big plans like nationalizing the province’s hydro-electric capacity (which worked - Quebec pays low electricity rates and exports a lot for extra cash). However, when the federal government also started making plans, like expanding health care insurance, it interfered with Levesque’s plans as the money coming from Ottawa came with lots of strings attached. It was this difference of opinion about how federal tax revenue should be allocated to provinces that drove the Quebec sovereignty movement, and still does. When in the 1980s and 1990s Quebec was negotiating Meech Lake and Charlottetown, it wasn’t about language rights, it was almost entirely about Ottawa just being a massive wallet for the provinces. Levesque objected strongly to the Charter because he believed it constrained his government’s authority, and he didn’t want that. That’s why he fought so hard against it. However, if you look at Meech Lake and Charlottetown, which Quebec’s government eagerly accepted as a condition of staying in Canada, none of that is there. Meech Lake Charlottetown So why was language a big deal? Well, even in the 1960s, French was considered a second-class language in Quebec despite it being, by far, the majority language. Rue St. Catherine in 1969. No French in sight. French Canadians were allowed to work at Eaton’s, but couldn’t speak to customers in French - even French Canadian customers. English was the commercial language even in neighbourhoods that were pretty much 100% French speaking. If you look at language in Quebec, it’s not about being able to speak it elsewhere in Canada, it’s about being able to communicate in French in your own province when immigrants want to learn English instead. That’s going to be an issue whether Quebec is in Canada or not.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is Social Security a welfare or a retirement program?
Answer: There is often so much misinformation about the Social Security system that it’s difficult to know where to begin but if I had to chose one, it’s overwhelmingly a “welfare” program. Thinking it’s a retirement program totally misunderstands how the system is funded. Now, to be fair, we’re often taught that Social Security is just like a savings account for your old age where you pay in now and get paid back later. Frankly, that’s what people think auto and home insurance are sometimes - a pot which you pay in and can draw from if you need it. But it works way more like a disaster insurance fund than a savings fund. Yes, right now, there’s $2.9 trillion in U.S. government bonds in the Social Security Trust fund, which also makes it look like it’s some sort of savings plan. But it isn’t. It’s an illusion and this situation of having a “surplus” really only started in the 1960s when actuaries realized that the way the program was funded, that in future there would be two people paying into it for every person drawing from it, and that just wasn’t sustainable. So instead the system actually collected more money than it needed to fund the program to put away for when all the boomers retired, which they’ve been doing for about a decade now. But at the beginning, Social Security was strictly funded on an “as you go” basis. The first person to receive a social security check was Ida May Fuller, who got her first monthly check for $22.54 on January 31, 1940. She collected benefits until her death in 1975. She received $22,888.92 over that 35 year period. Her total contributions to the program for the three years she paid into it - $24.75. In other words, she broke even two months into her retirement. And although Social Security currently has $2.9 trillion in liquid assets, its current obligations assuming it takes in no more money come to about $22.3 trillion. In fact, Social Security pays out about $1.2 trillion in benefits each and every year, and that number is growing. Luckily, Social Security taxes currently come to about $1.4 trillion a year. But there’s good news. The Social Security Trust fund regularly outperforms 401K and Keough plans. In other words, if you took your social security taxes and invested them, it’s likely that you would have less money at retirement. Heck, the guy who first proposed 401K plans for high income earners (rather than just raising the Social Security cap and benefits) and was a professional investment manager realized that his 401K was outperformed by Social Security. The other big benefit of the “welfare” plan rather than the “retirement savings” plan is that if, like Ms. Fuller, you live for 35 years after you retire, you will not have to worry about Social Security running out no matter how high (or low) your benefit. Trust me, if you live to be 100 you will exhaust all of your other retirement savings. Now, some people who pay into it may get no benefit (e.g. Shannon Dougherty, what a tragedy) but people who do live long lives (e.g. Dick Van Dyke, now 98) don’t have to worry about it running out. Oh, and Social Security also gets paid to you if you’re permanently disabled. That’s “welfare” not “retirement savings”. And everything will be fine as long as the government keeps collecting it. The U.S. is supposed to last forever (although sometimes I wonder) and there’s no reason to put an end to the program, even though there are some who are trying (mostly people who want to “manage your money” by taking most of it).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: If the English language were reformed so that the language were written strictly phonetically, (dunno how, maybe IPA. The "how" is a different question anyway) how many generations would it take for such a change to be fully implemented?
Answer: How about “never” Here you go - many common English words spelled with IPA, and we have a problem. Now, it’s not like British and American people don’t spell words differently (color/colour, realise/realize, tyre/tire) but if you broke it down word by word you could probably find no English word where, say, a person with a midwestern American accent would pronounce a word identically to someone with a Southern Standard British accent. Heck, Southern Standard British didn’t even exist a generation ago, and now both the Prince of Wales and his expat brother speak with that accent. Their dad still speaks with an RP accent, but their grandma spoke RP when she was young but spoke with an SSB accent in later life. And that’s just the two major ones. The United Kingdom has more English accent variation than the rest of the English speaking world COMBINED. As anyone from Northern Ireland will tell you, anyone who believes any differently must be an “idgit”. True, English in both the United States (with at least seven major regional accents) and the UK is getting somewhat more homogenous over time, but Americans can’t even reach consensus about what to call a sandwich on a long piece of bread. Or what to call a generic fizzy sugar water There’s also variation in Canada (which uses the schwa more than most English speakers do, i.e. “Tranna”), Australia (where “there” is a two syllable word) and New Zealand. Not to mention places like India, Singapore, Africa and the Caribbean where English is commonly spoken as a second language. So if you can’t even get LONDON to agree how to pronounce words (is it “British” or “Bri’ish”?) you can’t really expect the rest of the planet to go along.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What distinguishes a communist from a socialist? Is there a belief that communism could be successful if implemented correctly?
Answer: You can try to draw the line, but Marx, who coined both words, used them interchangeably. Moreover, there are at least two major branches of communism (we have two communist parties in Canada, one following each vision) and the Soviet Union and People’s Republic of China had a major diplomatic split in 1963 over the Soviets reforming some of their practices. In common use, “socialists” believe that it’s important that a lot of things are subject to at least some common ownership (e.g. factories, apartment buildings, transportation, etc.) while “communists” believe that this pretty much all of these HAVE to be subject to common ownership with no private ownership being involved. For example, it’s not expensive to live in Vienna because for decades the Viennese have believed private ownership of apartment blocks has to be supplemented by a good proportion of buildings that were totally publicly owned, plus encouragement of common ownership (e.g. co-operatives or non-profits). Private ownership isn’t forbidden, but neither is it seen as desirable. However, in the old Soviet Union, individual residential buildings could be owned, but being a landlord was prohibited - all residential buildings were appropriated by or owned by the state.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What movie is wonderfully awful?
Answer: FLASH! AH-AHH! “Flash Gordon” is not a well made movie. Its screenplay was written in English, translated into Italian for the Italian producer, and then re-translated back into English. The special effects are hokey (especially compared to “The Empire Strikes Back”, released the same year). The acting is sometimes just plain bad. The costume and set design are totally over the top. The star, yes the guy playing “Flash Gordon”, left before filming was completed over a contract dispute. But the movie is wonderfully entertaining from start to finish. If you’re willing to overlook its flaws, it’s story structure is solid, its pacing is great, its editing is amazing, and its use of a rock music soundtrack at key moments just works well. I saw it four times its opening weekend. It may not be something you want to show to film students (unless you want to point out its flaws) but people love it. It was Queen Elizabeth II’s favourite movie, and Charles III’s least favourite.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can the concept of "separation of church and state" in America be altered to allow prayer in school? Why or why not?
Answer: So let’s take what it actually says in the First Amendment, shall we? Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances Now, when this was written in 1791, many states had their own official religion and you weren’t allowed to hold public office unless you were a member. In addition, most European states also had an official religion (in England that was the “Church of England”, the head of which was George III, the king). Europe had been in several wars which were strictly about religion (most notably, the Thirty Years War, (1618–1648) the outcome of which allowed each king to decide their own religion. People were expected to follow their king’s religion. This really hadn’t been a problem before the 16th century, because prior to that all the kings in Europe were Catholics. And many Americans were members of non-official religions. Most were some form of outsider Protestant, but many were Catholics from Great Britain and Ireland where Catholics couldn’t serve in public office. Many colonies, like Pennsylvania, had strict rules allowing anyone to practice their own religion, and by the 1770s many of the founding fathers weren’t members of any particular religion. Now the concept of the First Amendment is often stated as “separation of church and state” but in practice as it’s been interpreted by the Supreme Court starting largely in the 20th century is that no state (thanks to the 14th amendment) nor the federal government can mandate any sort of religious practice. This does not mean “no prayer in school”. If you’re Muslim and want to have some space to pray privately at mandatory prayer times, many schools will accommodate you. If you want to form a Christian fellowship after hours and have a prayer to start and end, that’s fine too. But what you can’t do is require people to pray. That’s forbidden. Moreover, you can’t have a situation where people are forced to “opt out” of a prayer, by being put out in the hall, for example. And the school prayer cases of the 1960s weren’t started by atheists (although atheists have brought suits about government endorsed religion). One of the first school prayer cases was brought by a Lutheran, a Protestant religion that doesn’t believe in public common prayer. The #1 litigant in the Supreme Court over establishment of religion issues has consistently been the Jehovah’s Witnesses, who win about half the time. So, imagine for a while that you win and school prayer is returned, but you’re required to recite this prayer: Gracious St. Joseph, protect me and my family from all evil as you did the Holy Family. Kindly keep us ever united in the love of Christ, ever fervent in the imitation of the virtue of our Blessed Lady, your sinless spouse, and always faithful in devotion to you. Amen. If you’re Catholic, you would probably be fine with that. If you’re not Catholic, it’s most likely its something you find objectionable as most non-Catholic religions, including most Christian ones, don’t believe in saints. Similarly, any mention of “Jesus” in a prayer is not going to go over well with non-Christian theists, and any attempt to keep Jesus out of it will probably be objectionable to non-Christians. New York State actually tried. Here’s what they came up with: “Almighty God, we acknowledge our dependence upon Thee, and we beg Thy blessings upon us, our parents, our teachers and our Country.” As an atheist, I can see several problems with that, the biggest of which is that we’re supposed to be believe our parents, teachers and government have god’s endorsement, which we’ve just asked god to give them. And the court got it right. Here’s one of the things they said: “The history of governmentally established religion, both in England and in this country, showed that whenever government had allied itself with one particular form of religion, the inevitable result had been that it had incurred the hatred, disrespect and even contempt of those who held contrary beliefs.” And that’s come to be the truth. Many plaintiffs in many subsequent cases who “opted out” found out that their fellow students’ parents had accused them of being Satan worshipers. Or worse. Now, my heritage is Northern Irish, and Ireland had two separate school systems - one for Protestants and one for Catholics. It was commonly taught on both sides that the other side was going to hell. Even in Newfoundland, in Canada, well into the 1980s when the province had both Protestant and Catholic run schools, was for teachers to openly mock the religious beliefs of the other. In the program “Son of a Critch” about the life of comedian Mark Critch growing up in St. John’s, he recounts a visit of Princess Diana (who he met by the way) that his Catholic teachers openly mocked Henry VIII for “starting his own religion”. So be careful what you ask for. You just might get it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why are American cellphone plans cheaper than Canadian ones, even though the phones were purchased in Canada?
Answer: It’s a combination of factors, but it’s primarily the size of the market, the density of the population., bad government policy and the existing concentration of telecommunication infrastructure in Canada. The United States and Canada both took the same approach to allocating the frequencies used by cellular phones, which is a limited resource and essentially means you can’t just start up your own cell phone service company. Back in the 1990s, high channel UHF frequencies were taken away from television stations (here in Canada, Toronto’s channel 79 became channel 57) and were auctioned off in a complicated system where there were several rounds of bidding for each allocation of cell phone frequencies in a given locality. In a nutshell, holding just one allocation is pretty much worthless but holding a set of allocations in adjoining territories was ideal. Think of it like a game of draw poker where your share of the pot is determined by the final strength of your hand, there’s betting every round, but as long as there is betting, you can throw your bad cards away which are then available to other players. In this case, only your final bid counts and when the bids don’t change, the auction is over. Here is a map of all the areas covered by LTE in the United States. These all represents large numbers of people who live close to each other. Although coverage is spotty in mountainous areas, in flat heavily populated areas, it’s solid. But here’s the same picture for Canada As you can see, there are massive parts of the country that have no coverage at all. There is literally a thin line of coverage along the north shore of Lake Superior. Many cell providers are literally out in the middle of nowhere. As such, if you wanted to build a nationwide network in the United States, it’s probably doable. If you want to do the same thing in Canada, you probably need more frequencies. And when cell phones were starting to become popular, central Canada (Ontario and Quebec) which gives you the most customers for the fewest frequencies, were already dominated by two telecommunications companies - Rogers Communications (which started as a radio network that branched into cable television) and Bell Canada (which has been the largest telephone company in the country since the 1870s). It’s not like they’re the only providers in Central Canada, but the others, like Shaw Communication (also a cable company) are much smaller and often aren’t available in most places. The lowest rates are offered by SaskTel, which is owned by the Government of Saskatchewan. In 1947, under Tommy Douglas, the provincial government bought out the federal government’s interest in telecommunications in the province with the specific goal of providing better telephone service to people in the province. Private companies have never been interested in providing phone service to Saskatchewan, but the no-profit model works and when cell phone frequencies were being sold SaskTel bought up a whole bunch in Saskatchewan dirt cheap. But Rogers and Bell are both publicly traded companies and although in past years their rates were tightly controlled by legislation, in recent years the government has taken a “hands off” approach and their rates keep going up even though the cost of providing their services keeps going down. The federal government has pretty much gone with the “market solution” (more competition) but although some companies have tried, they just keep getting bought up by Bell or Rogers, which gives them even more leverage over the market. A good example was an independent who made a deal with Toronto’s TTC to provide free wi-fi in many busy subway stations to obtain the rights to build a cellular network in the TTC’s subway tunnels. The company hoped that they would be able to sell access to other cell phone providers to make it pay, but for years you could only access the TTC tunnel network on that company’s cell phones. The company went to the CRTC (which regulates telecommunications) but the “big two” said it was unfair to make them pay for that service and they should be able to build their own network. The TTC replied the tunnels simply didn’t have enough room or electrical power for more than one network. In the end, the company couldn’t make a go of it and sole out to Rogers, which started offering that service to its own customers with the hope that it could shut out Bell. However, the CRTC ruled Rogers has to make that service available to anyone who pays a reasonable rate (fixed by the CRTC). Service still isn’t; available in some tunnels, but the TTC carries 1% of the entire population of Canada on a daily basis, so it’s a valuable franchise. In the United States, there were so many regional companies after the AT&T breakup, plus very large cable companies, plus other big telecommunications companies that it was really impossi8ble for anyone to completely dominate the market anywhere in the United States. This has led to real competition and not very many cases where the small fry get eaten up. In addition, for a change, American government are a lot more friendly to small scale telecoms getting in on things like local internet companies, or other companies that aren’t telecoms with money to get into the business, like Google Fiber. Get too greedy and someone is going to undercut you big time.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it possible for a city to place a lien on your property?
Answer: Absolutely, and here’s the thing - they don’t even have to do any paperwork. Under the laws in most jurisdictions, any unpaid tax immediately attaches to the property on the tax roll and has the highest priority - it even outranks a mortgage. If you buy a property with unpaid taxes, you’re not personally liable for those back taxes, but the lien remains on the property which means it passes to anyone who is dumb enough to buy it without checking. If you pay the normal taxes, they’re applied to the back taxes first. When you buy a house, one of your lawyer’s jobs is to check the city’s tax rolls to see if there are any outstanding taxes. If there are, they will contact the seller and tell them those taxes will be paid to the city on closing and that they won’t be receiving that money. This is different from a tax sale. If the arrears are very large, the municipality is entitled to sell your property to collect those taxes, but they have to give notice to anyone else with an interest in the property, which would include any lender who has a mortgage. If your mortgage company finds out you have arrears, they have the option of paying them off and adding those arrears to your mortgage.

Question: What led to northern Canada becoming its own territories instead of being part of the provinces like Quebec or Ontario?
Answer: Oh, that’s complicated. “The Territories” used to be massive. It was pretty much the entire 1670 land grant to the Hudson’s Bay Company, which included the entire watershed of all rivers that emptied into Hudson’s Bay. That even included a bit of what’s now in the United States (it was traded for a bit of the Mississippi watershed in Canada). So let’s take a look at it. In addition, “The Bay” also merged with the North West Company, which pretty much got a grant of all the land where rivers emptied into the Arctic Ocean. In 1870 when the UK transferred all of it’s interest in the land to the new self-governing Dominion of Canada, it was almost entirely inhabited by Hudson Bay company employees, First Nations, Metis and Inuit. That was about to change rapidly. But here’s what the provinces looked like in 1869. Now, the Quebec-Labrador border hadn’t actually been set by this time (it was functionally the northeast coast along the Atlantic) but all this new land being added to the country after Canada bought out “The Bay’s” interest started provincial politicians in Ontario and Quebec rubbing their greedy little hands in delight. There were just a couple of hundred technical issues to sort out, the primary one of which was that although Canada owned what belonged to “The Bay”, the First Nations and Inuit in those territories were likely to fight over their rights to the land the same way that American Indians had done. The first fly in the ointment was the “Red River” or “Selkirk” settlement. A fellow named Selkirk got a land grant from The Bay to attempt to settle an area around Fort Garry, near a key junction of rivers, to keep Americans from claiming the territory of their own. However, the legality of the settlement was not clear and by 1870 most of the inhabitants were Metis - mixed European and Native peoples who were mostly French speaking Catholics. When the Canadian government surveyors showed up there was a massive misunderstanding about land ownership rights that led to a rebellion. The rebels declared a provisional government and had the law on their side. Eventually, Canada conceded and recognized “Manitoba” as a new province. Anyway, over the next fifty years, the Canadian government worked with the local First Nations populations on treaties (the “numbered treaties”) and despite a rebellion in 1885 (that was led by the same guy in charge of the 1870 rebellion, Louis Riel) settlement of the west was mostly peaceful. Over time the North-West Territory was split up into new provinces with bits going to Quebec and Ontario, more being added to Manitoba, and much of the rest going to the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905. More land was added to Manitoba and Ontario later after Treaty 9. Logistically, this was all making sense because really the only way that Canada could control all this territory was through its railway, which was completed from Ontario to British Columbia in 1885. A second railway was built by the early 20th century, but it wasn’t as lucrative and the Canadian government took it over in the 1960s, calling it “Canadian National Railways”. Yukon Territory was formed in 1896 in response to a flood of Americans crossing the border looking for gold in the Klondike so that the North-West Mounted Police had jurisdiction over the area. Right now, we have three territories. Yukon, which was the part of the North-West Company territory west of the Rocky Mountains that did not clearly pass to The Bay when the two companies merged. Most of it is unceded territory. Nunavut, which is recognized as being unceded Inuit territory. Some Inuit have ceded territory to Canada and that’s the yellow islands at top left. The Northwest Territories, which are mostly ceded First Nations land, but a small part of it remained unceded.

Question: What is the cost of applying for probate in Canada?
Answer: Here in Ontario, it’s one-half of one percent (0.5%) of the total assets of the estate, not including any jointly held assets that go automatically to the survivor. On a $100,000 estate, that works out to $500.

Question: What is the reason for Toronto's high property tax rate?
Answer: Good one. Oh, lord, you’re serious aren’t you. Now, my sister and I have just sold our late mom’s house in Scarborough (part of the City of Toronto) and bought a new one in Oshawa (outside the City of Toronto, but still part of the GTA). Our tax rate has actually gone up. Now, we pay less tax because the house is only about 70% the value of the old one, but the rate is higher. Moreover, we were looking at properties in Pickering, Ajax and Whitby too - the three communities east of Scarborough that are also outside of Toronto. In each case, the property tax rate was higher. In fact, Toronto has one of the lowest “mill rates” (tax rate per $1,000 value of property) in the province of Ontario. However, since Toronto prices are so high, that’s still a substantial tax bill. The problem is that for the last few decades, Toronto City Council has decided to defer a lot of infrastructure expenses to keep expenditures down. However, about 50% of Toronto’s infrastructure (roads, sewers, water mains, stuff like that) was built in the 1950s during a massive expansion boom. Most of the rest is far older. As such, compared to most cities in Ontario, Toronto’s tax rates are surprisingly low. That’s why the interim mayor, Olivia Chow, has called for a substantial tax hike - about 9%. Things got really bad when Rob Ford was mayor. He managed to bury about a billion dollars worth of liabilities by deferring them to future years. As such, instead of being paid off slowly over a four year period, they pretty much all came due the same year - the one after he stopped being mayor. But let’s face it, Toronto in 2024 is not the same as Toronto in 1954, the year ‘Metro Toronto’ was created. Back then the city was still mostly rural. Brown’s line and Queen Elizabeth Way, 1940 The same, from Google Earth Toronto is a big city with a lot to maintain, plus significant police services and transit. It all has to be paid for somehow.

Question: What is the breakdown of income tax distribution among the different levels of government in Canada?
Answer: Both the federal government and the provincial governments collect income tax, but under an agreement between them all the forms are federal, the federal government collects the money and then disburses it to the provinces. It varies by province but here in Ontario the provincial rate is roughly 25% of the federal rate across all income brackets, so 80% of the income tax you pay is kept by the federal government. For example, for the highest income earners, the top bracket is 53.53% of income for federal taxes, and 13.16% for Ontario taxes. Of course, municipalities get screwed because they don’t collect income tax. Almost all municipal revenue comes from property and commercial taxes collected locally, plus a few grants from the federal and provincial governments.

Question: Are there any Canadian restaurant chains similar to American franchise chains?
Answer: Loads of them. Most of them are named after the United States. Harvey’s is a long standing burger chain that’s part of a larger restaurant chain. It offers custom topped burgers and chicken sandwiches. New York Fries is an Ontario based chain that started just serving skin-on fries, but has mostly moved into poutine in the past few years. It’s trying to break into Quebec. Tim Horton’s is the ubiquitous coffee and donut chain. It tried to break into the American market, but hasn’t done well there. Meanwhile, here in Canada, it keeps on expanding. When it expanded into Quebec a decade or so ago, it totally steamrolled over Dunkin’ Donuts, which was well established in the province. Swiss Chalet is a long standing rotisserie chicken restaurant, and gets very good reviews. However, the pandemic really ate into business and it’s been contracting recently so they’re harder to find than they used to be. In Quebec, rival chain St. Hubert rules. They’re owned by the same company as Harvey’s and are often co-located. Boston Pizza is a national pizza and similar food chain based in Alberta. Montana’s is a barbecue restaurant. They’re not tremendously common and tend to be found in larger cities. Similarly, you have Jack Astor’s, an American style food sit down restaurant that mostly caters to groups. Manchu Wok is a ubiquitous Chinese fast-food chain, found largely in food courts. Mary Browns is a fried chicken chain based in Newfoundland & Labrador. They’re not very common, but are often found in smaller communities. Humpty’s is a diner chain found solely in western Canada, although they are known nationally thanks to their sponsorship of the Canadian Football League. On top of that KFC, known as PFK in Quebec (Poulet frit du Kentucky) was once run completely independently in Canada as Harlan Sanders retained a share in the Canadian franchise operations after selling his interests in the U.S. operations. Sanders lived in Canada until his death in 1980. However, the chain is now again linked to the U.S. chain. Popeye’s although founded in the U.S. and still based there, is owned by a Canadian company now. They have rapidly been expanding here in the last few years. A&W in Canada is a completely independent company that licenses the brand from its international owners. When the brand attempted to withdraw completely from Canada in the 1990s, the Canadian rights were sold to the Canadian management team who turned it around an it’s been expanding rapidly in the past few years.

Question: Is Tim Hortons really Canada's favorite coffee and compared to what?
Answer: Tim Hortons is popular because for roughly the past twenty years they went on an aggressive expansion phase, ignoring conventional wisdom about how many people you needed to support a donut shop (the conventional wisdom - 4,000) . You see, in the early 1990s many people in smaller communities with pretty much no franchises were being ignored because the conventional wisdom was “that community can’t support a donut shop”. This is Meaford, a community of about 4,000 in Ontario on Georgian Bay. Ignore the franchises for the moment. I am familiar with the town because my uncle lived here in the 1970s and 1980s and really the only thing they had was a KFC and that was pretty much only a takeout location. As you can see now, it has a McDonalds and a Dairy Queen, but they’re both pretty new. Anyway, some enterprising entrepreneurs decided to have a go of it with donut shops in communities of about 1,000 people or so. The donut chains predicted failure. They thrived. Anyway, back in the 1990s, Tim Hortons had a partnership agreement with Wendy’s where they would build co-locations. There are still a lot of them around. The theory was that Wendy’s would benefit from the lunch and dinner hours and Tim’s from other times while they shared the same space. When the data on small town donut shops started to come in, Tim’s realized it had made a mistake and it really hurt the partnership as Tim’s went on a massive expansion spree that Wendy’s thought was a total mistake. It wasn’t. Tim’s thrived while Wendy’s faltered in Canada. So, anyway, here are the Tim’s near where I work Here are the ones near where I live Here are the ones near where I grew up And the ones near where my sister lives And the ones near where I stay when I go to Niagara Falls Lots of other Canadian consumer companies have taken the same route with the same success Dollarama A&W Popeye’s But, to be fair, there’s only one Tim’s in Meaford.

Question: Is it possible for banks to access other people's credit scores in Canada?
Answer: Yes. Banks have access to credit reporting services and many bank personnel can get instant access to that information. However, a bank employee still needs your permission to access that information. Credit agency access is controlled by provincial law, but all provinces make it an offence to access someone’s credit information without their permission. The case that established the right to privacy in Canada involved a bank employee who accessed account information about a rival. The employee paid about $15,000 in damages for that breach. So despite the fact it’s an offence, you have a private right of action against someone who accesses your credit history without permission. However, note that in many contracts you sign with banks and credit cards, you grant them permission to look at your credit history any time they want to.

Question: Can you explain the difference between a P.Eng and C.Eng designation in Ontario, Canada?
Answer: Absolutely. The abbreviation “P.Eng.” for “professional engineer” is reserved to people who hold a full professional engineering license or temporary engineering license with the Association of Professional Engineers of Ontario (PEO). It is a provincial offence, punishable by a fine of up to $10,000, to use the abbreviation if you’re not licensed by PEO. You need to be licensed to engage in the independent practice of professional engineering in Ontario except in some very limited circumstances. “C.Eng.” for “chartered engineer”, is a designation given to people who are registered with the Engineering Council, the UK’s regulatory body for the engineering profession. It has no status in Ontario. You may not call yourself a chartered engineer in Ontario unless you’re also a professional engineer with PEO. You’re not allowed to practice professional engineering unless you also hold a PEO license, temporary license or limited license.

Question: In law, an Alford plea is given by a person who maintains their innocence, but admits that the evidence is such that they would probably be found guilty. They are then treated as guilty. In your opinion, isn't that just a cop out?
Answer: Nope. “Alford” solves a problem that plagues trial and appeal courts - once you have pled “guilty” or “no contest”, you are forever prevented from “takesy-backsies” by withdrawing that. The best you can hope for is a pardon. As such, people who are fighting an uphill battle are better off pleading “not guilty” and making the prosecution prove their case even though they have no ammunition to fight back. That’s pretty much a waste of time. From a legal standpoint, if you plead guilty, you can’t withdraw that, but if you’re FOUND guilty, you can continue the fight as, hey, you never admitted it. “Alford” gives you a “faint hope” that in the future evidence will come forward to exonerate you. Once it does, you can go back to court and argue you’re entitled to a new trial. Essentially you’re saying “There’s enough evidence to convict, but I still say I didn’t do it. Find me guilty now so I won’t have to plead guilty and waste all your time”. And it happens. Up here in Canada a guy was convicted of killing his girlfriend. The defence strategy was to say an unknown third party did it. The police scoffed and said “if there were someone here in Scarborough killing young women, we would definitely know about it.” And there was, and the police didn’t know about it, and when he got found out, the M.O. of the murder matched the way this fellow killed his victims. The probable murderer, who was already in jail serving three life terms, was a guy named Paul Bernardo. The convicted guy got a new trial luckily, and the prosecutor decided not to go ahead with another trial.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why do cops hate it when you “lawyer up”?
Answer: For the same reason you hate it when you’re ready to go on your donut break and someone comes in to order a burger, fries and a coke. Instead of taking it easy, you have to actually do your job for a change. Gathering evidence, talking to witnesses, consulting the district attorney’s office, filling out forms, that sort of thing. Instead, why not just spend 20 minutes convincing someone that it’s in their best interest to talk to you, when it isn’t, then only listening to the stuff that supports your theory rather than to the whole story. Did you know a third of the people who the Innocence Project eventually freed actually confessed to the crime? Bet you didn’t. Let’s get this straight. If you’re under arrest there is nothing, nothing you can do to satisfy the cops of your innocence. Particularly if you are actually innocent. If you’re actually guilty, it actually helps because they will listen to you pin the crime on someone else. Honestly, that happened in Canada where the trial judge actually said the main witness’s description of details at the crime scene proved he was telling the truth that someone else did it. Hell, one guy on death row in the states actually confessed to over 300 murders before someone caught on that he was making it all up to keep himself alive. He was interviewed later and said it was painfully easy - all he had to do was keep trying details until he got the ones that fit, and then blame memory lapses on the number of murders he committed. Think about it - over 300 killers got away because some nutbar claimed their crime and the police couldn’t be bothered to check. That’s why in civilized places like the UK, they assign an entire squad led by a detective inspector to a murder investigation. In the United States, they assign two detectives. Guess who has the higher clearance rate.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the difference between a plea of no contest and a guilty plea in a criminal case? Why did Scott Farmer plead no contest?
Answer: This is an American thing. It should be a British/Canadian thing too because it causes all sorts of problems but there you go. But, in a nutshell, a “guilty” plea is a complete admission to the fact situation put forward by the prosecutor. As such, you can not, in any subsequent proceeding of any kind, argue that you did not actually do the thing you were convicted of. A “no contest” plea is only an agreement that you will be convicted. It is not an admission of guilt for legal purposes. You get the same penalty, but you’re able to argue in a subsequent legal proceeding that you did not actually commit the offence. So let’s take a “for instance”. You’re driving along when some idiot plows into you from the side at high speed. You’re badly shaken and a little shocked, although uninjured, and when the police officer gets there you’re really in no condition to speak. The EMTs insist on taking you to a hospital to be checked out, but when you get there you start to feel better and you’re released the next morning. But the cop has quota to make and you’re charged with impaired as the cop says that when he saw you you were conscious but unresponsive and must have been on weed or something. Then the driver of the other car, a BMW, sues you for $1 million because he wasn’t wearing his seatbelt and was badly injured in the crash. So your criminal lawyer (who is paid for by you) and your accident lawyer (who luckily is being paid by your insurance) get together and unfortunately fighting the criminal charge is going to set you back $10,000 because the other guy in the crash donated money to the district attorney’s campaign. The fine is $1,000 plus a driving course - no prison, no driving suspension. Also, your criminal record will be suspended after you do your course. But if you pled guilty, you’ve admitted you were impaired when you were operating a motor vehicle. Even though the other driver may have been at fault, it’s likely that this is going to cost your insurance company some big bucks. So you plead “no contest”. You save $9,000 by not having to pay your lawyer and your insurance company is happy because at the deposition you can safely explain that you hadn’t been drinking but the collision was so bad you were badly shook up and couldn’t respond to questions at the scene. Win win. Mr. Farmer killed four people while driving, so it’s likely he’s on the hook for a big judgment against him. Admitting he was at fault in the accident won’t help. Best to let his accident lawyers make the best case they can and settle for whatever they can.

Question: What do you think of the lawsuit filed against the Museum of Ice Cream in NYC?
Answer: See, now this is why you Americans need universal health care. So, in a nutshell, someone is suing the museum because they jumped into a “sprinkle pool” which I assume is a large tub containing those yummy colored soft candy bits and broke his ankle. If that had happened at the Museum of Ice Cream in London, England, the tourist would be rushed to “casualty” where they would have been given really good care, a plaster cast and no bill (except maybe for the crutches). But I’m guessing our New York visitor is probably out of pocket like $50,000 for the stuff that isn’t covered by insurance and is facing financial ruin. Now, this is not a “frivolous lawsuit”. For all I know, it’s a really bad idea for a person to jump into a tub of soft candy bits with questionable footing and the museum should not have even considered having such a thing. I’m not going to guess how a jury will decide, but that is something a jury will have to decide unless it settles. And, honestly, given the way that states police public attractions for safety concerns, it’s surprising that there aren’t more of these suits. Over in New Jersey, there was a place that was called “Action Park” that earned the nickname “Class Action Park” due to the number of lawsuits against the park for people injured on their “rides” and I use that term loosely because a more accurate description would be “hazards”. Down south somewhere, someone was decapitated on a slide ride that was self-designed by the park’s owner who didn’t bother to hire a professional engineer, and the state didn’t bother to give it more than a cursory inspection. Frankly, I hope that kid’s family wins like $100 million. Both those parks are closed now. And, just in case your wondering, yes, the law protects the stupid and careless to much the same degree it protects the very intelligent and ultra careful. As it should. Children are stupid and careless and deserve the most protection.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What do I do or say at a restraining order hearing in California?
Answer: A good start is “This is my lawyer, and they will be representing me today”. Honestly, if you don’t show up with a lawyer who has briefed you on your chances, it’s best to just say “I consent to the restraining order” and then move to some other wonderful state in the United States like Arizona, Oregon or Nevada or, at the very minimum, make sure you stay as far away from the person as possible. Unless there are kids involved, fighting a restraining order is generally pointless. If there are kids involved, you should have a lawyer already. All a restraining order says is “don’t come near this person”. If a person is seeking a restraining order, whether for good reasons or bad ones, staying as far away from them as possible is good advice. For goodness sake do not think you can go into this alone and come out with some sort of victory. I don’t care if it’s Amber whatsername from the Aquaman movie who is asking for the restraining order - if you don’t have counsel you are only going to make things worse for yourself. If you’re alone, there is no way this is going to work out well for you. It may not even work out well for you if you have a lawyer, but it will work out slightly better.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it possible to be fired for serving on a jury in Ontario, Canada?
Answer: No. Firing a person because they’re tied up on jury duty is clearly dismissal without cause and in addition to collecting damages for the appropriate notice period, it’s likely a court will tack on punitive damages. It’s also an offence to do so and your employer can be prosecuted for it. If the judge is in a bad mood, he or she can also have your boss arrested to explain exactly what they were thinking when they did it. Mind you, your employer has no obligation to pay you during jury duty, although many employers will.

Question: How do I request a hearing in court?
Answer: Well, that’s not how this works. That’s not how any of this works. First, you have to start a “proceeding”. Proceedings come in two flavours - “claims” and “applications”. Claims are for ordinary routine run of the mill legal disputes like automobile accidents and breach of contract. “Applications” are generally for disputes that are tightly constrained by statutory requirements, like enforcing a judgement from another jurisdiction. If you don’t know which one applies to your situation, go get a lawyer. Now, there are two types of hearings in general - “motions” and “trials”. In order to get a trial, you have to go through a series of procedures outlined in “rules” that apply in your jurisdiction. Until you complete all those steps, you can’t have a trial. Once you’ve completed all the steps, you will be put on a list and they will call you, probably to show up in court, to set a trial date. “Motions” are generally to settle things that have to be determined before trial. This can include emergency actions like stopping a contractor from coming onto your property to work on your neighbour’s house. It can also include a hearing that will eliminate the need for a trial. In order to get a “motion date”, you have to follow “local rules” which are unique to every courthouse. For example, at the Superior Court here in Toronto, for a date to hear an application (which is a motion, not a trial, although the court can convert your application to a claim and a trial) you have to show up at a “case conference” with the other side to discuss what steps have to be taken before the motion date and pick a date after they’ve all been allowed to complete. Again, if it’s an emergency (i.e. your husband is an irreversible coma and his lawyer got an order to keep you from pulling the plug even though you’ve made arrangements to donate their organs - no that happened) there is a way to get a judge but short of that you wait your turn. What you can never, ever do is just walk into a courthouse and ask to see a judge. That’s a big “no”. If you carry on, they have security guards and nearby police who will remove you and, if necessary, arrest you.

Question: In which states is it illegal to pump your own gas in the United States? What is the reasoning behind this law and how does the process work in these states?
Answer: Right now, that appears to be limited to New Jersey, which is the only state that has laws that require gas to be pumped by an attendant. Oregon lifted their ban in 2023. And the reason is largely political. Gas isn’t all that expensive in NJ even with full service (self-service gas in neighbouring states is actually more expensive). The ban has been in place for more that 50 years so most people in New Jersey have never pumped their own gas anyway. Gas stations like it because they work on slightly higher margins than self-service pumps. Most of the reasons for disallowing it in the first place were weak. People pumping their own gas aren’t a fire risk, which led to a lot of states banning the practice in the 1960s. Gas stations, which used to do the bulk of seriously lucrative repair work, wanted to raise the barrier to entry so they wouldn’t be undercut on gas prices. But when gas stations pretty much got out of the repair business, it was just too much to keep a full time person on board to pump gas, so resistance to the change from industry disappeared. Nowadays, gasoline sales are a “break even” business and, as I’ve pointed out, most gas stations make most of their profit on their convenience stores, which means you want the customer out of the car and coming inside to grab a bag of chips or something.

Question: What is the most commonly practiced type of law in your area?
Answer: Here in Toronto, corporate/commercial work predominates. 25 years ago I worked for a general practice firm that did a lot of corporate/commercial for large corporate clients, and a few of my law school buddies have smaller corporate/commercial practices that help out medium sized business owners. One of my cousins did that work before going into regulatory work. A lot of it involves mergers and acquisitions. You have to do a lot of ground work to ensure you’re not buying a dead horse, such as ensuring the company isn’t facing massive litigation liabilities or that it hasn’t mortgaged or otherwise encumbered all of its assets to the hilt. All that information is publicly available and I used to do some searches when I was a paralegal, but back in the 80’s it was largely stored in massive ledgers or kept on microfilm. More of that’s available electronically now. For example, when I started, if you wanted to know if someone had been sued, you had to search through a massive ledger that was updated with a typewriter. It took about an hour. Now you just put the name into a computer and the results are available in seconds. One of our clients at the old firm was a major telecom company and they had installations all over the city which required agreements with building owners. If those were not carefully crafted, there was usually litigation over things like when technicians could visit the building or who paid for the electricity.

Question: What happens in a court if a lawyer says "Objection your honor" and the person charged or being tried gets up without their lawyer and yells "On what grounds? I demand the right to be heard so sit down and shut up!" in response without permission?
Answer: If I were a judge….. This isn’t a political debate here. Trials have rules. One of the rules is we take turns. Even though we take turns, the lawyers have the right to interrupt if the rules aren’t being followed. If a lawyer objects too frequently without cause, it’s the job of the judge to keep them under control too, and that can lead to contempt against the lawyer. It’s my courtroom. I’m always in charge. Now, it’s polite for an objection to be followed by the reason, but sometimes it’s blatantly obvious. When I rule on the objection, I generally have to give direction to someone, whether it be the lawyer questioning or the witness, that they’ve crossed the line.
