Question: For those who work in a law office: What is the craziest thing anyone wanted to sue someone about?
Answer: There was a rich businessman here in Toronto, a widower with three kids, all of whom he had already made arrangements to provide for so most of his estate was going to go to charity. He was getting on in years and found companionship with an older lady. Naturally, as people do when they get older, he became increasingly unable to handle his own affairs. However, he had thought ahead and had already created a committee of three other men, all titans of industry, to manage his affairs if that happened. So when it did, our rich man’s lady friend found that they were essentially putting her on a generous allowance rather than allowing her to buy whatever she wanted. So she came to us to go to court and install her as the rich man’s substitute decision maker. Now, please note that this would not have been a problem had they been married, and they were on the verge of doing so, but one of the rich man’s friends reminded him before the ceremony that if he did get married, his carefully laid out estate plan would be thrown into absolute chaos which would most likely attract massive tax consequences, so he backed out. Here’s the thing - we took on the case thinking we would get a big payout. There was a massive amount of money involved. But problems presented themselves immediately. First, if a person chooses a substitute decision maker, the court is unlikely to replace them unless they’re doing something self-serving. Like I said, these three guys were all of the highest reputation and they had all known the rich guy for decades. They were doing a first rate job and were working well together. However, our client had a series of old fraud convictions. Also, she stood to massively benefit if she was appointed. It took virtually no time for the court to reject our application entirely. Her previous fraud convictions were the nail in the proverbial coffin. The rich guy eventually passed and she worked out a settlement with the estate for ongoing support, which she was entitled to. The amount she received was about three times what I made in a year. And we never did get paid.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What causes combustion without oxygen? Why doesn't gas burn without oxygen even though it is present inside the substance being burned?
Answer: I heard one firefighter, who was briefing volunteers at an auto race, describe what he called “S.O.B.s” or “Self-Oxidizing burnables”. Chemically speaking, it’s not hard to include an oxidizer in a chemical that will cause it to burn even when there’s no oxygen in the atmosphere. That’s pretty much what an explosive is. For example, in gunpowder, potassium nitrate is a chemical compound with one atom of potassium one atom of nitrogen, and three atoms of oxygen. When combined with sulfur and carbon, it becomes highly unstable when set alight with the potassium combining with the sulfur, the oxygen combining with the carbon and the nitrogen being released. By itself, potassium nitrate won’t burn, but it will supply oxygen to anything that does. Most solid fuel rockets also use this, using an oxidizing chemical so they can burn even in space. Another common oxidizer is ammonium nitrate, which is generally used as a fertilizer. However, add it to diesel fuel and you get a bomb. But you’re right. In a vaccum or any atmosphere without oxygen, fuel won’t burn. Burning is a self-sustaining reaction once it starts, but it requires a constant supply of both fuel and oxygen. If the oxygen is cut off, the remaining fuel can’t combine with anything and the reaction stops immediately. When the reaction stops, there’s no more energy to push the fuel over the energy hump it needs to get the chemical reaction going.

Question: Has Israel ever attacked the United States or it’s military?
Answer: No, but it was a close thing. In 1956, the government of Egypt, which prior to World War II was pretty much under the thumb of Great Britain, having in 1951 broken a treaty granting the UK a military base to protect the Suez Canal, which the UK owned, moved to nationalize the canal, giving the UK Egyptian bonds in return. The UK didn’t take kindly to this as it was already rapidly losing its empire, so along with France, it decided to have one last go at imperialism and planned an invasion of Egypt to re-take the canal. And this is where Israel comes in. Egypt and Israel had both been involved in the Arab-Israeli war of 1947–48 and there was still no peace treaty, so Israel saw an opportunity to get on board and maybe take a chunk of Egyptian territory. At worst, they figured that the could deal Egypt a pretty good blow at little risk. It didn’t help that the Egyptians had been providing Palestinians with a base for attacks on Israel. Israel had already forged good relations with France as well. In addition, Egypt was playing a dangerous game, trying to play off the US and the USSR to see who would give him the best terms. However, both the US and USSR were not really enthusiastic about the relationship. Of course, the invasion was a disaster. The three aggressors totally telegraphed everything they planned to do, which meant the Egyptians were well prepared to receive them. The war was massively unpopular in both the UK and France. Moreover, it was about the only time the United States and the Soviet Union ever agreed on anything. The United States felt it couldn’t complain about the Soviet Union invading Hungary while letting an Egyptian invasion pass unnoticed. The Soviet Union also called for an end of hostilities and the only reason the issue wasn’t dealt with by the UN Security Council is because both the UK and France vetoed any resolution. Meanwhile, Israel had conquered some territory, but despite saying they would keep it, it became clear that doing so would mean losing all American support. Things got worse with the Soviet Union proposed sending help to the Egyptians, actually taking sides in the conflict. Eventually all sides agreed to a proposal where troops from neutral countries would take control of the occupied areas, eventually returning them to Egypt while preventing the Egyptians or Palestinians from taking occupation of them for military purposes. But had the conflict escalated, it is likely that the United States would have been supporting the Egyptians and not the Israelis. Honestly, the United States came close to taking military action against the UK and France. That’s one of the reasons Canada stepped in to propose the peacekeeping plan. The guy who proposed that plan, Lester Pearson, won the Nobel Peace Prize and later became Prime Minister of Canada.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it true that the climate of Los Angeles is mild to hot year-round, and mostly dry?
Answer: No, not really. Los Angeles has a Mediterranean climate - warm winters, warmer summers, but very dry in summer and more wet in winter. Typical daily highs in winter are in the high 60s Fahrenheit, rising to the mid 80s in the summer. That’s a fairly narrow band of highs. There are higher extremes, but what saves L.A. is that due its very low summer humidity, temperatures drop very quickly after sunset and it goes down to the mid 60s - very nice sleeping weather. In east coast cities with their high humidity, temperatures during warm periods can easily stay in the high 70s overnight. L.A. only gets about 14 inches of rain a year, but almost all of it falls from December to March. Outside of that, L.A. gets very little rain. From June to September, it’s unlikely you will get any rain at all. But L.A. can get immense rainstorms in the winter, sometimes lasting for several days. That can cause devastation, including landslides. On March 2, 1938, L.A. got over 5 inches of rain in one day - about one third the typical yearly total. That 14 inch average is very misleading too because in the winter of 1977–78 it got 30 inches during the winter alone.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the reason for the silent 'r' in the word "correction"?
Answer: English has some really weird rules for the use of a double consonant instead of a single one, and many of them don’t make immediate sense. However, this one does. As a rule, if you see a pattern CVC in a word, the vowel takes the short form. “Cut”. However, if you see the pattern CVCV in a word, the first vowel takes the long form and the second vowel is silent. “Cute”. This applies to longer words with more syllables. If the pattern is CVCVC, then the first vowel is the long form and the second vowel is silent or unstressed. “Silent”. If you want to make sure the first vowel is short form or unstressed, but the second vowel is stressed, It’s CV[CC]V. “Correct”.

Question: What was the 70s sitcom “Good Times” about?
Answer: It was largely about the struggles of an African-American family of five living in a two-bedroom apartment in the Chicago projects. James, the patriarch, is hard working, but frequently unemployed due to the economic problems of the era, as is his wife Florida, who has previously worked as a maid for the Findlay household in suburban New York City. Their children are the budding artist James, Jr. (J.J.), the straight-A student Michael, and their daughter Thelma, who hopes to become a fashion designer. James and Florida are constantly trying to keep their kids on the straight and narrow, which is difficult because they too face temptation and find it hard to set a good example. Once, James stumbles on a bag of money and returns most of it, but keeps some when the reward is a grocery voucher. J.J., the eldest, is recruited to a gang, but resists. So is Michael, and he at first gives in. Pitfalls are everywhere, and navigating them is difficult. On his birthday, J.J. is expecting art supplies, but gets a sweater and storms out of the apartment. While he’s out, he’s arrested, but it turns out he’s a victim of mistaken identity - for someone who doesn’t resemble him at all. J.J. falls in love and wants to marry his girlfriend, but when he’s denied permission (at 18, he’s too young under Illinois law) he and his girlfriend go to nearby Indiana only to find out there’s a waiting period. In the meantime, J.J. learns his girlfriend is a junkie, and she dumps him to get a fix. The family grows by one when they save a neighbour who is the subject of abuse, and save her again when her mother comes back only to threaten to beat her. But tragedy strikes as James finds a good job in Mississippi, only to die on the car trip back. So, think “The Honeymooners”, only with more emphasis on real life problems rather than get-rich-quick schemes that go bad.

Question: Were there police forces before the concept of government was established?
Answer: No. What we now think of as a “police force” is a rather modern invention. The whole idea of having full-time paid professionals with training is attributed to Sir Robert Peel who formed the Metropolitan Police Force in 1829. The new “police” wore unforms, carried truncheons and were paid to react to crime as it happened. The concept proved very successful and soon spread pretty much everywhere. Prior to that, you had a whole bunch of systems to deal with systemic disorder, but most of them consisted of irregular volunteers who may or may not have had training for their roles, and may or may not have paid for their services by being horribly corrupt. Back in London before police, there was actually a fellow who had a knack for recovering goods and charging the victim a small fee for their return. In truth, he was a fence who openly told thieves to bring him stolen goods, as well as the name of their owner, and he would split the proceeds with the thief. Eventually, someone figured it out and he was hanged. Crime went down too.

Question: How is "sphincter" pronounced in English?
Answer: Tricky. It’s “sfink-t’r” English has numerous words which are long (this one is nine letters) but have only one enunciated vowel sound. Many of them only have one syllable (e.g. “stretched”, “squirrel”). But that /sf/ cluster is really weird. It’s not uncommon for there to be an /s*/ consonant cluster in an English word but /sf/ is really rare. More common are /st/, /sk/, /sl/, /sm/, /sn/, and /sw/. That’s most likely because the word itself derives from Greek, where /sf/ isn’t an uncommon consonant cluster. You find it in other related words of ancient origin too, like “sphinx”. Of course, you find a lot of words in English starting with “PH” that are pronounced with the /f/ sound and they’re mostly of Greek origin too - Philosophy, Physics, Phonetics, Phoenicia.

Question: What are the differences between an ESL and an EFL speaker of English?
Answer: EFL is an academic discipline, so EFL students tend to speak in a very formal manner. However, they’re not very good at dealing with vernacular English. They often struggle with conversational English, although they can read, write and speak well above average, even better than many native English speakers. They also often avoid working on their accents. ESL is a practical discipline, so ESL students tend to speak in a more casual manner. That often puts them at a bit of a disadvantage in an academic environment where formality is important. However, they’re more likely to get training in listening to vernacular English and are more likely to understand spoken English from native speakers. They get more training in conversational English and are better at learning conventions like turn taking and interrupting. However, they often struggle with writing in particular as it’s not a stressed skill the way it is in EFL. However, an ESL student will most likely work on softening their accent, particularly if it’s going to cause confusion.

Question: What is the relationship between pronunciation and spelling in English (phonology vs. orthography)? If there is a relationship, how can it be explained scientifically or logically?
Answer: Look, it’s really quite simple. English words are spelled exactly the way they’re pronounced - or at least the way they were pronounced in and around London, England, in the 15th century before the printing press was introduced in England. Since then, there’s been a bit of divergence.. The worst of course is the combination “-ough” which has five common pronunciations, two less common pronunciations, and five rather rare pronunciations. That I know of. Prior to the introduction of the printing press, which more or less put an end to the “Middle English” period after a 400 year run, spelling was fluid, the pronunciation of words changed depending on which part of the country you were in, and vocabulary often changed from county to county. But the printing press pretty much arrived at the exact wrong time - right in the middle of when the English language was going through a massive change As such, spelling reflected the way words were generally pronounced and written in the late 14th century. By the end of the 17th century, pretty much every vowel sound had changed, and many sounds like the throaty consonant still heard in German words like “Bach” disappeared from the language. That sound used to be represented by the “WH” combination in words like “Why”, “Where” and “Whisper”. Similarly, it’s thought that the “ough” combination used to be pronounced consistently like /oug/. And let’s face it - English has never been a homogenous language. Famously, the word “sorry” changes it’s pronunciation entirely when you cross from Niagara Falls, New York, into Niagara Falls, Ontario. When you compare the United States to the United Kingdom, dozens of words are pronounced remarkably differently, and there are regional variations on top of that. Famously, people in Australia often pronounce words as if they have an extra syllable. The one syllable “there” becomes “they-ah” in Australia. French also famously has a disconnect between phonetics and orthography. For example “oiseaux” (birds) is pronounced “wa-zoh” in French, so literally none of the sounds match. However, overall, French orthography is at least more consistent with all the “-eaux” plurals at least having the same pronunciation. Conversely, simply English word endings like the plural “-s” and the past tense “-ed” each have two different pronunciations (/s/ and /z/; /ed/ and /et/) depending on the letter that precedes them. Native English speakers are oblivious to this fact. With so many local pronunciations of a simple word like “route” (root? rout?) English pronunciation has been sacrificed for consistent orthography across all versions, with only small variations like “color/colour”, “realize/realise”, “center/centre” and “tire/tyre”. But regional variations are everywhere. No one in Boston would say “Smart Park” or “Harvard Yard” or “Charles Emerson Winchester the Third”. The fun thing on “M*A*S*H” is every part of Major Winchester’s name is there to show you he deletes his terminal /r/ sounds. And Charles is no lower class yobbo like Captain America - he’s Boston elite. Of course, the English vocabulary is expanding all the time and most new words are spelled closer to what they sound like. “Covid”, “deepfake”, “e-bike”, “influencer”. The big exception is still borrowed words, which tend to retain their original foreign spelling even thought hey may be pronounced differently in English.

Question: How did Germanic languages evolve into modern English? Did they go through distinct stages or did they gradually change over time?
Answer: Old English was staggeringly similar in vocabulary and structure to Old Dutch and many of the Germanic languages of the northwest, including Old Danish. But 1066 changed all of that. It was at that point English started to sharply diverge from other Germanic languages. The major reason is that while other Germanic languages generally formed new words from compounding old ones, English instead started to borrow words from their Norman French invaders to make communicating with the aristocracy, which continued to speak French for 400 years while the commoners kept speaking the native language. For example, “Swine+Flesh” was used in English and early German, but in Middle English, English swapped out the term for “Pork”, from the Old French “Porc”. German kept Swinefleisch. English vocabulary started to expand greatly and it was common for both Old English and Old French terms to be used depending on level of formality - e.g. Old English “guts” and Old French “courage”. For about the next 400 years “Middle English” became quite a different language from “Old English”, but it was plagued with inconsistent spelling and was largely seen as a “gutter language”, not a sophisticated one like French or Italian. That started to change in the 1470s when an amazing technological breakthrough reached England - the movable type printing press. The arts and science soon started coming to the forefront in the country and they caused massive changes to the language. Printing started to standardize spelling and vocabulary nationwide (although there are still local variants to this day, like what you call a dinner roll). It took a while, but in the 17th century a playwright named William Shakespeare started a tradition of using more natural language in plays, with actors having something closer to having conversations rather than just given speeches. Shakespeare also liked throwing new words in the mix - 1,700 English words have their first written use in one of his plays, and he had a massive vocabulary of 20,000 words. Soon thereafter, English scientists started coming to the fore. Although England’s most famous scientist, Isaac Newton, did most of his important work in Latin, academic English started changing with scholars using more words based on Latin and Greek roots when they came up with new concepts. And at roughly the same time, England started sending settlers to the other side of the Atlantic where they formed a series of colonies along the Atlantic Coast. Naturally, they brought English with them and it wasn’t long before it started to diverge as they discovered new things that didn’t exist in Europe, like raccoons. Still, by the end of the 18th century and American independence, English was not considered very much of a high end language. Latin and French were still considered more important. That was to change very quickly as Great Britain went on an expansion spree. They already had a presence in the Caribbean where English was being adopted, but then they expanded to Australia, New Zealand, Africa and, finally, to Asia (like Singapore, Malaysia and Hong Kong). In the early 20th century, the United States went on an expansion binge too, spreading the language to the Philippines, which to that point had been largely Spanish speaking. Later in the century, English started to be introduced by Americans into Japan, Korea, and finally, Vietnam. As such, well before the end of the century, English was the dominant language of diplomacy, science, literature and, with the invention of mass media in the United States, film, radio and television too.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How is "Yosemite" pronounced in English? Is it pronounced with a closed or open mouth, similar to French?
Answer: It’s a bit of a tricky one given it’s spelling, but it’s “yoh-SEM-ih-tee”. Most of that involves keeping your mouth in an open position throughout because it doesn’t have any unstressed vowels, which is unusual for an English word where the vowels in the unstressed syllables are generally glossed over. But the word has four glorious syllables, one for each vowel. Based on it’s spelling and following usual spelling conventions, you might think it’s “Yoh-s’-might” or “Yoze-might”, but that’s just wrong. After all “Semite” is “Seh-might” not “Seh-mih-tee”. and “Vegemite” is “Veh-g’-might” not “Veh-geh-mih-tee”. The reason for the pronunciation is that it’s a borrowed Native American word, and a highly mangled one at that. It’s from the Miwok language and means “they are killers” which is how they referred to their rivals, the Ahwahneechee, who were the original inhabitants of the land that now encompasses Yosemite National Park. Originally it was “yohhe’meti”. Making it much more confusing is that the way we pronounce it makes it much closer to the Miwok for “grizzly bear”. Despite the unflattering name, the Ahwahneechee generally got along with their neighbours. There was a lot of trade and intermarriage. Unfortunately, they were largely wiped out by Europeans during the 1850s.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Which movie star was the first to be born in Canada?
Answer: That would be this little lady right here Mary Pickford, born in Toronto in 1892. The site of her childhood home has a marker on University Avenue near what’s now Sick Children’s Hospital. And when I say “little” it’s because she was just a shade over 5 foot tall. Otherwise, she was a giant. After her Broadway play ended its run and she was out of work, she auditioned for D.W. Griffith, who was already a filmmaking legend by that point. She didn’t get the part, but Griffith realized that she had a handle on the difference between stage and film acting and offered her the immense sum of $10 a day (twice the going rate) and a guarantee of $40 a week. Mary made her film debut in the 1909 short “Mrs. Jones Entertains”, one of about fifty films she made that year. The following year, she moved from New York to Hollywood. Back in those days, actors didn’t get credits, but audiences soon noted Pickford and in her first year they clamoured to find out who she was. In 1912 she moved back to Broadway, but realized she preferred film acting and was soon back in Hollywood. By 1914, her name was appearing above the title on most of her features, and she was often demanding further raises. By 1916, she was making the unheard of sum of $10,000 a week, plus profit sharing. By the late 1910s, only Charlie Chaplin matched her in popularity. She was soon running her own film production company. When her contract expired in 1918, she left for more money, but by 1919 she, Chaplin and Douglas Fairbanks Sr. had enough money to start their own studio, United Artists. Her films were soon grossing over a million dollars each. Unfortunately, she mad a poor transition to talkies, and by the time she was in her thirties she could no longer play the young spirited characters that had made her such a success with audiences. Although she racked up an Academy Award, she largely retired from film acting in 1933 and focused on producing the movies of other people.

Question: What led to the decline of Silent Films after the rise of Sound Films?
Answer: Mostly films like this The first “talkie”, using early non-synchronized sound where the soundtrack was played on a record along with the film, only had a few musical numbers in full sound, but it featured a massive Broadway star, Al Jolson. It was an insanely successful hit. It cost about half-a-million dollars to make and made that back several dozen times over. The success of synchronized film encouraged Broadway producers to take their show on the road to Hollywood where they essentially put on filmed versions of their incredibly successful Broadway reviews. In 1929, two musicals were nominated for Best Picture and “The Broadway Melody” won. It cost under $400,000 to make and did “boffo box office” as they said in the day. Opening to “The Broadway Melody”, a musical comedy with a plot. It would be a while longer before another musical won “Best Picture”, but that didn’t stop producers from embracing every new technology that came along. The first was pre-recorded songs, which “The Broadway Melody” pioneered. Producers of musicals found that trying to record live music was a pain so instead the stars pre-recorded their musical numbers which were played on loudspeakers on set with the stars lip synching. That became the standard going forward. Eventually, musicals embraced the expensive new color film technology. You may have heard of that film.

Question: What is the reason behind China's use of a script for their language instead of an alphabet like English or French?
Answer: Mutual intelligibility. French and English use the same alphabet, but have you ever noticed that as an English speaking person you can’t understand most things written in French despite recognizing the alphabet? Apparently, French people have the same trouble with reading English. However, if you speak any language in the Chinese language group that uses Chinese characters for writing, and you follow a set of standard rules, it’s easy for a Mandarin speaker to understand what a Cantonese speaker has written down even though they can’t understand each other’s spoken languages. Now Chinese is seriously weird this way. If you transcribe what a Mandarin speaker says word for word, it’s unlikely a Cantonese speaker would be able to understand it, and vice versa. However, there is a standard way of writing Chinese that preserves the meaning of a sentence perfectly. Here in Canada, with an English speaking majority and a substantial French speaking minority, you pretty much have to write everything twice. And in other countries, like Switzerland, it can be even worse Not a problem in Chinese. One written language fits all. Although the Chinese writing system is a lot more difficult to learn, and darn near impossible to write, it’s easier to read than write. I’m pretty sure those first two symbols mean “no doing this” Another benefit - as a rule, Chinese characters take up less space than words spelled with an alphabet.

Question: Civil war author Shelby Foote says that Confederate General Lee was misled by victory after victory against superior numbers to believe having Pickett charge on the third day at Gettysburg would be successful. Is he right?
Answer: Probably. The Army of Northern Virginia was, until July 1, 1863 completely undefeated in the field. They had consistently fought off larger Union armies and sent them running back to free territory. For example, the previous September, at Antietam (Sharpsburg), Lee’s army of 30,000 fought an army under George McLellan of 53,000 with more artillery to a draw. McClellan’s forces included a division led by George Meade, who would receive a promotion the week before Gettysburg to lead the entire army. The Union action was characterized by most of the units just sitting there doing nothing, allowing Lee’s forces to concentrate against any Union attack against his position. Similarly, at Gettysburg, Meade played defensively, doing very little to try to take on the Confederates facing him, preferring to let them come at him. To Lee, who preferred movement, he switched to his favourite tactic - flanking maneuvers to try to bring superior numbers to bear on a weak point of the Union lines. But Meade had chosen a good position with high ground on both sides and low ground on the middle. He expressed to his subordinates the importance of not abandoning the high ground to chase the Confederates. On Day 1, his subordinate in that position ignored that advice and nearly lost the hill to the south, only to be saved by a unit, thought destroyed, that was instead hiding behind a low wall and took advantage of a surprise textbook maneuver that pushed back the Confederates and restored Union momentum. On Day 2, Lee tried attacking the north hill, but the Union troops held firm. It was at this point that Lee convinced himself the reason why the attacks failed is because Meade had fortified his flanks to prevent such an attack and this must have meant Meade had weakened the middle of his line. Nothing was further from the truth as the Union middle contained pretty much all the Union artillery and the bulk of Meade’s men. Moreover, it appeared to Lee that Meade had absolutely no interest in trying to take the Confederate position. That was completely true but Meade was being careful as the site of the battle was not of his choosing and he felt his primary responsibility was to prevent a Confederate breakthrough which would leave the road to Washington wide open. He guessed, correctly, if he held his ground, Lee would be forced to retreat. But a retreat posed problem. With the Union likely to pursue, the larger Union force would most likely be able to pick off Lee’s units at leisure before they could re-organize. Lee, with his supplies and supply lines being stretched and a history of not thinking strategically became convinced of his own invincibility and against the advice of his immediate subordinates started making plans to attack the Union center despite a lack of reconnaissance. And it was a disaster of epic proportions. To be fair, Lee blamed no-one but himself, but his army was decimated as they tried to advance on a Union position over open ground with no cover. The Union simply blasted the advancing Confederate infantry and cavalry to pieces with grapeshot and rifle volleys. None of the Confederate personnel even got close. At the end of the day, both sides suffered about the same number of casualties, but the Confederates had smaller numbers to begin with and most of their units had been torn apart. As Lee figured, the retreat left them disorganized and it was nearly a disaster as their escape route was blocked by the swollen Potomac. However, Meade was slow to pursue and they were able to escape. Meade called it a day but Lincoln was not impressed and started looking for Meade’s replacement when he got some good news the same day from Vicksburg, Mississippi that General Grant had closed the last Confederate outpost on the river, cutting the Confederacy in half and preventing communication and trade over the river. Meade kept his rank for the rest of the war, but he soon had a new boss with a higher rank.

Question: When was the last Silent Movie released? When did sound completely take over in cinema?
Answer: The last silent movie was only released 13 years ago (this being 2024) “The Artist” was critically acclaimed and won five Oscar awards, including “Best Picture”. But it’s hardly the first such experiment. Mel Brooks went full comedy in “Silent Movie”, which unfortunately didn’t do terribly well critically or commercially. The film has only one piece of dialogue - famous mime Marcel Marceau being asked to be in the movie and replying “Non”. The last mainstream silent movie at the end of the silent era was Charles Chaplin’s “Modern Times” about a factory worker driven mad by his job who then has a series of adventures due to misunderstandings. By that time, silent movies were all but gone and this one was the first since 1931’s “City Lights”, also by Chaplin. But silent films pretty much died immediately once sound technology was introduced to film. “Wings”, which won the first Academy Award for “Best Picture” in 1929 was the last silent film to win that award until “The Artist”. In subsequent years, talking pictures dominated. In 1930, four of the five “Best Picture” nominees has synchronized sound and two, including the winner, were musicals. The fifth nominee, “The Patriot” had non-synchronized sound. As such the complete list of silent films nominated for best picture are “Wings” (1929), “The Artist” (2012) and “The Racket” (1929).

Question: What is the difference in pronunciation between "th" and "f" in English? Is the pronunciation of these letters the same in French, even though they may be written differently?
Answer: English has two sounds that are represented by the letters “TH”. Both of them are “dental fricatives” because the tongue has to extend past the teeth to make the sounds. The first is the sound in a word like “the”. It’s made by holding the tip of the tongue against the front of the top row of teeth. The second is the sound in a word like “thin”. It’s made by holding the tip of the tongue just through the teeth. The /f/ sound is made quite differently, by holding the teeth over the lower lip. The tongue remains entirely within the mouth. Most languages, including most European languages and even all the Germanic languages, don’t have dental fricatives. That means if you’re not an English speaker, you’re not used to moving your teeth, lips and tongue in that manner to make the sound. It’s quite a difficult sound to make and most English speakers don’t master it until they’re around five years old - that’s fairly late for a language sound that’s very common in English. In Germanic languages, the words that take a dental fricative usually use a /t/ sound instead (e.g. “thousand” versus “tausend”). The /t/ sound is made by holding your tongue at the back of your top teeth where they meet the roof of the mouth, entirely different. When trying to pronounce dental fricatives, most Germanic languages just substitute a /t/. Dental fricatives don’t exist in French either, and most French speakers also make substitutions. If you’re from France, you tend to substitute a /z/ sound, which is made by holding your tongue just behind your closed teeth. “The” and “thin” become “ze” and “zin”. If you’re French Canadian, you tend to substitute a /d/ sound, which is made similar to a /t/ sound by holding your tongue slightly farther back. “The” and “thin” become “de” and “din”.

Question: What is the reason for the difference in spelling of "colour" between American and Canadian English?
Answer: “Colour” is the standard British spelling, immortalized by Samuel Johnson in his late 18th century dictionary, which pretty much became the standard for British spelling thereafter. “Color” was a spelling reform introduced by American Noah Webster in his early 19th century dictionary, which became the American standard. Through this, Canada didn’t really have a standard. Most English speaking Canadians had been born in the United states, and Webster’s spelling reform hadn’t become a standard yet even in the United States. One of Webster’s goals was to standardize spelling because Americans spelled words in all different types of ways. But as standardized education became more common in the 19th century, most Canadians were taught by British teachers with British books. British spellings became the standard in Canada even though Canadian accents were closer to American ones than British ones even as more British people started arriving in Canada. The huge influx of British immigrants had a massive effect on things like spelling, but not on vocabulary or pronunciation, which remained solidly in the American camp. My dad was born in the 1920s to a mother with a Manchester accent and a father with a Northern Irish accent. His accent, and those of his four siblings, was solidly Canadian even though most of the adults he grew up around were British immigrants. My mother’s father was pretty much the first adult my dad met who had been born in Canada.

Question: What is the origin of the term "Anglais" used by the French to refer to English speakers?
Answer: Same source as the word “English” - the group of people from what’s now northwestern Germany who inhabited the territory that was then known as “Britain” in the 5th century, C.E., the “Angles”. In Britain, the vowel changed and “Angles” became “Engles” and “English”. In French, they also called the people “L’angles” and the people and language eventually became “L’anglais”. The name of the country underwent a similar development going from “Angle Land” to “England” in English and from “Angle Terre” to “Angleterre” in French.

Question: When should 'favour' be used instead of 'favor'? Which spelling is more commonly used in Canada, American English or Canadian English?
Answer: As a rule, where British English uses “-our” and American English uses “-or”, Canadian English will use the “-our”. As such, British and Canadian English users use “favour, colour, honour, labour” while our American cousins use “favor, color, honor, labor”. And while Canadian English mostly favours British spellings (e.g. “-re” instead of “er” in words like “centre/center”), it’s not entirely consistent. Canadian English prefers “tire” to “tyre”, but “cheque” to “check”. It also tend to favour “-ize” over “-ise” in words where the “S” has the /z/ sound like “realize, analyze, etc.”

Question: Why do we use Latin letters to write in English instead of using a different set of letters that are more closely related to the language's Germanic origins?
Answer: Early English, as has been noted, had it’s own alphabet, borrowed from the Norse. It was called Runic and was made to be easily carved with all straight lines. But as England became Christian, the most literate people you had were monks and priests, and they started doing all the royal paperwork. The priests and monks knew Latin, and were more familiar with that alphabet, so they adapted it to English - rather poorly as it turned out, but there you go. By the time of the Norman Conquest the Latin alphabet was widespread throughout Europe so it largely became the standard. English just followed suit and adapted it to their own needs, including about half-a-dozen English only letters that have since become obsolete.

Question: Why do so many Americans have a problem with alcohol?
Answer: This has literally been a problem since before the United States was an independent nation. 19th century European authors frequently noted that everyone in the United States appeared to be pretty much drunk all the time. And the reason was that even though the United States government raised most of its revenue from alcohol taxes for over 130 years, alcohol was and remains dirt cheap in the United States thanks to the fact that the raw material for it is plentiful. In the early days of the United States when shipping goods across the coastal mountains from the midwest was prohibitively expensive, it was a much better idea to turn corn and wheat into alcohol which sold for a substantial premium and remained cheap. As you can see, the United States is currently in about the middle of the table for beer prices. That wasn’t the case in its early history - booze was dirt cheap, plentiful and widely available. About half of U.S. corn production, and that’s a lot, is converted to alcohol either for human consumption or for fuel. Now, that’s part of it, but the other part is that for most of its history, the United States has been majority Protestant. Most American Protestants are alcohol adverse - it isn’t a normal part of socialization the same way it is with Catholics. There really has not been a tradition of social drinking in the United States the same way there has been in Germany, France or even the UK. In the United States, you drink to get drunk. Add to that the fact that non-adults legally drinking, even a little, is pretty much non-existent in the United States. Prohibition just made things worse, driving alcoholism underground and making it even a worse problem. It’s still a factor in the United States because alcohol can still be banned on a county by county level in the United States, but it’s still plentiful in “wet” counties, which means drunks often have to drive and consume alcohol away from home. Car culture in the United States is also a problem because in most of the United States, it’s pretty much impossible to walk to a bar or liquor store. You need a car for that. Alcoholism is also widely seen in the United States as a personal failing rather than a systemic problem. If you drink, you should be able to deal with it. Despite the U.S. being largely a temperance culture where you don’t drink socially, in business it’s quite the reverse and you’re expected to drink if you’re in sales or many other field. Once you’re 21, it suddenly becomes expected that in large social gatherings, like a party or wedding, you will be drinking. You’re pretty much expected to go from zero to sixty on your 21st birthday. Now, the Americans are hardly unique in this. Alcohol abuse is common in Russia, Japan and Korea too. It’s just that America has a number of combined factors that makes it a bigger problem than it otherwise would be.

Question: How much does a car cost as a percentage of a household in the US?
Answer: Well, these figures are readily available, so let’s do some math. The average cost of owning a car in the United States has been worked out to be $10,728 per year. That includes ownership costs, depreciation, insurance, and fuel, but not parking. It’s highly variable of course, but we can work with this. In 2022, the median real household income in the United States was $74,850. Again, that’s highly variable (people from Massachusetts have about twice the income of people from Alabama). Doing the division, that means your car takes up about 14% of your income. But it’s not quite that simple because a lot of households have, and need, more than one car. Only 8.3% of U.S. households don’t have a car. That’s a staggeringly low figure. Manhattan accounts for a big chunk of that, as does New York City proper and some other very walkable cities like San Francisco. And, like I said, that’s for “one car”. Averaging out the figures for every household, there’s 1.88 cars for every household in the United States. I’m going to adjust that to eliminate the households without cars, so for households with a car, the average is 2.05 vehicles per household. Think about it - many households have two people who work, or a child that works, and in many parts of the United States if you don’t have a car, you rely on people who do. So when you account for the fact the average household with a car has two of them, double the 14% and you get about 29% of income going to automobiles. Not “transportation” but “automobiles”. Public transit would be on top of that.

Question: Does the United States military waste money? If so, how much and what are some examples of this?
Answer: No, not really considering its size. The military is actually quite efficient in how it handles its budget and the things it buys with it. The problem is not at the military level. It’s due to three things: So, let’s take a look at these things one by one. Accounting You’ve all heard of things like the “$1,000 hammer” or some such thing, but figures like that are just accounting simplifications. Here’s how it works. The military spends tens of billions of dollars on tanks, a ship or aircraft. When they’re delivered, they generally come together with a lot of spare parts. Those spare parts may come itemized, but since they are often sent to several different locations as a matter of convenience the accountants simply add up the number of parts, divide them into the cost, and when they’re sent out they’re assigned an equal dollar value whether it’s something like a helicopter rotor blade or a special fitting to hold things together. In fact, the U.S. military does a much better job of inventorying things than most armed forces do. Famously leading up to the invasion of Ukraine, it appeared the officers had sold all the food and the hungry soldiers had sold all the fuel. Try that in the U.S. military and you will get caught. That’s amazing considering the sheer scope of what the U.S. military has to handle on an annual basis. Congressional allocations The military requests certain equipment and systems, trying to stay ahead of the curve of developing technology and obsolescence. Then Congress ignores them and funds programs that bring employment to their constituents. For example, no-one in the military wants tanks. Tanks have been obsolete since the 1990s. They’re too easy to destroy now and it’s a lot cheaper to build anti-tank weapons. During the Yom Kippur War, Soviet anti-tank missiles hit every Israeli tank they were aimed at. Israel only won that war because they started sending infantry ahead of their tanks to clear out the anti-tank missile crews. But Congress still allocates tons of money for tanks, which sit in a location in Arizona because they’re no use for them. Similarly, Congress is spending billions on an advanced military plane that doesn’t work and no-one wants because it provides jobs in about 40 states. Congress also keeps allocating money to store obsolete equipment (generally of a non-military nature, like medical supplies) that couldn’t even be given away because it’s so obsolete. The amount of money spent each year exceeds the value of the goods being stored, and the military still has to keep track of it. Foreign Policy One of the reasons military budgets are so high is because the United States keeps a lot of forces all over the planet, often for doubtful reasons. For example, World War II ended nearly 80 years ago, but the Americans still have over 70 bases in Japan. It’s got even more in Taiwan, a country the U.S. doesn’t even recognize. The reason they still have a base in Guantanamo Bay, where they’re clearly not wanted and serves no functional use, is pretty much a matter of habit. There are also over 6,000 bases in the United States, and no-one wants to close any because they’re mostly in rural areas where they provide an important boost to the local economy.

Question: Were any languages influential in the development of written Chinese characters?
Answer: No. Like Egyptian and even our own alphabet, Chinese characters were originally ideographs - visual representations of what they were supposed to represent. Over the roughly 3,000 years that Chinese has been a written language, the characters have become more stylized than representative, and the written language remained ideographic while Egyptian and Phoenician (and later Greek and Latin) became phonetic. As you can see, “horse” looked like a horse, “cart” looked like a cart and so on. However, about 2,300 years ago the hard to draw ideograms were morphed into slightly easier to draw abstract characters. Similarly, in the middle east, Egyptian started as a completely ideographic language, then sounds were assigned to some of the ideographs. For example, the /i/ sound was represented by an ibis, a very common bird in Egypt. Phoenician script was originally based on representing trade transactions that were often put on clay tablets, then they too started using the symbols to represent sounds. For example, “Aleph”, meaning “Ox” came to represent the /a/ sound. If you turn the Phoenician character 90 degrees counterclockwise, you can see the head and horn of an ox. The Chinese never switched to a phonetic alphabet because the ideographic characters work for all spoken forms of Chinese, which are otherwise unintelligible. Take this warning label Seven of the warnings are in the Roman alphabet, but they all have to be different because the languages are different. However, there’s only one Chinese warning that can be understood by anyone who can read Chinese writing, whether they speak Mandarin, Cantonese or Hakka. Japanese and Korean speakers were so impressed they adapted Chinese ideographs to represent sounds in their own language. The Japanese set, kanji, is still in common use but Korean has more recently abandoned that script in favour of Hangul, which is easier to learn.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it true that there is only one language in China, or is it actually a group of languages known as "Chinese"?
Answer: There are a group of languages that use a common writing system. That’s “Chinese”. Because of the common structure of each language, concepts can be communicated in the same written script. However, there are about a dozen major languages that use this script that in their spoken form are mutually unintelligible and have major structural differences in the way they are spoken. Moreover, if you transcribe what a Chinese person says into characters, it may not make sense to anyone except someone who speaks that Chinese language. When you’re writing Chinese, you have to be very careful how you express yourself to make sure that people who have a different form of spoken Chinese can understand it. The two major variants are Mandarin (which by far has the most speakers, and is growing) and Cantonese (which also has a massive number of speakers, but is declining a bit in favour of the Chinese government’s preference for Mandarin). So although the concept behind a sentence can be written down, how its pronounced it the different Chinese languages can change a lot As you can see, these sentences are structurally similar, but there are pronunciation differences. Also, tone is important in Chinese to distinguish different sounds, and Cantonese has more of them than Mandarin does.

Question: How will the completion of the Gordie Howe International Bridge contribute to infrastructure development in both Canada and the United States?
Answer: The current route over the Ambassador Bridge is a massive bottleneck for trade. About 20% of all U.S./Canada trade goes over the Ambassador Bridge, which has tiny customs plazas and is poorly connected to freeways. That small section of Highway 3 from the river to Northwood Street is a regular surface road with traffic lights and normal neighbourhood traffic. It’s also the oldest part of Windsor (Sandwich was where the first settlement was before it moved east) so they can’t just bulldoze it. Here’s the new route for the Gordie Howe Bridge It will cross largely industrial land and will directly connect I-75 to Ontario 401, bypassing Windsor’s narrow streets. At present, all truck traffic has to go over the Ambassador and as such most cars and buses use the tunnel, which is right in the heart of the downtown of both cities and can often be a nightmare if you’re going somewhere else. Making this crossing easier should have a knock-on effect for the highways on both sides. Ontario 401 is pretty much four lanes (2 in each direction) all the way from Windsor to Milton where it now spreads into 12 lanes. Eventually, it connects to Quebec’s Autoroute 20, which goes through Montreal. Toronto is a big bottleneck despite the highway being 12 lanes wide, but the 407 toll road is on the expensive side. One of the proposals (which is facing opposition) is Highway 413, which bypasses a heavily congested part of the GTA from Milton to north Vaughan. It would also connect the 410 and 427, as well as the existing 407 toll route. Originally, the 401 was built to bypass Toronto in the 1950s, but the city grew around it instead. The 407 is really expensive and it’s unlikely to be an alternative in the future. A bypass route could really help with trucks that otherwise have to pass through the city.

Question: What is the likelihood of a mini ice age occurring in our lifetime? Should we be concerned about this in relation to climate change and global warming?
Answer: Probably about 90% in favour. When Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted in 1991, the second biggest eruption in the 20th century, the ash from it was so widespread and deflected so much sunlight from the earth’s surface that global temperatures dropped about 1 degree Celsius for a year. That might not sound like a lot, but it means crop failures and crop damage become more common. The “Little Ice Age”, which affected the North Atlantic for about 400 years was tiny by comparison, a drop of about 0.3 degrees Celsius at most, and wasn’t felt worldwide. The cause of that event is uncertain, but it could be anything from the sun cooling off a bit to a fluctuation within the norms for climate. It could also have been caused by volcanic activity or deforestation. This period of time was marked by the appearance of frozen ice where none had been seen previously and years where it wasn’t warm enough to grow crops in the summer. But any event that might cause a mini-ice age is likely to be short lived compared to what excess carbon dioxide is doing to the atmosphere. As in 1991, we might get a short break from rising temperatures, but as long as we keep adding CO2 to the atmosphere, it will continue to get warmer, and if it does get cold we do tend to burn more fossil fuels in response.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the options for using public transportation or taxis to navigate Montreal's underground city?
Answer: Montreal’s underground network, the RESO, is very spread out and some of the connections aren’t close to one another so it’s not easy to do the whole thing on foot. As is obvious, several Metro Stations serve the RESO, but there’s a problem - some are served by the Green line near Sherbrooke Ave., and some are served by the Orange Line near Boul. Rene Levesque. Those two streets aren’t terribly close together, and the two subway lines only meet at Berri-UQAM, which is at the far eastern end, and Lionel Groulx, which is off to the west. Navigating the RESO by car or bus is difficult because many of Montreal’s downtown streets are one-way and are interrupted by pedestrian plazas (like the one near Place des Arts all year, or the one in the Golden Square Mile during summer). Traffic also sucks, even if there’s no construction. Lastly, several clusters are ONLY connected by the Metro, not by pedestrian tunnels. Place Alexis Nihon is a good example. On the other hand, the heart of RESO with the most interesting destinations are all clustered around St. Catherine St. in the Golden Mile. I suggest you start there. Most of the best shopping is on the north side of St. Catherine between Peel and McGill where you will find The Bay, Simons and most of the other major retailers. Most of the rest of the system is just there for convenience. There’s also good shopping at Place Ville Marie south of St. Catherines, which also conveniently connects to Gare Centrale, the main intercity/commuter rail station.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is Long Beach, NY considered part of the greater New York City region in terms of commuting distance to Manhattan and its connection to the city's culture and economy?
Answer: Yes. All of Long Island is considered “downstate” and all of Nassau and Suffolk County are considered part of the New York Metropolitan Area because of their railway and highway links to central Manhattan. As you can see, the Long Island Rail Road pretty much stretches to the farthest parts of Long Island and one of the branches of the Montauk line actually terminates in Long Beach. The community is isolated from heavy traffic, but as you can see it’s a breeze to get to JFK airport by car. Far Rockaway is in NYC proper and Long Beach is directly connected to it.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can you recommend a movie filmed in Toronto, Ontario, Canada and explain why it is your favorite?
Answer: Lots of movies are filmed in Toronto, but Toronto rarely plays itself in a movie. So I’m going to recommend a great movie that totally celebrates Toronto, at least as it was 15 years ago. Scott Pilgrim is a 23 year old slacker who’s dating a 17 year old after his breakup with his ex-girlfriend “Envy” (N.V.) who has gone on to become a massive rock star. However, he immediately falls head over heels for Ramona Flowers, a recent 24-year old immigrant from New York City who works doing Amazon deliveries. Ramona is interested, but there’s a problem - she’s hounded by her seven evil exes who, unbeknownst to anyone, have been banded together by Ramona’s most recent ex, a New York record executive, to keep Ramona from finding happiness. Among her exes are a skateboarder turned movie star And Scott’s ex-girlfriend’s vegan bassist with vegan super powers. Scott gets involved in an increasingly escalating series of battles against the exes, culminating in the final boss battle against the New York City record executive. Fans of the anime series that inspired the movie avoided it because it jammed all the books into one movie, but its DVD release found new life among movie fans who appreciated Edgar Wright’s approach to visual storytelling and his ability to cast some actors who turned out pretty well for themselves. So, a rollicking visual treat for the senses that keeps you guessing until the end.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What was the reason for building bridges across Niagara Falls when it was possible to cross by boat before they were built?
Answer: Ferry services between Niagara Falls, Ontario and Niagara Falls, New York were very common in the early 19th century. The Ontario side still has a “Ferry Street” The problem is that the safer part of the river, a little downstream of the falls, is in a deep, deep gorge about 150 feet deep. It’s getting passengers down to the boats and up again on the other side that’s the major problem. Here’s the docks for the Hornblower Cruise on the Canadian side, which is pretty much where the ferries use to operate. They recently spent a bundle adding a funicular railway to bring passengers down to replace the passenger elevators, which had limited capacity But that’s beside the point. The first bridge over the Niagara Gorge wasn’t for people on foot or horses, it was for railways. The old Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge was built for railway traffic and was designed and built by the same fellow responsible for the Brooklyn Bridge (which is still in use). The Falls were popular before this but the railway increased both tourism and industrial use by many times because it now made it easy to get to the location from both Toronto and New York City. Currently, a double steel arch bridge is located at roughly the same site, but only one arch is in use for rail and car traffic (no pedestrians). The first pedestrian bridge, the “Honeymoon”, wasn’t completed until 1898 and was just down river of the ferry docks, pretty much putting them out of business. It also carried those newfangled “automobiles” and streetcars. The Niagara River area had an extensive system of trams well into the 20th century. The Honeymoon Bridge collapsed due to an ice jam in 1938 and was replaced by the current Rainbow Bridge in 1941. The Rainbow was directly connected to a new highway system running from the Falls to Toronto that was started in 1939, so it was primarily built for cars even though pedestrians can cross it .

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the best location to view Toronto's skyline without being inside a building? How high do you need to be for a good view, regardless of weather conditions?
Answer: Casa Loma Casa Loma sits at the top of an escarpment that used to be the shoreline of an ancient glacial lake that eventually shrunk to become Lake Ontario. There aren’t any high buildings immediately to its south so it’s view is largely uninterrupted until you get to the downtown skyline. It’s not the easiest place to get to though. It’s about a 10 minute walk from the nearest transit stops, and a lot of that is uphill. These are the Baldwin Steps, which lead from Davenport Avenue to Casa Loma. There are observation platforms. There’s no bus serves on Davenport Road in this area, and the Dupont subway stop on Line 1 is the nearest subway.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are the reasons for the high levels of humidity in Ontario, Canada?
Answer: We’re surrounded by giant inland seas Ottawa is pretty much the only major city in Ontario that isn’t next to or near one of the Great Lakes, and it’s humid because it’s within shouting distance of the Atlantic Ocean. Cities as far east as Kingston generally have the Great Lakes and westerly winds as the major driver of weather, but for Ottawa and east of there, the Atlantic Ocean drives most of the weather. Ottawa is kind of unlucky because western weather systems and eastern weather systems often meet there. Montreal is also noted for its humidity, which is punishing in summer months even though temperatures are limited by its latitude.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How is Greenwich Village in New York City pronounced?
Answer: The same as its Greater London England counterpart, “GREN-itch”. New York also has a “Soho” that’s also pronounced the same way as the London neighbourhood, but has a different etymology. The one that can really throw you in New York is “Houston”. It’s got a completely different etymology from the city in Texas, although they’re both based on the last name of a person but if you don’t want people to know you’re a tourist you will pronounce the New York version “HOW-st’n” not “HEWS-t’n”. “SoHo” means “South of Houston”. There are lots of Dutch place names in New York City but even New Yorkers mispronounce those. Some of the mispronunciations are now the official names like “STAH-t’n” (from the Dutch “Staaten”).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Have any ships been lost at Niagara Falls?
Answer: Yes. The most famous one is still there. A dredging scow was being towed in a safe part of the river when it broke loose from its tug. It got trapped on large rocks about a half-mile from the Horseshoe Falls. Through superhuman efforts by people on both sides of the river, the two men aboard it were eventually rescued, but the scow was trapped on the rocks by the pressure of the water. In 2019 during a time where water levels were up and there were stormy winds left over from Hurricane Olga, the scow actually moved about 50 yards downstream from the position where it had been trapped. In 2022, several pieces of the scow fell off, but remained trapped in the rocks. The best guess is that it will probably break up and be swept over the falls in a reasonably short period of time. The other is the “Sunbeam”, a World War I submarine patrol boat that was sold to private owners. While trying to navigate the ship into the Erie Canal in 1923, the crew became lost and instead navigated into the Niagara River. They managed to moor the boat a few miles upstream of the falls, but it was late and they decided to fix everything in the morning. However, the boat slipped out of its mooring and actually became entangled in rocks near the scow. It completely broke up in the 1930s and was swept over the falls, although there are reports that at very low water levels parts of it can still be seen by helicopter.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is December a good time to visit Niagara Falls from Toronto?
Answer: Any time is a good time, but December has some advantages. First, when ice forms on the falls, that’s really spectacular and that starts in December. Second, they have the Festival of Lights, which is a display you can walk or drive through at your leisure. Third, accommodation prices generally plummet in the area, except for special events like New Years. Expect to pay half what you would in peak season. The bad news? Many of the major attractions are closed through the winter, which includes the boat cruise, the zipline, the White Water Walk and the slowly dying Marineland.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Are Lake Ontario beaches in Toronto crowded during the summer? If so, which ones are less crowded and more relaxing to visit?
Answer: Long gone are the days when Torontonians flooded to Lake Ontario beaches in the summertime to escape the heat. Sunnyside Beach, 1920s. Sunnyside Beach, 2020s Yes, Sunnyside is still there and still accessible, including one of the largest outdoor heated pools on the planet. But it’s harder to get to. In it’s heyday, the streetcars AND trains used to stop right next to what used to be an amusement park (it was demolished in the 1950s to make way for an expressway). Now, it’s a six minute walk over a pedestrian bridge which crosses a rail line, a freeway and a boulevard. The site mostly now caters to special events like corporate luncheons and weddings although, like I said, there’s still changing facilities. Also, there’s air conditioning and pools now. Toronto beaches are often contaminated by sewage after heavy rains, closing them for swimming. However, in addition to Sunnyside, there’s “The Beach” (west of Woodbine Avenue) and Centre Island, which has beaches on the Lake Ontario side which don’t get polluted, including Hanlan’s Point, which is clothing optional. “The Beach” is well over a mile long and it has lifeguard stations throughout. They might be busy for special events (fireworks, the Caribbean festival) but that’s the exception, not the rule.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why is human feces being found on Canadian beaches?
Answer: Because too many municipalities, including what used to be the old City of Toronto and the old City of North York, didn’t maintain separate storm and sanitary sewer systems. As such, in heavy rain, like the one we had a couple of weeks ago, storm water floods the sewage treatment plants. They overflow and dump raw sewage into bodies of water. Here in Toronto, pretty much every beach is unswimmable after a heavy rain, although things have been improving as more sewers are separated. The big exception are the beaches on the far side of Toronto Island, which are far away from sewage treatment plants. The worst is “The Beach”, the area of Toronto south of Queen Street and east of Woodbine Avenue. It’s very near the Ashbridge’s Bay treatment plant, which always overflows when there’s heavy rain. It’s not a problem with some cities. The old cities of Etobicoke and Scarborough, west and east of the old City of Toronto respectively, from the beginning built separate sewer systems. Their treatment plants are never overwhelmed, so the beaches there are pristine.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: In Canada, does it get hotter in Toronto, Ontario or Winnipeg, Manitoba?
Answer: Winnipeg has worse extremes, but Toronto is warmer in normal conditions. Historical summer data for Toronto Historical summer data for Winnipeg From top to bottom - record Humidex, record high, normal high, and normal average. For all three summer months, Toronto is warmer on average, but temperatures in Winnipeg are more likely to soar. So why when Winnipeg is a good 7 degrees further north than Toronto? It’s mostly Lake Ontario, which doesn’t heat up as fast as the land around it, and because of that temperature difference between land and water, there are constant breezes on and off the lake that moderate the temperature. Winnipeg is pretty much landlocked, so nothing moderates it’s temperature - it heats up evenly with the sun in summer, and stays hot.

Question: How does blood nourish and oxygenate organs in the body? Where does it come from and where does it go after leaving the capillaries in each organ?
Answer: Red blood cells originate in the bone marrow - the soft part inside the bones. They’re constantly being manufactured from raw materials that are usually created in the liver. Once created, they enter the bloodstream. Their sole job is to deliver oxygen to the body’s tissues. In lower forms of life, like bacteria, oxygen diffuses through the cell wall, or in insects it enters through cavities through the body. However, oxygen can only travel so far so this only works if your body tissues are all directly exposed to air or water. The main component of red blood cells that does the heavy lifting is a molecule called hemoglobin. Hemoglobin has a unique characteristic - where there’s lot of oxygen it likes to attach to oxygen molecules, but where there’s lots of carbon dioxide, it likes to attach to carbon dioxide molecules. It can freely exchange one for the other in those circumstances. So let’s start with a blood cell in the lower left ventricle of the heart. It’s pumped by the heart into the aorta, which is the largest artery (arteries carry blood from the heart, veins carry it to the heart). Some of that blood flow is diverted to the nearby coronary artery, which provides blood and oxygen to the heart muscle. From the aorta, red blood cells go down increasingly smaller arteries until they reach capillaries, which are just big enough for one red blood cell to squeeze through. Here, they’re pretty much in direct contact with cells which are constantly dumping carbon dioxide into the bloodstream as a waste product. At that point, since the concentration of carbon dioxide is so high, the red blood cell releases its oxygen molecule and takes up a carbon dioxide one. The oxygen molecule diffuses through the cell wall for use in metabolic processes. To this point, the blood has been under pressure from the heart (that’s “blood pressure”) but that’s lost in the capillaries so the return trip through veins takes advantage of a series of one way valves (arteries don’t need those) and muscle movement (which squeezes the veins and forces blood through them). The veins get larger and larger until you get to the inferior vena cava (from below) or the superior vena cava (from above), which leads into the upper right atrium of the heart. From there, it’s pumped into the lower right ventricle which forces it into the pulmonary artery, which leads to the lungs. Again, the arteries, now carrying de-oxygenated blood, get smaller and smaller until they reach pulmonary capillaries. These don’t run by living cells, but through the small air sacs of the lungs, which if you’re breathing properly should contain about 100 times more oxygen than carbon dioxide. With so much oxygen, the hemoglobin lets go of its carbon dioxide molecule and absorbs an oxygen molecule. The gases in the blood diffuse though the membrane of the air sac, and the amount of CO2 in the lungs increases - until you breathe out which gets rid of most of the CO2. Your feedback mechanisms will make you breathe harder if CO2 builds up in your lungs, and less hard if there’s lots of oxygen. From the lung capillaries, the pulmonary veins again start to converge into the pulmonary vein which enters your heart in the upper left atrium, which is pumped into the lower left ventricle and your blood cells are off again. Total time to make one lap - about one minute. Of course, red blood cells break down with use. The waste products eventually pass through the spleen and the liver where they’re recycled to make more raw materials for more red blood cells. The first guy to figure this out was a fellow named William Harvey, who drained a dead body of blood, then squeezed the heart to see how much blood it could pump. Knowing how fast the heart pumped (about 60–100 times a minute), he came up with the figure that all the blood could be pumped in one minute. The prevailing theory was that the heart made blood and the cells consumed it, but Harvey realized that it was impossible for the heart to create seven pints of blood in one minute. He did more dissection of dead bodies and discovered the answer - blood circulates. There are lots of diseases that effect red blood cell production. I had one - pernicious anemia. Vitamin B12 is a key component in blood production and if you don’t have any, your body can’t make enough blood. I wasn’t getting enough B12 in my diet (probably because I constantly microwave food - long story) so I started taking supplements and now I’m fine. Blood only provides nourishment by allowing nutrients, mostly sugar, to float around the body where it can be taken up by cells. Food is just along for the ride.

Question: What happens to a will in Ontario when one of the beneficiaries has died before the person who made the will dies?
Answer: Well, ideally, the will should account for that by saying who that money goes to. That’s why it’s important to get a lawyer to draw up your will. So let’s say there are three kids and only two survive the deceased. Depending on the will, the money could be (1) split two ways among the remaining children or (2) split three ways with the third share going into the estate of the deceased child. Actually, in the absence of language to the contrary, scenario (2) would be the default. One common clause is that a beneficiary has to outlive the deceased by thirty days. That’s specifically to prevent money payable under a will from being paid to the estate of a deceased person. Its quite common for the deceased and the main beneficiary to die at the same time (car crash, house fire, etc.). The last thing you want is to try to figure out if the money should flow through to a person who survives a little longer. There’s actually a provision in most civil codes (i.e. Quebec) that if you can’t determine which of two people died first, you assume that they died at the same time. That’s for this very scenario. It’s really difficult if the beneficiary is the “residual beneficiary”, i.e. one who gets everything once everyone else gets their share. In a case like this, that part of the estate, in the absence of other specific intention in the will, is treated as if the deceased died without a will and is distributed according to the default rules for an intestate - spouse first, if no spouse children, if no children surviving grandchildren, if none of those siblings, if none of those parents, if none of those, cousins (first, second, third, etc.).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Can an employer ignore a wage garnishment request?
Answer: Sure. But if they do, they become liable for any money they pay their employee during the period the garnishment is effective, up to the entire amount of the debt, plus interest and costs. Anyone served with a garnishment has to either (1) start making payments as directed or (2) file a document with the creditor explaining why they don’t have to make payments. If you do neither of these things, the creditor can apply for judgment against the employer. We’re in civil court here so the burden pretty much shifts to the employer to prove they don’t have to pay. If they try not to cooperate, the court will consider just awarding the entire amount owed by the debtor against the employer and then letting them duke it out. The debtor can attempt to obtain a variance (there’s a limit of about 30% of take home pay, 50% for child and spousal support orders) but the employer may not.

Question: What is the difference between using "tu" and "vous" when speaking to someone who is not known personally? Is there a rule for when to use each form?
Answer: Mr. Budd is correct and the general rule is that you shouldn’t use “tu” with anyone you’re unfamiliar with. It’s the “familiar” form of the English word “you” while “vous” is the “formal” and plural pronoun. This rule is more strictly enforced in Paris than anywhere else and the further you get away, the less strictly it’s enforced. In Quebec, “vous” is often seen as pretentious and elitist, particularly among young people who tend to use “tu” with pretty much everyone. But “vous” is always safer. Using “tu” is the equivalent of calling someone in English “buddy”, “lady” or “guy” when addressing someone you don’t know (e.g. “hey buddy!”) rather than using “sir” or “ma’am”. For example, if you’re ordering from a bartender in most of France, use “vous” unless you’re a regular and it’s clear the bartender will accept “tu”. In Quebec, the bartender isn’t likely to mind you using “tu” and will probably respond in kind. Always use “vous” with police officers, customs officials, court officials (particularly judges), bureaucrats, CEOs and priests (although as the chart shows, God may safely be referred to as “tu”) as well as potential in-laws.

Question: If a younger person was in the running to be leader of the Republicans, and promised to be 'tougher than Trump' on several issues e.g. illegal immigration, would they prove popular amongst the broad USA electorate for the 2024 election?
Answer: Maybe, but the problem is that they would never get the Republican nomination because they could never get broad party support. Ron DeSantis (45) put out feelers to become president, but the Republican establishment sees him as toxic and unable to win anywhere outside of Florida. Scott Walker (57) also made a run for president and got practically zero support. It doesn’t help that the Democrats now control Wisconsin despite every attempt to gerrymander the state. Again, his brand is toxic in and out of Wisconsin. Similarly, Sam Brownback (68), the former governor of Kansas, made a big push in Kansas to cut taxes in the hope of attracting business. It backfired because businesses wanted good public schools and they withered on the vine as state revenues went bad. Again Kansas, a seemingly solidly red state now has a Democrat as governor again. A good example is a young Republican with extreme views is J.D. Vance (39) who most of the Republican establishment are cringing about because he says stuff even Trump won’t. Trump has a unique ability to be made out of teflon (TM) so nothing sticks to him, and managing to convince voters he’s not part of the establishment he’s obviously 100% behind. And when you go back you get Mitt Romney (65 when he ran), John McCain (72), George W. Bush (54), Robert Dole (76), George H.W. Bush (68 when he last ran against Clinton) and the literally granddaddy of them all, Ronald Reagan (69). It was Eisenhower who realized the Republican leadership skewed older, and in an act of desperation went with the youngest credible candidate for vice-president he could find, but that turned out to be Richard Nixon, who was barely older than John Kennedy.
